study_id: 01_Adedinsewo et al. - 2023 - Non-invasive detection of cardiac allograft rejection among heart transplant recipients using an ele
study_metadata:
Non-invasive detection of cardiac allograft rejection among heart transplant recipients using an electrocardiogram based deep learning model
Adedinsewo, D. et al.
EUROPEAN HEART JOURNAL - DIGITAL HEALTH / 2023
algorithm_name: AI-ECG
section1_comments: The study included heart transplant recipients “at three Mayo Clinic US sites” and retrospectively identified patients “between January 1988 and April 2021.” The paper states support from NIH in the article end matter and includes an explicit disclosures/conflict statement section, so COI declaration was present. The data source was three Mayo Clinic sites rather than a registry.
section2_comments: The final retrospective study sample was “1427 unique heart transplant recipients and 7590 unique ECG-biopsy pairs.” Table 1 reports median age at last biopsy 58.3 years and female sex 28.9%, so mean age was not reported. Race/ethnicity and post-transplant comorbid conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, cancer, and connective tissue disease were reported in Table 1.
section3_comments: The paper says it “initially conducted a retrospective cohort study,” then a prospective proof-of-concept study after model development. The model was “a convolutional neural-network model” using the “12-lead ECG signal as input.” The retrospective data were split into training/validation/test sets. Figure 2 describes the architecture, and the paper states the best model was chosen after “a randomized hyperparameter search over optimizer, learning rates, class weights, batch size, and regularization.” The comparator was not a single clinical rule or human reader; the paper compares against standard ECG variables alone, which had inferior AUC 0.579.
section4_comments: Missing-data handling was not described for model inputs. Class imbalance was addressed at least in part because the hyperparameter search included “class weights.” Preprocessing was described: ECGs were digital 12-lead recordings at 500 Hz, and the model input was a “12 by 5000 array,” with random noise and translation layers. The paper does not report code release. The training and test sets contained “6074/758 unique ECG-biopsy pairs,” respectively.
section5_comments: Allograft rejection was defined as “moderate or severe acute cellular rejection (ACR).” On the held-out test set, the AI-ECG achieved “AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.78–0.90),” sensitivity 95%, specificity 52.6%, PPV 5.1%, and NPV 99.7% using threshold 0.4. The prospective proof-of-concept study showed AUC 0.78 and sensitivity 100%, but the prompt asks for held-out test/validation-set metrics, so the primary extracted model performance is from the retrospective test set. Figure 3 shows the ROC curve, and Figure 4 shows subgroup AUC performance; performance was better within 7 days of biopsy (0.87) than >7 days (0.77). Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a retrospective study from “three Mayo Clinic US sites,” and patients were restricted to those with digital ECGs and EMBs within 30 days, which may limit representativeness and introduce selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were standardized 12-lead ECG waveforms acquired at 500 Hz and recorded before EMB, so the predictor measurement process was objective and clinically plausible.
qa_outcome_comments: ACR was defined using ISHLT criteria, and the final classification groups were “reviewed and approved by a cardiovascular pathologist and transplant cardiologist.”
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include patient-level partitioning, held-out testing, and hyperparameter search, but uncertainty remains because missing-data handling for clinical variables was not described, clustering was simplified by assuming repeated EMB independence, and no calibration analysis was reported.
qa_applicability_comments: Table 1 for demographics/comorbidities; Table 2 for ECG characteristics; Figure 1 for study flow; Figure 2 for CNN model architecture; Figure 3 for ROC performance; and Figure 4 for subgroup performance.

study_id: 02_Agasthi et al. - 2020 - Machine learning helps predict long-term mortality and graft failure in patients undergoing heart tr
study_metadata:
Machine learning helps predict long-term mortality and graft failure in patients undergoing heart transplant
Agasthi, P. et al.
Gen Thorac Cardiovasc Surg / 2020
algorithm_name: Gradient-boosted machine (GBM)
section1_comments: The data source was the “ISHLT Registry,” described as including “223 centers in 18 countries,” making this an international registry study. The modeling cohort was restricted to OHTs “outside the window 2005–2009” being excluded, and the paper states, “Funding No funding was available” and “The authors have no conflict of interest to declare.”
section2_comments: The final study population included “15,236 OHT patients.” The article states continuous variables were summarized by mean/SD and categorical variables by count/percent, but the retrieved article text does not report an overall cohort table with mean age or female percentage in the main paper. Clinical history and transplant variables were included among the 342 initial variables and 87 modeled variables, including functional status, inotrope use, creatinine, bilirubin, graft function at discharge, and immunosuppressive therapy.
section3_comments: The paper describes a retrospective registry cohort and states that endpoints were evaluated “using the gradient-boosted machine (GBM) algorithm.” The dataset was split into “training cohort” 80% and “validation cohort” 20%, with “tenfold cross-validation repeated 5 times” used within training to tune hyperparameters. Feature selection was automated by removing variables with >50% missingness and near-zero variance, with recoding of sparse categories, resulting in 87 variables for modeling. No explicit clinical-rule comparator was tested in the main analysis.
section4_comments: Missingness was handled primarily by excluding variables with more than 50% missingness and filtering out patients missing survival/graft-failure time; blank categorical categories were recoded to “No” or equivalent, but no imputation was reported. Preprocessing steps were described, including exclusion filters, recoding, and near-zero-variance removal. The 80/20 split implies approximately 12,189 training and 3,047 validation/holdout patients from 15,236 total. The paper does not report code availability, and no class imbalance method was described.
section5_comments: The two primary endpoints were “all cause mortality and graft failure at 5 years after OHT.” Figure 1 and the Results report AUC 0.717 (95% CI 0.696–0.737) for 5-year mortality and 0.716 (95% CI 0.696–0.736) for graft failure. The user asked for tables and figures, and Figure 2 shows subgroup ROC analyses: graft-failure prediction was significantly better when recipient age was >60 years, and mortality prediction trended better when ischemic time was >4 hours. Although the methods say sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV were provided, these numerical values were not present in the retrieved main-article text, so they are NR. Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: The cohort came from the ISHLT international registry with “223 centers in 18 countries,” which reduces single-center selection bias, although eligibility restrictions were applied.
qa_predictors_comments: The model included both pre- and post-transplant variables, including “hospital length of stay,” “graft function at discharge,” and discharge immunosuppression, which limits interpretability for purely pre-transplant risk prediction and creates predictor-timing concerns.
qa_outcome_comments: The primary outcomes were explicitly defined as “all cause mortality and graft failure at 5 years after OHT,” and graft failure was further defined using the ISHLT reporting definition.
qa_analysis_comments: The analysis treated each endpoint as a binary outcome and “time-to-event was not taken into account,” and patients lost to follow-up before year 5 were treated as not having had the event, which is a substantial risk of bias.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly studies machine learning for heart transplant outcomes using donor-recipient and transplant variables, which is closely aligned with the review question.

study_id: 03_Ahady Dolatsara-2020-A two-stage machine learn
study_metadata:
A two-stage machine learning framework to predict heart transplantation survival probabilities over time with a monotonic probability constraint
Ahady Dolatsara, H. et al.
Decision Support Systems / 2020
algorithm_name: Two-stage framework with Stage I ML models and Stage II isotonic regression; selected implementation reported in main results: UP-LASSO-logistic regression
section1_comments: The paper states, “Our UNOS dataset covered 103,570 heart transplant events up to and including September 30, 2016,” and the registry/process described are explicitly U.S.-based through UNOS. Funding was supported “in part by the Ohio Supercomputer Center” and the “National Science Foundation,” and the paper declares “Declaration of Competing Interest None.”
section2_comments: The main article reports a UNOS dataset of “103,570 heart transplant events,” but because censoring was applied separately at each time point, the effective sample size varies by prediction horizon. The paper does not report an overall mean age, female proportion, or race/ethnicity summary in the retrieved main-text tables/figures. Clinical history and transplant factors were included among the 494 variables and engineered features used for modeling.
section3_comments: Stage I examined seven algorithms: “LR, LDA, ANN, CART, SVM, RF and XGB,” along with variable selection methods including “fast feature selection, LASSO, and random forests,” and the paper reports holdout performance for the “UP-LASSO-logistic regression implementation.” Stage II applied isotonic regression to calibrate survival probabilities over month 1 and years 1–10 so they are monotonically decreasing. Figure 3 summarizes this workflow. The framework used internal training/holdout evaluation plus 5-fold cross-validation for model selection.
section4_comments: Missing data were handled through a structured cleaning strategy rather than a single standard method: variables with high missingness were removed, and the authors compared models with no imputation versus median/mode imputation; categorical missingness could also be imputed as “unknown.” Class imbalance was explicitly addressed with several subsampling methods: “none, DOWN, UP, SMOTE and ROSE.” Data preprocessing was described in detail, including removal of intra/post-transplant variables, censoring rules, engineered features, regrouping categorical levels, and encoding choices. Code availability was stronger than a simple yes/no because the paper states that “our code, analysis and results are detailed in an R Markdown document” and also provides a public web app; however, algorithm weights were not reported. Exact training/test N for the selected final model at each time point were not provided in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The target outcome was multi-period post-transplant survival probability at month 1 and years 1–10 rather than a single fixed endpoint. Table 4 reports holdout performance for the selected UP-LASSO-logistic regression model: AUC rose from 0.608 at month 1 to 0.702 at year 10; year-10 accuracy was 0.627, sensitivity 0.752, and specificity 0.533. Figure 7 presents observed-versus-forecast survival probabilities after isotonic regression, so calibration was reported graphically. Table 5 shows isotonic regression slightly improved AUC at all time points. No PPV, NPV, F1-score, or DCA were reported. Since the prompt asks for the test/validation set, I used the holdout results from Table 4; the single numeric AUC field here is the year-10 holdout AUC of 0.702, while the article reports a range across time points.
qa_participants_comments: The study used a large national UNOS registry with 103,570 heart transplant events, which lowers single-center selection bias, although censoring varied by time point.
qa_predictors_comments: The authors intentionally removed intra- and post-transplant variables in the main prediction framework, keeping a pre-operative decision-support orientation, and also engineered clinically motivated donor-recipient features
qa_outcome_comments: The survival outcome at each time point was explicitly coded using G-TIME and G-STATUS, with censoring rules clearly described for whether the recipient was alive or dead at the time point of interest.
qa_analysis_comments: trengths include extensive preprocessing, class-imbalance handling, multiple algorithms, cross-validation, holdout testing, and post hoc monotonic calibration; however, the very large analytic design space and time-point-specific censoring introduce complexity and possible instability, and exact final training/test sample sizes per horizon were not clearly reported in the retrieved text.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly concerns AI/ML for heart transplant outcome prediction using donor-recipient pre-operative variables and is highly aligned with the review question.

study_id: 04_Ayers et al. - 2021 - Using machine learning to improve survival prediction after heart transplantation
study_metadata:
Using machine learning to improve survival prediction after
heart transplantation. Brian Ayers. et al. Journal of Cardiac Surgery / 2021
algorithm_name: Final ensemble ML model combining deep neural network, logistic regression, AdaBoost, and random forest
section1_comments: The study used the “United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry” and included adult patients undergoing OHT “between 2000 and 2019.” A disclosures section was present, listing industry relationships for several authors, so COI was declared. I did not identify a funding statement in the retrieved article text, so funding is marked Not Reported.
section2_comments: The study included “33,657 OHT patients,” and “the majority of study participants were male (75%) with an average age of 52.8 ± 12.4 years,” implying female sex 25%. Table 1 reports race as White 70% and includes multiple clinical-history/support variables such as prior cardiac surgery, dialysis, ventilator, ICU, inotropes, ECMO, IABP, LVAD/RVAD/TAH, bilirubin, creatinine, and waitlist time.
section3_comments: The paper describes a “retrospective study” using UNOS data with patients split into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets. The final model was an ensemble of four algorithm classes: deep neural network, logistic regression, AdaBoost, and random forest, built from 400 total models. Inputs were preoperative donor and recipient registry variables. The main explicit comparator in reported results was a “singular logistic regression,” which best fits the review option of a linear risk-score comparator rather than human expert/guideline. Feature selection combined clinician review and random-forest importance, producing 47 final variables. The paper does not describe SHAP/LIME-style explainability or an explicit hyperparameter-tuning process.
section4_comments: Missing continuous data were imputed with the median and categorical data with the mode. Class imbalance was addressed using “over-sampling (SVM Smote) and under-sampling (Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbors).” Preprocessing was clearly described, including exclusion of non-preoperative variables, clinician review, grouping sparse categories, one-hot encoding, and standardization of continuous variables. The paper states models were trained in Python using Keras/Tensorflow but does not provide code release, so code availability is No. Table 1 gives training n=26,926 and validation n=6,731.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “1-year post-transplant survival,” with 1-year mortality 11% (n=3738). In the validation cohort, AUROCs were 0.649 for logistic regression, 0.691 for random forest, 0.691 for deep neural network, 0.653 for AdaBoost, and 0.764 for the final ensemble ML model. The ensemble improved predictive performance by 72.9% ± 3.8% by NRI and had better DCA across the full risk spectrum. Calibration was evaluated visually by plotting predicted versus observed risk by decile. The paper did not report accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1-score numerically in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_comments: The study used a large national UNOS registry cohort of 33,657 patients, which reduces single-center selection bias, although exclusions for prior transplant, multiorgan transplant, age <18, and incomplete 1-year survival were applied.
qa_predictors_comments: The authors explicitly excluded variables that “would not be available in the preoperative setting,” which supports appropriate predictor timing for clinical use.
qa_outcome_comments: The primary outcome was clearly defined as “1-year post-transplant survival,” and Figure 1 classified patients as alive vs dead at one year.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include a separate validation cohort, resampling for imbalance, multiple algorithms, AUROC/NRI/DCA evaluation, and calibration assessment. However, there was no external validation cohort, and the authors acknowledge this as a limitation.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly studies machine learning for heart-transplant survival prediction using donor-recipient preoperative variables, matching the review question closely.

study_id: 05_Barbosa et al. - 2018 - Machine Learning Algorithms Utilizing Quantitative CT Features May Predict Eventual Onset of Bronchi
study_metadata:
Machine Learning Algorithms Utilizing Quantitative CT Features May Predict Eventual Onset of Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome After Lung Transplantation
Barbosa, Jr., E. J. M. et al.
Acad Radiol / 2018
algorithm_name: Support vector machine with radial basis function kernel
target_outcome: Chronic Lung Allograft Dysfunction (CLAD incl. BOS)
section1_comments: The patient cohort came from a local IRB-approved retrospective study and the lead academic clinical site was the University of Pennsylvania; the article states that data were selected retrospectively and transferred “to an outside facility for computational imaging analysis,” which supports a single-center clinical source with external image processing. I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved article text. Calendar study years were not reported; only follow-up intervals after transplant were provided.
section2_comments: Table 1 states there were 71 subjects total, with 41 BOS and 30 non-BOS, and the text reports 53 men and 18 women with mean age 57 years. Female sex is therefore 18/71 = 25.4%. Race/ethnicity was not reported. Clinical background was reported through pretransplant diagnoses including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, cystic fibrosis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and other.
section3_comments: The article explicitly says the scans were analyzed retrospectively and that “supervised ML with support vector machines (SVMs) was used.” The model used significant qCT features derived from Student t tests, and a “radial basis functional kernel with default tuning parameters was used.” Inputs were qCT/FRI imaging features from paired inspiratory-expiratory CT scans. The main comparator was not another clinical model but rather baseline clinical/PFT variables, which the paper states could not significantly distinguish BOS from non-BOS at baseline. Validation used repeated random train-test partitions (90/10 for 1D and 2D, 80/20 for 3D), so “Other” is the most exact category.
section4_comments: For the baseline prediction cohort, “patients with missing values for certain regional parameters… were not included,” which is best classified as complete case analysis. Class imbalance handling such as weighting, oversampling, or SMOTE was not reported. Data preprocessing was described extensively: CT segmentation, central/distal airway definitions, lung/lobar volume extraction, and computational fluid dynamics-based resistance calculation. The paper reports train-test ratios, but because the absolute sample counts vary across repeated random partitions and dimensions, exact training and test N are NR. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: The clinical outcome was eventual BOS after lung transplant, which is the obstructive phenotype of chronic lung allograft dysfunction, so the closest restricted category is CLAD. Table 5 reports the best 3-feature SVM classification accuracy as 85%, using RML lobe volume at TLC, RUL airway resistance at FRC, and central airway surface at FRC. One-feature accuracy reached 76%, and the best two-feature model reached 83%. The paper did not report AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA. Figure 7 summarized significant baseline qCT predictors, and Figure 8 showed that baseline FEV1 and FEV1 percent predicted were not significant predictors of future BOS.
qa_participants_comments: This was a small retrospective cohort of 71 patients selected using several imaging and data-availability criteria, and only 41 patients were eligible for the baseline prediction analysis because incomplete datasets were excluded.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were objective qCT/FRI imaging biomarkers extracted from paired inspiratory-expiratory CT scans with standardized segmentation and computational methods.
qa_outcome_comments: BOS was defined using standard clinical criteria requiring a sustained decline of at least 10% in FEV1 from best baseline postoperative measurement, and BOS status was reviewed clinically by a board-certified pulmonologist.
qa_analysis_comments: The study used a very small baseline prediction sample, selected features using univariate testing before SVM modeling, used default SVM tuning parameters, and reported repeated random split accuracies without an external validation cohort.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly addresses AI/ML prediction in thoracic transplantation, specifically lung transplant recipients and later BOS/CLAD development using imaging biomarkers.

study_id: 06_Brahmbhatt-2022-The lung allocation score and
study_metadata:
The lung allocation score and other available models lack predictive accuracy for post-lung transplant survival
Brahmbhatt, J. M. et al.
J Heart Lung Transplant / 2022
algorithm_name: LASSO regression, Random Forests, and the Chan et al. (2019) model.
section1_comments: The study used the “United Network for Organ Sharing database (2005-2017)” and included adults receiving their first lung transplant between “May 1, 2005, and May 1, 2017.” The registry is a U.S. national dataset.
section2_comments: The cohort included “19,900 adults who received their first LTx between May 1, 2005, and May 1, 2017.” Table 1 reports age means of 55.1 and 56.5 years in the two 1-year outcome groups; the weighted overall mean is about 55.3 years. Female sex is reported separately by outcome group (41% vs 37%) rather than as one overall cohort percentage in the retrieved text, so I marked the single overall female percentage as NR rather than infer it. Table 1 also reports race and multiple clinical variables, including diabetes, dialysis, steroid use, mechanical ventilation, BMI, GFR, bilirubin, creatinine, oxygen requirement, pulmonary arterial pressure, and diagnosis.
section3_comments: This was a retrospective cohort study comparing five models: LAS, Chan et al., a clinician logistic model with 27 a priori covariates, LASSO, and Random Forests. Because the paper centers on evaluating machine-learning approaches alongside existing risk scores, the primary ML component is Yes. The machine-learning architectures explicitly reported were LASSO and Random Forests. Inputs were pre-transplant recipient covariates from UNOS, with donor covariates added in secondary analyses. The main comparators were LAS and Chan’s risk score, both best categorized here as linear risk-score comparators. The validation approach used an 85% development set and 15% validation set. No SHAP/LIME-type interpretability or hyperparameter-tuning details were reported in the retrieved tex
section4_comments: The paper states that “for binary and categorical variables, patients with missing measurements were grouped into their own category” and “missing measurements for continuous variables were estimated using mean imputation,” so this is best classified as simple imputation. I found no mention of resampling, weighting, or other imbalance handling. Preprocessing/model-building details were described, including a priori variable selection for the clinician model and alternative ML approaches. Code availability was not reported. The development/validation split was 85%/15%, which corresponds to approximately 16,915 training and 2,985 validation patients from 19,900 total.
section5_comments: The modeled outcome was “death or re-transplant within the indicated timeframe,” primarily at 1 year and secondarily at 3 years, so the closest allowed label is Other. Figure 1 and the Results state that all 1-year models had low AUCs ranging from 0.55 to 0.62. The paper also states that all models had NPV 0.87-0.90 and PPV <0.25, but the retrieved text does not provide model-specific numeric PPV/NPV/sensitivity/specificity values for a single chosen model, so I leave those fields NR rather than guess. Calibration was clearly reported through calibration slopes and Figures 2, 4, and 5. DCA was not reported. The LAS post-transplant survival measure had calibration slope 0.38 (95% CI 0.03-0.73), indicating overestimation of mortality risk
qa_participants_comments: This was a large national UNOS registry cohort including 19,900 adult first lung transplant recipients, reducing single-center selection bias, although patients lost to follow-up were excluded.
qa_predictors_comments: The models were based on pre-transplant covariates from UNOS, and donor covariates were tested separately in secondary analyses, which is appropriate for allocation-related prediction.
qa_outcome_comments: The study explicitly used “death or re-transplant within the indicated timeframe” as the modeled outcome, which is clearly defined.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include a held-out validation set, calibration analysis, and multiple comparative models; concerns include mean imputation, exclusion of patients lost to follow-up, limited details on tuning, and persistently poor discrimination across all models.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly studies prediction modeling, including machine learning, for lung transplant post-transplant survival using national recipient data.

study_id: 07_Chang-2025-Patterns of Left Ventricular Region
study_metadata:
Patterns of Left Ventricular Regional Wall Motion Abnormalities After Brain Death and Their Clinical Significance
Chang, A. J. et al.
JACC Heart Fail / 2025
algorithm_name: k-means clustering
section1_comments: The study was the “Donor Heart Study,” coordinated at Stanford and “conducted at 8 organ procurement organizations across the United States,” so the data origin was U.S. multicenter rather than a registry. Funding was from the “National Institutes of Health (NIH)/National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (R01 HL125303),” and the authors stated that they had “no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.” Specific calendar start and end years for donor enrollment were not reported in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: Although the Donor Heart Study enrolled 4,333 potential heart donors, “the final analytical cohort included 913 initial TTEs.” Table 1 reports mean age 34.3 years and female sex 42.6% for the analytical cohort, and also reports race/ethnicity plus medical-history variables including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, tobacco use, Public Health Service risk status, and cause of death.
section3_comments: The paper states that the Donor Heart Study was a “5-year multicenter observational prospective cohort study.” The machine-learning method was unsupervised “k-means clustering,” using all 17 segment-level wall motion scores from transthoracic echocardiography to identify RWMA phenotypes. The number of clusters was chosen using the cubic clustering criterion, but no held-out validation, SHAP/LIME-style interpretability method, or hyperparameter-tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: The analysis excluded donors without adequate initial TTE quality and then excluded 70 outliers after cluster analysis, which is most consistent with complete case analysis plus exclusions rather than imputation. Class imbalance handling was not relevant because this was unsupervised phenotyping rather than a binary classifier. Data preprocessing was described: only donors with RWMA on initial TTE entered clustering, 17 segment-specific WMS values were used, 8 preliminary clusters were generated and then consolidated into 4 clinically plausible phenotypes, and 70 outliers were excluded. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: This was not a supervised prediction model with held-out discrimination metrics. Instead, the clinically relevant outcomes associated with the RWMA phenotypes were donor-heart acceptance, changes in LVEF/WMSI on follow-up TTE, and recipient survival after transplantation. Table 1 reports donor-heart acceptance was highest in FBS (68.2%), and recipient 2-year survival among transplanted hearts was similar across phenotypes. Figure 3 shows all phenotypes improved in LVEF on second echocardiogram. Because no AUC, accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA were reported for a predictive model, those fields are NR/No.
qa_participants_comments: The final analysis was restricted from 4,333 enrolled donors to 913 initial TTEs with RWMA and complete pre- and post-transplant data, and 70 outliers were additionally excluded after clustering, which may introduce selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: The clustering inputs were standardized echocardiographic wall motion scores for all 17 LV segments, interpreted by a blinded expert core reviewer, which supports objective predictor assessment.
qa_outcome_comments: Clinical outcomes (acceptance and survival) are objective endpoints verified through registry and clinical records.
qa_analysis_comments: The analysis used unsupervised clustering followed by investigator consolidation into 4 clinically plausible phenotypes and exclusion of outliers, without external validation or a separate test set, which raises concern about stability and reproducibility of the phenotypes.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly involves machine learning in the cardiac transplant donor setting and evaluates clinically important transplantation outcomes, so it is relevant to a thoracic organ transplantation AI review.

study_id: 08_Chao et al. - 2024 - Improving prognostic accuracy in lung transplantation using unique features of isolated human lung r
study_metadata:
Lung Transplantation Advanced Prediction Tool: Determining Recipient's Outcome for a Certain Donor
Zafar, F. et al.
Transplantation / 2022
algorithm_name: InsighTx (augmented with computer vision)
section1_comments: The cohort came from “Clinical EVLP cases performed from 2008 to 2022 at Toronto General Hospital,” which makes this a single-center study rather than a registry. The country is not one of the prompt’s fixed options, so “Other” is the closest fit. I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study included “n = 650 clinical EVLP cases” and “n = 1300 radiographs.” The analysis was centered on isolated donor lungs on EVLP rather than recipient cohorts or waitlist candidates. No overall age, sex, or race/ethnicity summary was reported in the retrieved text. Donor information was correlated with principal components, but the excerpt does not clearly establish a structured comorbidity/history table, so that item is best marked Unclear.
section3_comments: The paper used CNNs including “ResNet-50, ResNeXt-50, RexNet-100, EfficientNet-B2, EfficientNet-B3, and DenseNet-121,” with the best model being CADLab-pretrained ResNet-50. The image-analysis task used EVLP radiographs, while the multimodal stage combined image PCs with physiological and biological EVLP data in an XGBoost-based “InsighTx” model. Comparator performance was reported against manually labeled radiographic scores rather than a clinical rule or human decision-maker directly. The cohort was split “temporally” 80:20, with training from 2008-2020 and validation from 2020-2022, which is best categorized as external temporal. Explainability was present via Grad-CAM and “Shapley Additive explanation values.” The extracted text does not describe explicit hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: Missing-data handling was not described in the retrieved text. I found no statement about class weighting, oversampling, or imbalance correction. Data processing was described in detail, including temporal image pairing at 1 h and 3 h, pretraining/fine-tuning, latent-feature extraction, PC analysis, Grad-CAM, and multimodal fusion with tabular EVLP data. The EVLP case split was 80:20 into training “n = 520” and validation “n = 130.” Code availability is best marked “Other” because the paper states that source code and data are being worked toward and that the authors will make best efforts for access, but the data are not publicly available.
section5_comments: The modeled outcome was a 3-class donor-lung endpoint: “(1) recipient time to extubation of <72 h, (2) ≥72 h, and (3) lungs unsuitable for transplantation,” so the closest fixed category is Other. For the multimodal model, Table 2 reports improved performance from 73 ± 5% to 78 ± 4% accuracy and from 88 ± 2% to 94 ± 2% AUROC after adding radiographic PCs. The paper also states that both “precision (73% vs. 64%)” and “recall (79% vs. 72%)” improved significantly with image PCs added. Table 1 reports that the imaging-only CNN achieved 62.7 ± 1.8% accuracy and 76.1 ± 1.2% AUROC, while the best validation-set donor-lung outcome classification for ResNet-50 was 66.9% accuracy with AUROC 78.4%. Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: The study included all bilateral EVLP cases with both 1 h and 3 h radiographs from a single center, which is systematic but still narrow and potentially selective relative to all donor lungs.

Within the 117-case study cohort, 80%, 10%, and 10% were randomly assigned to training, validation, and test datasets. section4_comments: The first 117 cases were split into training dataset n=93, validation dataset n=12, and test dataset n=12, as shown in Figure 1. section5_comments: The target was next-step tacrolimus trough level forecasting, so the closest category is Other. section2_comments: The waitlist analysis included “13,204 candidates,” and the post-transplant analysis included “20,763 adult transplant recipients.” Table 1 reports female sex as 41% in the baseline waitlist cohort. Race/ethnicity was reported, and multiple clinical factors were included, such as diagnosis group, 6-minute walk distance, respiratory support, pulmonary arterial pressure, oxygen use, creatinine, BMI, bilirubin, insurance, and education. A single overall mean age for the full analytic cohorts was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The study compared seven models for each outcome: current LAS/CAS Cox models, updated Cox models, nonlinear spline-enhanced Cox models, random survival forests, logistic models, linear discriminant analysis, and gradient-boosted trees. The main comparators were the current LAS/CAS survival models, which are linear risk-score models. The data were “randomly partitioned into 10 training and test samples for cross-validation.” Predictors came from SRTR candidate/recipient tabular data available at allocation. The retrieved text did not report SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or explicit hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: The Methods state that the authors used “multiple imputation to account for missing predictor data,” and inverse probability-of-censoring weighting to address informative censoring due to transplant. They also describe reconciliation of relisted patients and construction of residual cohorts. The study used repeated cross-validation folds rather than one fixed train/test split, so exact training and test counts are NR. Code availability was not reported in the retrieved text. Class-imbalance handling was not described.
section5_comments: The primary outcomes were waitlist death or removal as too sick, and post-transplant death or retransplantation. For waitlist models, discrimination was strongest in the baseline cohort, with AUC about 0.92-0.93 at 1 month, declining to about 0.87-0.89 at 3 months and 0.84-0.85 at 6 months. For post-transplant models, discrimination remained poor across models, generally “0.58-0.61,” including at 1, 3, and 5 years. Figure 1 shows subgroup AUC patterns, especially worse variability among Medicaid patients. Because the paper centers on AUC/C-statistic-style discrimination across many models and time horizons rather than a single deployed model, and because the prompt asks for held-out test/validation metrics, I leave the single numeric AUC field as NR rather than choose one arbitrary value. Calibration and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_comments: The study used large national SRTR cohorts of waitlist candidates and transplant recipients in the United States, which reduces center-level selection bias, although exclusions for missing key variables were applied.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were derived from SRTR variables available at allocation or cohort time points, consistent with the clinical use case for LAS/CAS modeling.
qa_outcome_comments: The outcomes were clearly defined as time from waitlist placement to death or removal as too sick, and time from transplant to death or retransplantation.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include TRIPOD-aligned internal validation, 10-fold cross-validation, multiple imputation, inverse probability-of-censoring weighting, and comparison of several model classes; however, only internal validation was performed and post-transplant discrimination remained poor across all models.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly evaluates machine-learning and alternative modeling approaches for lung transplant allocation-related prediction, making it highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 11_Davalos-Yerovi et al. - 2024 - Factors Influencing the Attrition Rate of a 10-Week Multimodal Rehabilitation Program in Patients Af

algorithm_name: Artificial neural network (ANN) using the nnet function
section1_comments: The study was conducted in “a tertiary university hospital in Barcelona (Catalonia, Spain)” and “took place between January 2022 and September 2023,” which supports Europe and single-center classification. I did not identify an explicit funding or conflict-of-interest statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The Results state: “Of the 41 patients referred to the multimodal rehabilitation program (mean age of 55.8 [SD 9.7] years; 22 men).” This implies 19 women, or 46.3%. Table 1 reports comorbidity and clinical-history-related variables including Charlson Comorbidity Index, transplant indication, malnutrition, sarcopenia, muscle strength, exercise capacity, and quality of life. Race/ethnicity was not reported.
section3_comments: The paper explicitly states this was a “prospective observational study” and that “an ANN and regression analysis were used.” The ANN was implemented in R using the nnet package, with “30 neurons, a decay of 0.001, ‘tanh’ activator, and linear output relationships,” so architecture details were reported. Garson’s algorithm was used to quantify variable contribution and select variables with relative importance >0.5 for subsequent regression, which supports both explainability and automated feature selection. No explicit train/validation/test split or cross-validation was reported.
section4_comments: The primary analysis used “23 common baseline variables that were complete (with no missing data points) for all participants,” which is best classified as complete case analysis. Data preprocessing was described: variables were defined by type, attrition classes were encoded as 1/2/3, numeric and ordinal variables were rescaled between −1 and +1, and categorical variables were dummy coded. I found no mention of class-imbalance handling and no released code repository; only function names and package details were provided. Because a separate training/test split was not reported, training and test sample sizes are NR.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was attrition rate in the rehabilitation program, classified as low (<5% missing data), medium (5–10%), or high (>10%), so the closest allowed category is Other. Table 2 shows significant variables: low age-dependent BMI (p = 7.08 × 10−5), end-stage respiratory disease requiring LT (p = 0.000111), EQ-5D VAS (p = 0.0009078), low handgrip strength by Mediterranean reference values (p = 0.0230351), and low handgrip strength by EWGSOP2 cutoffs (p = 0.0455796). No calibration or DCA was reported.
qa_participants_comments: The study included only 41 patients from a single center, all referred to one rehabilitation program, which limits representativeness and creates substantial selection risk.
qa_predictors_comments: Baseline predictors were clinically relevant, but only the 23 variables with no missing data were analyzed in the ANN, so potentially important factors were excluded.

Table 1 reports recipient sex, race, BMI, blood type, donor demographics, and Table 2 reports medical history, hemodynamics, lab tests, life support, and operative variables. Recipient age was reported as median (IQR), not mean, so mean age is NR.
section3_comments: he study describes a retrospective ML workflow using UNOS data and states, “we implement and apply a multi-layer perceptron (MLP).” It compares MLP with logistic regression, GBDT, decision tree, LightGBM, and SVM. The paper reports “5-fold cross-validation.” For explainability it uses “Integrated Gradient CITE” to compute feature attributions and interactions. Feature selection relied on “expert’s domain knowledge” plus exclusion of features with >40% missingness, with additional engineered donor-recipient pair variables. Explicit hyperparameter tuning was not described in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: Missing data were handled with “the kNN imputer,” which is best classified as Other. Preprocessing is described: categorical variables were encoded numerically, patients with multiple transplants during the index hospitalization were excluded, features with >40% missingness were filtered, and donor-recipient pair features were generated. section5_comments: The outcome was PGD after heart transplantation. Table 3 reports the best model, MLP, with AUROC 0.868 ± 0.006 and AUPRC 0.794 ± 0.015. The paper does not report accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA.

qa_predictors_comments: Predictor domains were clearly described in Tables 1-2 and included recipient, donor, operative, pair, and life-support variables available around transplantation; no obvious post-outcome leakage is described in the retrieved text.
qa_outcome_comments: The paper states that y indicates “the diagnosis of PGD after a heart transplant,” but the retrieved excerpt does not provide a full operational definition or ascertainment algorithm within the Methods.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include multiple model comparisons, kNN imputation, 5-fold cross-validation, and explainability analyses, but uncertainty remains because hyperparameter tuning, calibration, and exact split sizes were not reported.
qa_applicability_comments: This study directly addresses AI/ML for heart transplant PGD prediction using donor-recipient variables and is closely aligned with the review question.

Inputs were donor, recipient, intraoperative, and postoperative clinical variables listed in Table 1. The paper states the model exceeded “classical statistical methods,” but it does not report a clear external or internal validation framework or explicit hyperparameter tuning procedure.

study_id: 15_Glass-2024-A machine learning algorithm improv
study_metadata:

algorithm_name: ResNet50 convolutional neural network with transfer learning
section1_comments: The biopsies were “previously as pAMR2 as part of routine standard of clinical care between 2018 and 2021 from Duke University Medical Center Department of Pathology,” so the data source was single-center in the USA. The paper includes a “Declaration of competing interest” stating “None.” I did not identify a funding statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study used “300 hematoxylin and eosin slides” from cardiac transplant endomyocardial biopsies. It did not report recipient mean age, sex distribution, race/ethnicity, or baseline comorbidity data in the retrieved text. The unit of model development was annotated biopsy regions rather than a clinical cohort table.
section3_comments: The study used annotated H&E pathology image patches and a “convolutional neural network approach utilizing transfer learning.” The ResNet50 model was initialized with pretrained weights and fine-tuned. The model was compared against blinded human pathologist review in a separate curated set of slides. Regions of interest were manually annotated by experts, which functions as manual/clinical feature selection at the region level. Training settings including Adam optimizer, learning rate 0.0001, cross-entropy loss, and stopping on validation-loss plateau were reported.
section4_comments: The dataset contained 4,212 annotations split 70%/10%/20% into training, validation, and testing. That corresponds to approximately 2,948 training annotations and 842 test annotations. The four classes were balanced at 1,053 regions each, so explicit class-imbalance correction was not reported and was likely unnecessary. Preprocessing was described through de-identification, whole-slide scanning at 40X, annotation, extraction of non-overlapping 224×224 windows, and train/validation/test splitting. Code availability was not reported. Missing-data handling was not relevant to image patches and was not described.
section5_comments: The task was histologic diagnosis of pAMR-H in cardiac transplant biopsies. The closest category in the allowed list is Acute Rejection. The algorithm achieved “98% overall validation accuracy.” Figure 3 shows multiclass AUROC 0.982 and binary AUCs of 0.995 for pAMR-H vs normal endomyocardium, 0.992 for pAMR-H vs healing injury, and 0.992 for pAMR-H vs ACR. The paper also reports pAMR-H classification accuracies of 99.5%, 99.2%, and 99.2% against those three categories, respectively. PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1-score, calibration, and DCA were not reported. I used the highest explicitly reported AUC value for the single AUC field.
qa_participants_comments: The training material came from previously diagnosed Duke cases from 2018–2021, so this was a retrospective single-center pathology dataset and not a broad clinical recipient sample.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were standardized digital H&E pathology image patches scanned at 40X, with expert consensus used to define ground truth and expert annotation of regions of interest.
qa_outcome_comments: Ground truth for pAMR-H was based on expert consensus plus cases confirmed as pAMR2 with immunologic evidence such as “>50% positive C4d immunofluorescence and/or >10% CD68 positive intravascular macrophages.”
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include balanced classes, predefined train/validation/test splitting, transfer learning, ROC/AUC reporting, and human-reader comparison. Limitations acknowledged by the authors include patch-level rather than whole-slide development and single-institution staining/scanning, with ongoing external verification still needed.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly applies AI to heart-transplant pathology and rejection diagnosis, which is clearly within thoracic organ transplantation AI.

section3_comments: The paper proposes “Taelcore,” combining autoencoders, multilayer perceptron (MLP), and topological data analysis tools. It compares Taelcore-enhanced performance against AE, PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, RF, KNN, and GNB. The nine measured clinical variables from the first 72 hours after transplant were used as input features. The evaluation is based on success percentages and dimensionality-reduction quality metrics rather than a conventional held-out train/test clinical validation framework, so “Other” is the most accurate validation label. The retrieved text does not describe SHAP/LIME or hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: Figure 1 and the text describe preprocessing including standardisation, box-plot outlier detection, denoising using the sCD31–ACR relationship, Rips filtration, persistence diagrams, and entropy vectorisation. The lung cohort is imbalanced (7 ACR vs 33 non-ACR), but the retrieved text does not describe reweighting, oversampling, or other imbalance handling. Missing-data handling is not reported. The paper states: “The code associated with this study is publicly available,” which supports Other rather than “algorithm weights available.” Exact train/test sample sizes are not given in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The target was ACR within 1 year after lung transplantation. Table 1 reports percentage success before and after topological improvement: RF 50%→80%, MLP 80%→90%, KNN 50%→50%, and GNB 90%→90%. No AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA were reported. Because the paper presents “percentage of success” rather than a richer held-out metric set, I report 90% as the model accuracy figure and leave the others NR.
qa_participants_comments: The clinical lung-transplant dataset included only 40 patients, with 7 ACR cases, which creates substantial risk of selection instability and limited generalisability.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were clearly defined early post-transplant clinical measurements collected at 24, 48, and 72 hours, including sCD31, PaO2/FiO2, and SOFA respiratory scores.
qa_outcome_comments: The paper clearly targets “acute cellular rejection,” but the retrieved excerpts do not provide the operational diagnostic definition or biopsy/grading criteria used to label ACR.
qa_analysis_comments: The study is methodologically innovative, but it relies on a very small dataset, reports “percentage of success” rather than a full clinical validation framework, and does not provide exact train/test sizes or standard clinical performance metrics such as AUC and calibration.
qa_applicability_comments: The paper directly addresses AI-based prediction of acute rejection after lung transplantation, which is strongly aligned with the review question.

algorithm_name: Machine learning decision tree model / multivariate decision tree analysis
section1_comments: The study was conducted “at our center” at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center and included ACHD patients “evaluated for heart or heart + additional organ transplant between 2004 and 2014.” Funding is explicitly listed from the National Institutes of Health and the American Heart Association, plus HeartFest. I did not find a visible COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The paper states, “We identified 58 patients meeting criteria.” Baseline characteristics show mean age 35.8 years, and 65.5% male, implying 34.5% female. Race was reported as 91.4% White, 3.4% Black, and 5.2% Asian. Table 1 also includes multiple comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, pulmonary hypertension, portal hypertension, chronic renal insufficiency, and tobacco history.
section3_comments: The Methods describe “a retrospective chart review” and state that “a machine learning decision tree model was used to evaluate multiple clinical parameters correlating with 1- and 10-year survival.” Input data were clinical, hemodynamic, laboratory, and CPET variables from chart review. The model was “verified… using K-fold cross validation.” The variables entered into multivariate analysis were those previously significant on univariate analysis, which is best categorized as manual/clinical feature selection. No hyperparameter tuning or explainability method was reported.
section4_comments: Of 71 identified patients, “58 patients had all relevant data… available for evaluation and were included in the study,” which is most consistent with complete-case analysis. The paper mentions K-fold cross-validation but does not report fold sizes, explicit train/test counts, imbalance handling, code availability, or preprocessing/normalization steps typical of ML pipelines.
section5_comments: The paper evaluates both 1-year and 10-year survival. Figure 1 and the text report clinically interpretable decision rules rather than AUC-style performance. For 1-year outcomes, transplanted patients with SVP <14 mmHg had 100% survival, and non-transplanted patients with PCWP <15 mmHg had 100% survival. For 10-year outcomes, all waitlisted/declined patients with PCWP ≥17 mmHg died, and all transplanted/deferred patients with SVP <10 mmHg were alive. Kaplan–Meier curves in Figure 2 show 1-year survival of 100% for deferred, 85.7% for transplanted, 42.1% for waitlisted, and 54.5% for declined patients. No AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA were reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a single-center retrospective cohort of only 58 included patients, and 13 of 71 identified patients were excluded because not all relevant data were available.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors included clinically relevant pre-listing hemodynamic, laboratory, and functional variables collected during transplant evaluation, especially catheter-based measurements such as PCWP, SVP, and EDP.
qa_outcome_comments: The outcomes were clearly defined as 1- and 10-year survival after transplant evaluation/decision, and the paper reports group-specific survival at multiple time points via Kaplan–Meier analysis.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include use of univariate analysis, multivariate decision-tree analysis, and K-fold cross-validation, but the small sample size, complete-case inclusion, and lack of standard predictive performance metrics limit robustness.
qa_applicability_comments: The paper directly studies machine-learning-assisted outcome prediction in heart transplant evaluation, albeit in a congenital heart disease subgroup rather than a general thoracic transplant population.

study_id: 22_Johnston et al. - 2025 - Estimating Calibrated Risks Using Focal Loss and Gradient-Boosted Trees for Clinical Risk Prediction

algorithm_name: Focal-aware XGBoost / focal-aware LightGBM with Ψγ calibration transformation

The extracted text does not provide a main baseline table with overall age or sex percentages for the lung cohort in the main results section I could verify. The features included demographics, immunosuppression, viral infections, and HLA variables, so clinical history was included.
section3_comments: The study used gradient-boosted decision trees, specifically XGBoost and LightGBM, trained with focal loss and then calibrated using the “Ψγ transformation.” It also compared against standard XGBoost, logistic regression, Platt scaling, and isotonic regression. The lung-transplant task used 54 tabular SRTR features. Evaluation used repeated 10-fold cross-validation experiments, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization was explicitly described. I did not find SHAP/LIME or a separate feature-selection step beyond using the defined feature set.
section4_comments: The lung-transplant datasets were described as “high degree of class-imbalance,” and the focal-loss strategy was explicitly motivated as a way to handle imbalanced or skewed class distributions. Preprocessing/exclusion steps were described in Figure 2 and Section 4.1.1. However, I did not find a clear statement on missing-data imputation for the SRTR lung dataset, nor explicit fixed training/test sample counts because the study relied on repeated 10-fold cross-validation rather than a single holdout split. I also did not identify a code-availability statement in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The lung-transplant outcome was PTLD, which is not one of the preset transplant-outcome categories, so the closest allowed choice is Other. The abstract states that the calibrated focal-aware XGBoost achieved “AUROC, Brier score, and calibration slope of 0.700, 0.128, and 0.968 for predicting the 10-year cancer risk.” The paper also reports that for 1-year PTLD prediction, “XGBoost-Focal calibrated using the Ψγ transformation achieved the best sensitivity (0.631).” Calibration plots, calibration slopes/intercepts, and Brier scores were central to the paper; DCA was not reported. I did not infer PPV, specificity, or NPV because they were not clearly stated in the retrieved excerpts.
qa_participants_comments: The lung-transplant analysis used a large national SRTR cohort and applied transparent exclusion criteria, reducing single-center selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were structured SRTR variables available in the registry, including demographics, immunosuppression, viral infection history, and HLA data.
qa_outcome_comments: The binary outcome was explicitly defined as PTLD, derived from the SRTR malignancy file, with time-to-PTLD calculated from transplant date to diagnosis date.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include repeated 10-fold cross-validation, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, and detailed calibration assessment. Remaining uncertainty comes from the lack of a fully independent external validation cohort and the absence, in the retrieved text, of a clear missing-data strategy for the SRTR lung dataset.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly addresses AI-based clinical risk prediction in lung transplant recipients using SRTR data and is highly relevant to the review question.

section1_comments: Patients were drawn from the “University Hospital of Lausanne, Switzerland, between 1990 and 2020,” making this a European single-center study. I did not identify a funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.

Table 2 reports age at transplantation, but only by BOS group, not an overall cohort mean. Race/ethnicity and comorbidity tables were not reported.
section3_comments: The paper states, “We trained a DNN to detect BOS in CT scans,” using a co-training method and late-fusion architecture tailored to low-data settings. Inputs were chest CT scans. The paper compared DNN performance with radiology-report detection in the narrative results, so human expert is the closest comparator. Evaluation used five-fold cross-validation. Visual interpretation techniques were used to reveal disease-relevant image regions, which counts as interpretability, although not specifically SHAP/LIME. I did not find explicit hyperparameter-tuning details in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The study excluded scans with large pixel size, too few slices, and scans of patients with extensive infiltrates, which is most consistent with complete-case/exclusion-based handling rather than imputation. Class imbalance was addressed in the design and evaluation by patient-level five-fold splitting and weighted ROC analysis to avoid bias from patients with more scans, but no oversampling was described. Data preprocessing and acquisition details were described in depth, including scan inclusion/exclusion, reconstruction type, and late-fusion slice handling. Because the study used five-fold cross-validation at the patient level, fixed training/test N were not reported. Code availability was not reported in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: BOS is the obstructive phenotype of chronic lung allograft dysfunction, so the closest restricted category is CLAD. The main result was aggregated ROC-AUC 0.90 (95% CI 0.840–0.953) for BOS versus non-BOS. Performance by stage was 0.88, 0.91, and 0.94 for BOS stages I, II, and III, and 0.87 for at-risk patients with FEV1 80–90% of best. The paper did not report accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA.
qa_participants_comments: This was a small single-center cohort of 75 patients, with only 26 BOS cases, and additional scan exclusions were applied, which raises selection concerns.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were chest CT scans processed with a defined DNN pipeline, and CT acquisition/reconstruction details were explicitly described.
qa_outcome_comments: BOS was defined according to “current diagnostic guidelines,” with onset defined when FEV1 consistently fell below 80% of best FEV1.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include patient-level five-fold cross-validation, bootstrapped confidence intervals, stage-specific evaluation, and at-risk detection analysis. Uncertainty remains because this is a low-data, single-center study without external validation.
qa_applicability_comments: The study directly addresses AI-based BOS detection after lung transplantation using CT imaging and is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 29_Linse-2023-A machine learning model for predic
study_metadata:
A machine learning model for prediction of 30-day primary graft failure after heart transplantation
Linse, B. et al.
Heliyon / 2023
algorithm_name: Fully connected multilayer perceptron artificial neural network (ANN/MLP)
section1_comments: The study used the “ISHLT registry,” described as “a global collaborative effort and the largest repository of heart transplant data in the world,” and included transplants from “January 1, 1994, and December 31, 2013.” I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The final study population comprised “64,964 patients,” with mean age “51.4 ± 11.9 years” and “22% (N = 13,607) of the transplanted patients were female.” Table 2 reports extensive donor and recipient clinical-history variables, including diagnosis, vascular disease, stroke after listing, dialysis, ventilation, ECMO, prior transplantation, prior cardiac surgery, bilirubin, creatinine, PRA, donor hypertension, smoking, cocaine history, and cause of death. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved excerpts.
section3_comments: The authors developed “a non-linear artificial neural networks (ANN) model” using fully connected MLP architectures with up to three hidden layers, and compared it with the RADIAL model. The model used donor-recipient tabular variables available at transplant. Validation used an internal “nested K-fold cross-validation approach” with an outer and inner stratified 5-fold loop. Model selection used random search over hyperparameters. Variable selection was automated via permutation testing and model-based ranking. No SHAP/LIME-style interpretability was reported.
section4_comments: Missingness was substantial, and the authors explicitly evaluated “multiple probability imputation (MPI)” as well as mean imputation; MPI during training with mean imputation during validation is best aligned with multiple imputation among the restricted choices. Class imbalance was addressed with a weighted error function, where positive samples were weighted threefold. Preprocessing included normalization of continuous variables to zero mean/unit variance, binary coding, and one-hot encoding for categorical variables. Fixed train/test counts were not reported because validation used nested 5-fold cross-validation across the whole cohort. The software stack was reported (Theano, Lasagne, scikit-learn), but I did not see a public code-release statement, so code availability is marked Other rather than No.
section5_comments: The primary endpoint was PGF within 30 days, defined as death due to graft failure or cardiovascular causes, or retransplant within 30 days for causes other than rejection. In the extraction framework, PGF maps most closely to PGD. The best ANN achieved a test AUROC/C-index of “0.70 (95% CI: 0.68–0.71).” The paper also reports that the score-based RADIAL model had AUROC 0.53 and recalibrated RADIAL 0.61, both significantly worse. No classification accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA were reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_comments: The cohort came from the ISHLT registry, “the largest repository of heart transplant data in the world,” with 64,964 adult recipients after prespecified exclusions, which reduces single-center selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were donor and recipient variables available “at the time of transplantation,” supporting appropriate timing of inputs for risk prediction.
qa_outcome_comments: The primary endpoint was explicitly defined as PGF within 30 days based on death from graft failure/cardiovascular causes or retransplantation for non-rejection causes.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include nested stratified 5-fold validation, hyperparameter search, imbalance weighting, and comparison with RADIAL. Uncertainty remains due to substantial missingness, mixed imputation strategies, and lack of external validation or calibration reporting.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly addresses machine-learning prediction of early graft failure after heart transplantation using a large transplant registry, which is strongly aligned with the review question.

Predictors were chosen “based on expert opinion and literature review.” The data were split 90% training and 10% holdout, with nested repeated cross-validation within the derivation set and random-search hyperparameter tuning. There was no SHAP/LIME-style explainability.
section4_comments: The authors used “multiple imputation with chained equations,” z-score standardization, and one-hot encoding, while excluding predictors with >20% missingness. A 90/10 split implies about 6,444 training and 716 holdout patients. I found no resampling or class-weighting for imbalance. The paper explicitly states that “The code used in the analysis can be found” on GitHub.
section5_comments: The outcome was “one-year all-cause mortality,” so the closest extraction label is 1-year survival. In the post-policy holdout set, Random Survival Forests had the highest C-index at 0.628, followed by Cox Boost at 0.627. Table 2 shows the other post-policy holdout C-indices: CoxPH 0.585, Ridge 0.586, Lasso 0.613, Elastic Net 0.613, XGBoost Linear 0.600, and XGBoost Tree 0.612. Calibration plots were not described for this paper in the retrieved text, and DCA was not reported.

qa_outcome_comments: The outcome was clearly defined as “one-year all-cause mortality assessed from the time of heart transplantation to death or end of the one-year follow-up.”
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include nested repeated cross-validation, a holdout test set, multiple imputation, and comparison across several model classes. Uncertainty remains because discrimination was only modest and the retrieved text did not document calibration results for the final models.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly studies machine-learning-based mortality prediction after heart transplantation in a contemporary registry cohort and is closely aligned with the review question.

study_id: 31_Lipkova et al. - 2022 - Deep learning-enabled assessment of cardiac allograft rejection from endomyocardial biopsies
study_metadata:
Deep learning-enabled assessment of cardiac allograft rejection from endomyocardial biopsies
Lipkova, J. et al.
Nat Med / 2022
algorithm_name: CRANE (Cardiac Rejection Assessment Neural Estimator)
section1_comments: The study combined a U.S. cohort with external cohorts from Turkey and Switzerland, so it is multinational and multicenter. Figure 1 states the U.S. train cohort spanned 2004–2021, the Turkish cohort 2002–2020, and the Swiss cohort 2014–2020, making the overall time span 2002–2021. I did not identify funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study population comprised heart-transplant recipients undergoing EMB assessment. The retrieved text reports 1,690 patient biopsies in the U.S. cohort, 585 patients in Turkey, and 123 patients in Switzerland, totaling 2,398 patients/biopsies across cohorts used for development and external testing. I did not find a cohort-wide mean age, sex percentage, race/ethnicity, or comorbidity summary in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: CRANE is a deep-learning system operating on H&E-stained whole-slide biopsy images using a pretrained CNN encoder plus attention-based multiple instance learning. It was compared with expert pathologist assessment in a reader study, and it was externally evaluated on Turkish and Swiss cohorts, which makes external geographic validation the strongest validation label. The system also generated attention heatmaps for interpretation. Hyperparameters and architecture details are described in Methods.
section4_comments: The internal U.S. cohort was split into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% hold-out testing. Since the U.S. dataset contained 5,054 WSIs, this corresponds to about 3,548 training WSIs and about 1,011 hold-out WSIs; adding the external Turkish and Swiss test cohorts gives 1,717 + 123 + 1,011 = about 2,851 total test WSIs, but for the strict held-out internal test field I report the internal U.S. holdout only as 1,011 if only internal is desired. However, because the prompt asks for test/validation size and the paper emphasizes rigorous external testing, I instead used the clearly reported external test cohorts separately in the narrative and note this ambiguity. Tissue segmentation, patching, transfer learning, and multi-magnification fusion were clearly described. Class imbalance was handled partly by balanced cohort partitioning rather than conventional reweighting; hence “Other.” Missing-data handling and code availability were not reported in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: On the U.S. hold-out set, the model detected overall rejection with AUC 0.962 and accuracy 0.899. It detected cellular rejection with AUC 0.958 and accuracy 0.893, antibody-mediated rejection with AUC 0.874 and accuracy 0.899, Quilty B lesions with AUC 0.939 and accuracy 0.920, and low-grade versus high-grade rejection with AUC 0.833 and accuracy 0.818. No PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, calibration, or DCA were reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_comments: The study used a large internal U.S. dataset plus two independent external international cohorts from Turkey and Switzerland, reducing single-center selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were standardized H&E whole-slide biopsy images, and the workflow for segmentation, patching, and model inference was clearly defined.
qa_outcome_comments: EMB labels included rejection presence, subtype, grade, and Quilty B lesions, and all AMR cases were confirmed with C4d immunohistochemistry.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include a large internal development set, hold-out testing, two external geographic validation cohorts, multiple tasks, interpretability heatmaps, and a reader study. Remaining uncertainty is minor compared with most studies in this review.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly addresses AI-based assessment of rejection after heart transplantation using biopsy pathology, which is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 32_Lisboa et al. - 2022 - Enhanced survival prediction using explainable artificial intelligence in heart transplantation
study_metadata:
Enhanced survival prediction using explainable artificial intelligence in heart transplantation
Lisboa, P. J. G. et al.
Sci Rep / 2022
algorithm_name: Partial Response Network (PRN-Lasso); benchmarked against IHTSA deep learning model, IMPACT, and Explainable Boosting Machine
section1_comments: The study used UNOS cohorts from 1997–2018 and an external Scandinavian cohort from 1997–2018, so the data origin is multinational and best classified as international registry data rather than a single-country registry alone. I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The UNOS cohorts included derivation n = 31,315, test n = 6,120, and blinded external validation n = 4,750, totaling 42,185 UNOS recipients; the Scandinavian cohort added 2,293 recipients, for 44,478 total across all cohorts described. Female sex was 26% in the external validation cohort and 24% in the derivation cohort; I report 26% because the primary external-validation cohort is the main focus of performance reporting. Race and multiple comorbidities/clinical variables were reported, including diabetes, dialysis, infection, ECMO, IABP, VAD, ventilator use, bilirubin, creatinine, and diagnosis. A single overall mean age across all cohorts was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The paper developed a self-explaining neural network, the Partial Response Network, and benchmarked it against the previously published deep learning IHTSA model, IMPACT, and EBM. Inputs were tabular recipient and donor variables. The main study design was a temporal derivation/tuning/validation framework: 1997–2013 for training, 2014–2016 for testing/hyperparameter optimization, and 2017–2018 as blinded external validation. Explainability was intrinsic to the PRN design through explicit partial-response functions rather than SHAP/LIME, but it still meets the user’s category of explainability used.
section4_comments: The Scandinavian external dataset had missing values imputed using the median for each column, which fits best under simple imputation. The model-development workflow clearly described derivation, test, and external validation cohorts and standardization around medians for partial responses. I did not find any resampling or class-weighting approach for class imbalance, nor a code-release statement. The derivation cohort size was 31,315 and the primary blinded external validation cohort size was 4,750.
section5_comments: The modeled outcome was 1-year mortality after heart transplantation, which maps to 1-year survival in this extraction framework. In the blinded external UNOS 2017–2018 cohort, PRN-Lasso achieved AUROC 0.628 [0.602, 0.654], compared with 0.635 [0.609, 0.662] for IHTSA; calibration for PRN was good with Hosmer–Lemeshow chi-square 15.01, p = 0.135. In the Scandinavian cohort, AUROC was 0.626 with imputed data and 0.634 with observed-only data. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_comments: The study used large registry-based cohorts from UNOS plus an external Scandinavian dataset, with clear temporal separation for derivation, testing, and blinded validation, which reduces major selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were clinically relevant recipient and donor variables commonly used for 1-year mortality prediction, including age, creatinine, ischemic time, ventilator status, diagnosis, infection, and transplant year.
qa_outcome_comments: The paper explicitly modeled 1-year mortality after heart transplantation and reported event rates and AUROCs consistently across cohorts.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include temporal external validation, comparison with multiple benchmarks, calibration assessment, and additional external validation in Scandinavia. Remaining uncertainty is limited compared with many studies in this review.
qa_applicability_comments: This study directly addresses explainable AI for prediction of 1-year mortality after heart transplantation and is highly relevant to the review question.
