algorithm_name: 3D ResNet (SE ResNet50 3D) with multimodal fusion; EfficientNetB7 and ResNet50 comparator imaging pipelines
section1_comments: The study included patients undergoing bilateral lung transplantation “at Washington University in St. Louis between January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2019,” making this a U.S. single-center cohort. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: “In total, 160 patients were eligible for inclusion,” and Table 1 reports female sex in 67 of 160 recipients (41.88%). Age was reported as median 61 years rather than mean, so mean age is NR. Race, diagnosis, hospitalization status, ICU status, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, LAS, BMI, pulmonary artery pressure, and donor characteristics were reported.
section3_comments: The study tested four computer-vision architectures, including ResNet50 montage approaches, EfficientNetB7 slice-based extraction, and a pretrained “3D ResNet model (SE ResNet50 3D).” Clinical and imaging data were then fused by early, joint, and late fusion. Feature reduction used repeated LASSO with selection frequency thresholding. Model training used stratified 7-fold cross-validation plus held-out validation/test sets. Hyperparameters included focal-loss gamma testing and were selected during cross-validation.
section4_comments: The paper states, “Missing clinical data was median imputed,” which is simple imputation. The cohort was split “75%:12.5%:12.5% train:test:validation,” so for 160 patients this corresponds to about 120 training and 20 held-out test patients. Preprocessing included DICOM handling, grayscale normalization, automatic exclusion of the top 15% and bottom 5% of scan series, resizing/cropping, and feature ablation. Class imbalance was addressed using focal loss optimized for AUPRC. Code availability was not reported in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “severe PGD (grade 3) at any time within the first 72 hours after transplantation.” Among imaging-only approaches, the best model had median AUROC 0.63 and AUPRC 0.48. The best overall model was late fusion of imaging and clinical data, with median AUROC 0.74 and AUPRC 0.61, significantly better than clinical EHR data alone (AUROC 0.64, AUPRC 0.43). The paper also reports F1, recall, PPV, NPV, and accuracy in tables, but the provided excerpt does not show all final fused-model numeric values clearly enough for me to extract them without risk of error, so I leave them NR. Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a single-center cohort of only 160 recipients, restricted to transplanted donors with available CT scans, which limits representativeness and introduces selection risk.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were clinically relevant recipient/donor EHR data and routinely reviewed donor-lung CT scans, and the image preprocessing pipeline was explicitly described.
qa_outcome_comments: Severe PGD was defined according to “International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation criteria” and graded by two board-certified pulmonologists.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include TRIPOD+AI reporting, held-out validation/test sets, bootstrap analysis, repeated LASSO, and multimodal comparison; uncertainty remains because the sample size is small for deep learning and external validation was not reported.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly applies AI/ML to lung transplantation, specifically donor-CT-enhanced prediction of severe PGD after transplant, which is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 34_Mardini et al. - 2024 - An explainable machine learning approach using contemporary UNOS data to identify patients who fail

An explainable machine learning approach using contemporary UNOS data to identify patients who fail to bridge to heart transplantation
Mardini, M. T. et al.
Front Cardiovasc Med / 2024
algorithm_name: eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
section1_comments: The study “utilized the UNOS registry” and identified candidates “listed between 2018 and 2022 as UNOS Status 2,” making this a U.S. national registry study. I did not identify an explicit funding or competing-interest declaration in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The cohort included “4,178 patients listed as Status 2.” From Table 1, mean age was 52.3 in failures and 54.3 in non-failures; weighted overall mean is about 54.1 years. section3_comments: The authors “used the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm” and developed one comprehensive model plus region-specific models. Inputs were structured UNOS tabular clinical features. Model interpretation used SHAP. Predictors were chosen from clinically different features between groups and then reduced to 19 inputs after removing highly correlated variables and creating missingness indicators. Validation used 5 × 5 nested cross-validation with grid search.
section4_comments: The study explicitly compared several imputation methods, including “XGBoost’s built-in imputation mechanism,” and Supplementary Table S1 determined the best strategy per model; among the restricted categories, “algorithm handles natively” fits best. Class imbalance was addressed by testing under-sampling, SMOTE, and increased class weights. Fixed train/test counts were not reported because evaluation used nested cross-validation folds. Code availability was not stated.

qa_participants_comments: This was a contemporary UNOS national registry cohort of 4,178 Status 2 candidates with explicit inclusion criteria, which reduces single-center selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were clinically relevant pre-listing/support variables measured near MCS initiation, including hemodynamics, labs, support devices, medications, and demographics.
qa_outcome_comments: The primary outcome was clearly defined as Status 2 failure, including death, too sick for transplant, Status 7 inactivation due to high transplant risk, or upgrade to Status 1.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include nested cross-validation, grid search, SHAP-based interpretation, and explicit handling of missingness and imbalance. Uncertainty remains because performance was only moderate and varied substantially across regions.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly studies machine-learning prediction in heart transplant candidates awaiting transplantation and is clearly relevant to the review question.

The text mentions CART was used by IHTSA developers to assess relative feature importance, but not as a main explainability framework in this paper. Hyperparameter tuning was not described in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The derivation cohort contained 22,263 transplants and the test cohort 5,597. The tables repeatedly report “N, number of transplants with non-missing values,” which indicates analysis on available cases rather than explicit imputation, so complete-case style handling is the best fit. No class-imbalance strategy or preprocessing/normalization details were reported. A web calculator for IHTSA is mentioned, but no code repository or released weights were identified, so code availability is marked Other.
section5_comments: In the 2009–2011 test cohort, recalibrated IHTSA achieved AUROC 0.65 (95% CI 0.63–0.68) for 1-year mortality, compared with 0.61 (0.58–0.63) for IMPACT. For long-term survival, recalibrated IHTSA had C-index 0.63 (0.61–0.65) versus 0.58 (0.56–0.61) for IMPACT. Calibration was reported through predicted versus actual mortality and Hosmer–Lemeshow statistics, with IHTSA closer to observed 1-year mortality than IMPACT. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a large UNOS national registry cohort of adult heart transplant recipients with explicit temporal separation into derivation and test eras.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were clinically relevant recipient and donor variables available in UNOS, and the models compared recipient-only versus recipient-plus-donor approaches.
qa_outcome_comments: The study explicitly modeled one-year mortality and long-term survival after heart transplantation, with follow-up summarized over 165,206 patient-years.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include large scale, temporal test validation, comparison with an established score, ROC/C-index evaluation, and calibration analysis. Uncertainty remains because missing-data handling and full modeling details were not extensively described in the retrieved text.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly addresses AI/deep-learning prediction of post-heart-transplant survival and is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 35_McInnis-2022-Chronic lung allograft dysfunctio
study_metadata:
Chronic lung allograft dysfunction phenotype and prognosis by machine learning CT analysis
McInnis, M. C. et al.
Eur Respir J / 2022
algorithm_name: CALIPER-based Lung Texture Analysis tool (Imbio)
section1_comments: This was a “single-centre retrospective study” from the Toronto Lung Transplant Program, University Health Network, Toronto, Canada, including transplants from “ January 2010–December 2015” with CLAD censored “31 December 2019.” Funding and COI were not visible in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The final CLAD cohort “consisted of 88 patients: 57 BOS, 12 RAS, eight mixed, eight undefined and three unclassified.” From Table 1, approximate weighted mean age at transplant is about 47.3 years, and females were 31 + 8 + 6 = 45 of 88 patients, or 51.1%. Race/ethnicity was not reported. Clinical history included native lung disease, CMV serostatus, time to CLAD onset, graft-failure type, immunologic variables, infection score, rejection score, and DSA status.
section3_comments: The study used the “Lung Texture Analysis tool (Imbio, Minneapolis, MN, USA) based on CALIPER,” previously trained outside the transplant cohort, to quantify CT textures and PVV. This was compared with independent scoring by two fellowship-trained thoracic radiologists. The work is best characterized as imaging biomarker evaluation rather than conventional train/test ML development on this cohort, so validation is “Other.” No SHAP/LIME or hyperparameter-tuning process was reported.
section4_comments: Patients were required to have a qualifying thin-section inspiratory CT near CLAD diagnosis, and cases with failed segmentation were excluded, which is most consistent with complete-case/exclusion-based handling. Preprocessing was described in detail: lung segmentation, removal of large airways/central vasculature, voxel texture assignment, radiologist review of overlays, and normalization of ML variables by CT total lung capacity. No class-imbalance method, code release, or train/test split was reported because this was not a new model-training study in this cohort.
section5_comments: The main diagnostic outcome was CLAD phenotyping. ROC analysis showed that GGOML, RETML, and especially PVVML identified the RAS/mixed phenotype, with PVV having the strongest AUC of 0.85. Using a 3% cut-point, PVV had sensitivity 90.0% and specificity 70.1% for RAS/mixed phenotyping. Machine-learning hyperlucent lung identified BOS on inspiratory CT alone with AUC 0.76. Prognostically, PVV was the strongest independent CT predictor of graft failure in multivariable Cox analysis (HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.05–1.44; p = 0.01). Accuracy, PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a single-center retrospective CLAD cohort, and from 211 CLAD patients only 88 were included after CT availability/quality and segmentation exclusions, which creates substantial selection risk.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were clearly defined CT-derived machine-learning texture variables and blinded radiologist scores obtained near CLAD diagnosis.
qa_outcome_comments: CLAD phenotype assignment was based on previously described methodology and considered the “gold standard,” and graft failure was explicitly defined as death or retransplantation.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include blinded radiologist comparison, ROC analysis, interrater reliability assessment, and multivariable Cox models adjusted for key confounders. Uncertainty remains because this was a relatively small retrospective cohort without external validation.
qa_applicability_comments: This article directly addresses AI-assisted CT phenotyping and prognosis in CLAD after lung transplantation and is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 37_Michelson-2024-Developing machine learning mod
study_metadata:
Developing machine learning models to predict primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation
Michelson, A. P. et al.
Am J Transplant / 2024
algorithm_name: K-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression (LR), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and support vector classifier (SVC); final selected model = KNN
section1_comments: The cohort included bilateral lung transplant recipients “at our center between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2019,” which makes this a U.S. single-center study. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The final cohort “consisted of 576 patients.” Table 1 reports recipient sex as 237 female of 576 total recipients, or 41.15%. Recipient age was reported as median 59 years rather than mean, so mean age is NR. Race, BMI, diagnosis, LAS, ICU status, ventilation, ECMO, donor variables, and pulmonary artery pressure were reported.
section3_comments: The study used donor and recipient pretransplant structured data from UNOS, UNet, and the local EHR. Four prediction algorithms were trained: LR, KNN, XGB, and SVC. Feature reduction was done with lasso regression, and hyperparameters were optimized using 5-fold cross-validation with random grid search. Feature importance was assessed using SHAP. The cohort was split 75%/25% into train/test sets.
section4_comments: The paper states that “missing data were median imputed for continuous data and mode imputed for binary data,” which is simple imputation. Preprocessing included binary encoding of categorical variables and MinMax scaling fit on the training data and applied to the test data. The population was divided into a 75%/25% train-test split, which corresponds to about 432 training and 144 test patients from 576 total. I did not see explicit class-imbalance mitigation. The model was deployed on a secure website, but no source-code release was stated, so code availability is best classified as Other.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “PGD grade 3 at any time within 72 hours of transplantation,” which maps to PGD. The abstract states that the final selected KNN model had “an area under the receiver operating characteristics curve of 0.65.” Table 3 shows KNN among the better-performing models, and Table 4/Figure 4 show explicit calibration assessment using Cox intercepts, slopes, and calibration curves before and after sigmoid calibration. The retrieved text does not provide clear final held-out PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1 values for the selected final KNN model, so I leave those as NR. DCA was not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a retrospective single-center study of 576 recipients from one institution, which limits representativeness despite a decent sample size.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were donor and recipient variables “known at the time of donor offer acceptance,” making them appropriately timed and clinically relevant for prediction.
qa_outcome_comments: PGD grade 3 was defined according to International Society for Heart and Lung Transplant criteria and graded by two board-certified pulmonologists.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include lasso feature reduction, train/test splitting, 5-fold CV with random grid search, 50 bootstrap iterations, and formal calibration assessment. Uncertainty remains because discrimination was only modest and no external validation was reported.
qa_applicability_comments: The study directly addresses AI/ML prediction of PGD after lung transplantation using donor-recipient clinical data and is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 38_Miller et al. - 2019 - Predictive Abilities of Machine Learning Techniques May Be Limited by Dataset Characteristics Insig
study_metadata:
Predictive Abilities of Machine Learning Techniques May Be Limited by Dataset Characteristics: Insights From the UNOS Database
Miller, P. E. et al.
J Card Fail / 2019
algorithm_name: Neural networks, naïve-Bayes, tree-augmented naïve-Bayes, support vector machines, random forest, stochastic gradient boosting; compared with logistic regression, ridge regression, and LASSO
section1_comments: The study queried the “UNOS database… since its inception in 1987 through 2014” for adult cardiac transplant recipients, making this a U.S. national registry study. Disclosures were explicitly reported, and one author was “supported by grant K12 HS023000-04 from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality,” which fits government/public funding.
section2_comments: The final analytic cohort included “50,453/62,621 patients” after excluding those with >20% missing data. The retrieved text did not provide an overall age or sex summary for the full cohort, so these remain NR. The paper did report major clinical predictors such as age, renal function, BMI, liver function tests, bilirubin, creatinine clearance, hemodynamics, donor blood pH, and candidate diagnosis. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The study explicitly compared traditional statistical methods with machine-learning methodologies and identified neural networks as the best-performing advanced model. Inputs were structured UNOS clinical variables, including donor and recipient factors. The data were “trained on 80% of the data and then tested on the remaining 20%,” so the validation method is internal split. No SHAP/LIME-style explainability or hyperparameter-tuning strategy was described in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The authors “excluded patients with >20% missing data,” which is best classified as complete-case/exclusion-based handling. The train/test split was 80%/20%, corresponding to about 40,362 training and 10,091 test patients from 50,453 total. I did not find any explicit class-imbalance mitigation, code-release statement, or detailed preprocessing/normalization description in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “1-year survival.” The neural network had the highest C-statistic at 0.66, while logistic regression, ridge regression, and LASSO each had C-statistic 0.65. Calibration was evaluated using calibration curves, Hosmer–Lemeshow testing, and Brier scores; traditional models plus random forest and stochastic gradient boosting showed good calibration, whereas some other advanced models were inferior. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported in the retrieved text. DCA was not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a large national UNOS cohort of adult first single-organ heart transplant recipients across multiple eras, which reduces single-center bias, though exclusions for missingness were applied.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were clinically relevant donor and recipient variables from UNOS, including renal function, BMI, liver function, hemodynamics, donor blood pH, and diagnosis.
qa_outcome_comments: The outcome was clearly defined as 1-year survival after heart transplantation.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include comparison across multiple traditional and advanced models, train/test splitting, bootstrapping, ROC/C-statistics, and calibration assessment. Uncertainty remains because the paper provides limited detail on preprocessing and tuning, and all models showed only modest discrimination.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly evaluates machine learning for outcome prediction after heart transplantation using a national transplant registry and is clearly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 39_Ozcan et al. - 2022 - Artificial intelligence-derived cardiac ageing is associated with cardiac events post-heart transpla
study_metadata:
Artificial intelligence-derived cardiac ageing is associated with cardiac events post-heart transplantation
Ozcan, I. et al.
Eur Heart J Digit Health / 2022
algorithm_name: AI-ECG age algorithm / ECG-age convolutional neural network
section1_comments: The study was performed “at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, MN” and included “564 consecutive cardiac transplant patients who underwent HTx in our institution between 1990 and 2018,” so this is a U.S. single-center cohort. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: “A total of 540 patients with available pre- and post-transplantation ECG data were included.” Table 1 reports recipient age 49 ± 14 years and recipient sex male in 366/540, implying 32% female. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text. Clinical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, ischemic cardiomyopathy, lipid measures, ischemic time, immunosuppression, rejection, CAV grade, and pacemaker implantation.
section3_comments: The paper used “an AI-ECG algorithm that was previously developed and validated in the non-transplant population” and states that “the convolutional neural network model was developed using Keras with a TensorFlow and Python backend.” Raw 12-lead ECGs were input to estimate ECG age. The model was applied without additional training to this transplant cohort. No SHAP/LIME-type explainability or hyperparameter-tuning process for this study cohort was reported. Validation here is best marked as not reported because this paper is primarily an application/prognostic study of a previously developed model rather than a new derivation-validation paper.
section4_comments: The analysis included only patients “with available pre- and post-transplantation ECG data,” which is most consistent with complete-case inclusion. The ECG-age algorithm had been previously trained on 774,783 subjects outside this study, but this paper did not retrain or provide study-specific train/test counts for the transplant cohort. Data handling was described, including averaging ECG ages from ECGs obtained within 1 year before and after HTx and excluding ECGs used in the original training/validation sets. Class imbalance is not applicable to this prognostic exposure analysis. The network architecture was “available on request,” so code availability is best classified as Other rather than Yes.
section5_comments: The study outcome was MACE, defined as “any incident of coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, re-transplantation, and all-cause mortality,” so the closest allowed category is Adverse Events. During median follow-up of 8.8 years, 307 patients experienced MACE. The main reported performance/result metric was association strength rather than discrimination: ΔECG age ≥ 0 was associated with MACE in multivariable Cox analysis, HR 1.58 (95% CI 1.18–2.10, P = 0.002). No AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, or DCA were reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a retrospective single-center Mayo Clinic cohort, and only patients with both pre- and post-transplant ECG data were included in the final analysis.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were standardized 12-lead ECGs processed by a previously developed CNN, and the study clearly defined pre- and post-transplant ECG age windows.
qa_outcome_comments: MACE was explicitly defined as coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, re-transplantation, and all-cause mortality, with events collected by detailed chart review.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include multivariable Cox models, competing-risk analysis, and long follow-up. Uncertainty remains because this was a prognostic application of an existing AI tool rather than a full derivation/validation study within the transplant cohort, and no discrimination/calibration metrics were reported.
qa_applicability_comments: The study directly applies AI to post-heart-transplant risk stratification and cardiac events, which is clearly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 40_Pelzer-2023-The Accuracy of Initial U.S. Heart
study_metadata:
The Accuracy of Initial U.S. Heart Transplant Candidate Rankings
Pelzer, K. M. et al.
JACC Heart Fail / 2023
algorithm_name: Random survival forest (RSF); comparator Cox proportional hazards (CPH)
section1_comments: The data source was the “Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients,” with a prepolicy training set from “2010-2017” and a postpolicy test set from “November 1, 2018, and March 1, 2020.” I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The final cohort contained “32,294 adult heart transplant candidates (mean age: 53.0 years; 73.7% male),” implying 26.3% female. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text. Clinical history included malignant disease, cerebrovascular disease, tobacco use, diabetes, diagnosis categories, and supportive treatments.
section3_comments: The study compared therapy-based “6-status” ranking with two multivariable methods: “Cox proportional hazards models and random survival forest models.” Predictors were clinically chosen listing-time variables including age, diagnosis, laboratory measurements, hemodynamics, and supportive treatment. Models were trained on prepolicy data and evaluated on a later postpolicy cohort, which is best classified as external temporal validation. No SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or hyperparameter-tuning details were reported in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: “Other missing data were imputed with the multiple imputation by chained equations algorithm,” so missing-data handling is multiple imputation. The prepolicy training cohort included 27,200 candidates and the postpolicy test cohort 5,094. The authors also specified assumptions for missing indicator variables and exclusion of obvious data-entry errors. I did not identify class-imbalance mitigation or code release.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “death before receipt of a heart transplant,” which maps to waitlist mortality. In the postpolicy test set, the best-performing model was the Cox model with treatment variables, C-index 0.76, followed by the random survival forest with treatment variables, C-index 0.74; the 6-status system had C-index 0.67. Calibration was assessed with Kaplan–Meier survival by predicted 90-day risk groups and Brier scores. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. DCA was not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a large national SRTR cohort of adult heart-transplant candidates, which minimizes single-center selection bias, although some candidates with data errors were excluded.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were listing-time physiologic measures, treatments, diagnoses, blood type, and medical history variables that are clinically relevant to urgency ranking.
qa_outcome_comments: The outcome was clearly defined as “death without receiving a heart transplant,” including death while waitlisted and after delisting, with transplant treated as censoring.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include temporal train-test separation, multiple imputation, comparison of CPH and RSF, bootstrap CIs, calibration assessment, and variable-importance analysis.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly addresses ML-based urgency ranking among heart-transplant candidates and is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 41_Raji and Safna - 2022 - Computational methods for predicting the outcome of thoracic transplantation
study_metadata:
Computational methods for predicting the outcome of thoracic transplantation
Raji, C. G. and Safna, A. K.
Journal of Big Data / 2022
algorithm_name: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with back-propagation; Radial Basis Function (RBF) network
section1_comments: The study states that data were collected from the “United Network for Organ Sharing database,” so the source is a U.S. national registry. The paper says “Funding: Not applicable,” but also notes the OPTN data source support contract in the ethics section; I therefore classify the study-specific funding as None. The exact calendar years of the included thoracic transplant records were not reported in the retrieved text. The paper uses the broad term “thoracic transplantation,” not a clearly separated heart-only or lung-only cohort.
section2_comments: The paper reports an initial UNOS thoracic dataset of 148,509 records, then after removing pediatric cases and validation steps, “24 important attributes with 485 records were extracted.” Age, donor age, creatinine, serum albumin, ECMO, IABP, rejection episodes, ischemic time, HLA mismatch, infection resistance, and graft-failure cause were included, so clinical history was incorporated. Mean age, sex distribution, and race/ethnicity were not reported for the final 485-case dataset.
section3_comments: The paper’s main proposed model is the “multi-layer perceptron algorithm,” and it also implemented “the Radial Basis Function Network model to prove the accuracy of proposed model.” Inputs were donor, recipient, and transplantation tabular variables selected from UNOS using InfoGain Attribute Eval with ranker search. The comparison was against an earlier published computational system rather than a clinical guideline or human reader. The paper discusses “validation” but the retrieved text does not clearly describe a standard split or CV protocol, so I classify validation as Other rather than guessing. No SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or explicit hyperparameter tuning was reported.
section4_comments: Data preprocessing was described extensively: multi-organ records were filtered to thoracic transplantation, pediatric records were removed, relevant attributes were selected, and InfoGain-based ranking reduced the feature space to 24 inputs. However, the retrieved text does not describe a missing-data method, class-imbalance handling, public code release, or explicit train/test counts. Because those details were not reported clearly, I left them as NR/No rather than inferring them.
section5_comments: The study outcome was graft/survival status after thoracic transplantation, represented by GRF_STAT, but the exact clinical horizon was not clearly specified in the retrieved text, so the safest category is Other. The paper reports “accuracy of 97.1%” for the MLP and “92.37%” for the RBF model. Table 6 reports sensitivity 0.966 and specificity 0.984 for the proposed MLP. AUC/C-statistic, PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_comments: Although the source was UNOS, the final analytic sample was reduced from a very large registry to only 485 records after multiple filtering and validation steps, and the paper does not clearly describe cohort assembly in a clinically transparent way.
qa_predictors_comments: The included predictors are clinically plausible donor, recipient, and transplant variables, but several choices are not well justified clinically and one top-ranked variable was recipient sex, suggesting possible dataset-driven instability.
qa_outcome_comments: The outcome variable was GRF_STAT, with “N” indicating graft failure and “Y” success, but the paper does not clearly define the exact time horizon for this success/failure endpoint in the retrieved text.
qa_analysis_comments: The reported accuracy is very high, but the retrieved text does not clearly document dataset split strategy, external validation, calibration, or robust modern reporting standards, which creates substantial risk of optimistic performance estimation.
qa_applicability_comments: The study is directly about computational prediction after thoracic transplantation and uses UNOS data, but it mixes broad “thoracic transplantation” terminology with heart-focused background and does not clearly define a heart-only or lung-only clinically interpretable cohort.

study_id: 42_Rodriguez et al. - 2022 - A Framework for Using Real-World Data and Health Outcomes Modeling to Evaluate Machine Learning-Base
study_metadata:
A Framework for Using Real-World Data and Health Outcomes Modeling to Evaluate Machine Learning-Based Risk Prediction Models
Rodriguez, P. J. et al.
Value Health / 2022
algorithm_name: Super learner ensemble ML model for 2-year mortality; patient-level microsimulation framework
section1_comments: The real-world cohort came from the “Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry” linked to UNOS data, and the cohort was followed “until December 31, 2016,” with simulation starting January 1, 2012. I did not identify an explicit funding or conflict-of-interest statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The patient-level simulation used the “40% validation set (n = 4247).” The retrieved text does not report a cohort-wide mean age or sex percentage for this validation sample. Clinical history and longitudinal disease data were included through repeated encounter-level CFFPR variables, including lung function, contraindications, visit history, waitlist status, and transplant outcomes. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The ML referral policy used a previously developed “super learner, an ensemble ML approach that optimally combined multiple underlying models (lasso, elastic net, ridge, XGboost, random forest, and support vector machine).” It was compared against referral based on FEV1 and usual care. The 40% validation set was used for the simulation, so internal split is the best validation label. The paper focuses on downstream clinical utility rather than interpretability, and I did not find a clear feature-selection or hyperparameter-tuning description in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The cohort of 10,615 adults was previously split into training (60%) and validation (40%) sets; this corresponds to about 6,368 training and 4,247 validation/test patients. The paper describes imputation of missing ABO and LAS-related variables and synthetic extension of trajectories, and explicitly uses “multiple imputation by chained equations” for some modeled quantities, so multiple imputation is the best fit. I did not find any class-imbalance strategy or code-release statement.
section5_comments: The modeled clinical decision was lung-transplant referral, and the downstream patient outcome was 5-year survival under different referral policies; because this does not map neatly to the preset categories, the best label is Other. The ML model’s baseline AUROC for 2-year mortality was 0.914 versus 0.876 for FEV1. Calibration is discussed because the paper states that the ML model had “better calibration than FEV1.” The paper’s main outcome results were survival and referral consequences in simulation rather than standard test-set accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1. DCA was not reported.
qa_participants_comments: The study used a large national CFF registry linked to UNOS, covering a substantial proportion of the U.S. cystic fibrosis population, which reduces major center-level selection bias.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were longitudinal real-world clinical variables collected at repeated encounters and used dynamically over time, which closely matches intended clinical use.
qa_outcome_comments: Outcomes were clearly defined, including referral, transplant, pretransplant death, post-transplant death, and 5-year overall survival, with explicit state transitions in the microsimulation model.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include linked real-world registries, dynamic decision modeling, patient-level microsimulation, and explicit accounting for organ supply and heterogenous treatment effects. Uncertainty remains because many downstream effects were simulated rather than directly observed, and results depend on structural assumptions such as organ allocation and post-transplant survival modeling.
qa_applicability_comments: Although the paper is highly relevant to lung transplantation and ML-based referral decisions, the population is adults with cystic fibrosis rather than a general thoracic transplant candidate population, and the article is mainly a methodological framework rather than a standard transplant prediction-model development paper.

study_id: 43_Sage et al. - 2023 - A machine-learning approach to human ex vivo lung perfusion predicts transplantation outcomes and pr
study_metadata:
A machine-learning approach to human ex vivo lung perfusion predicts transplantation outcomes and promotes organ utilization
Sage, A. T. et al.
Nat Commun / 2023
algorithm_name: InsighTx; eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
section1_comments: The study used EVLP data “collected in our center over the past decade,” specifically from the Toronto Lung Transplant Program/University Health Network, Toronto, Canada, with cases spanning “2008 to 2022.” I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The cohort included “n = 725 eligible clinical EVLP cases.” From Table 1, donor mean age was 45, 48, and 47 years across the three cohorts, which is approximately 46 overall. Male sex was 65%, 64%, and 64% across cohorts, implying about 35% female overall. This is an organ-assessment cohort rather than a recipient cohort. Race/ethnicity and comorbidity history were not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The paper states that the authors “evaluated eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)” and developed “our ML model, termed InsighTx,” using donor features plus biological, physiological, and biochemical EVLP assessments. The model was then examined in a retrospective blinded implementation study involving EVLP specialists, so human expert is the best comparator. Because the development cohort preceded two later consecutive validation cohorts, external temporal is the best validation category. SHAP importance values were explicitly used to assess feature importance. The retrieved text does not describe a separate feature-selection stage or explicit hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: The development dataset contained 504 EVLP cases, and the two independent temporal validation cohorts contained 97 and 124 cases, totaling 221 test cases. Data preprocessing is described at a high level through donor plus EVLP biological/physiological/biochemical feature extraction and temporal cohort separation. I did not find a clear missing-data strategy, class-imbalance method, or code-availability statement in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The model predicted EVLP suitability and post-transplant duration of mechanical ventilation; within the extraction framework, the closest postoperative adverse-outcome category is PGD because the paper also linked predictions to PGD grade 3 at 72 h. For the overall model, the best held-out AUROC was 85 ± 3% in test dataset 2. For unsuitable lungs, AUROC reached 95 ± 2%, and for extubation <72 h it reached 83 ± 4%. The paper reports model precision of 81% for identifying any unsuitable donor lung and 72% for suitable donor lungs. For donor lungs predicted to have extubation <72 h, the NPV for PGD grade 3 at 72 h was 88%. Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This is the largest clinical EVLP cohort reported, but it comes from a single expert center, which may limit generalizability to other EVLP programs.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were rich EVLP biological, physiological, and biochemical features collected longitudinally during standardized ex vivo assessment, and SHAP-based importance was examined.
qa_outcome_comments: Outcomes were clearly defined as three clinically meaningful categories after EVLP—extubation <72 h, extubation ≥72 h, and declined for transplant—with additional linkage to PGD grade 3 at 72 h.
qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include a sizable development cohort, two consecutive temporal test cohorts, and blinded implementation analysis. Uncertainty remains because the retrieved text does not clearly describe missing-data handling, hyperparameter tuning, or multicenter external validation.
qa_applicability_comments: The article directly studies ML-guided assessment of donor lungs during EVLP and its relationship to post-transplant outcomes and organ utilization, which is highly relevant to thoracic transplantation AI.

study_id: 44_Seraphin-2023-Prediction of heart transplant r
study_metadata:
Prediction of heart transplant rejection from routine pathology slides with self-supervised deep learning
Seraphin, T. P. et al.
Eur Heart J Digit Health / 2023
algorithm_name: Self-supervised learning attention-based multiple instance learning pipeline using RetCCL encoder and Marugoto; comparator CRANE
section1_comments: The data came from “three different medical centres in Germany,” with cohorts from Regensburg, Hamburg, and Aachen. Table 1 shows recruitment years spanning 1999–2014, 2016–2018, and 2019–2021, so the overall study period was 1999–2021. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The four cohorts included 107, 95, 86, and 37 patients, totaling 325 patients, with 1,079 slides. Age was reported as median by cohort, not as a single mean. Table 1 reports female:male per slides as 55:338, 55:301, 70:121, and 47:94, which totals 227 female slide-labels out of 1,079, about 21%; patient-level female percentage was not directly reported. Race/ethnicity and comorbidity summaries were not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The authors trained “our own deep learning pipeline using an SSL-based feature extractor combined with attention-based MIL” on H&E whole-slide pathology images and compared it against the CRANE method. The ground truth came from “two expert pathologists… grading the degree of rejection in consensus,” so human expert is the best comparator. Validation included hold-out and separate cohorts from other German centers, so external geographic is the strongest label. Interpretability came from attention maps and Grad-CAM visualizations. The paper reports optimizer choice, learning-rate finding, early stopping, and training settings, which count as hyperparameter/training-procedure reporting.
section4_comments: Only samples “with information on ISHLT grading” were eligible, which is most consistent with complete-case inclusion. The primary training cohort had 393 slides, and the three validation cohorts had 356, 189, and 141 slides, totaling 686 test slides. The paper describes digitization, tessellation, patch extraction, feature extraction, bag construction, and training procedures. No class-imbalance correction was described. The code repositories for preprocessing and deep learning are explicitly provided, satisfying code availability. The retrieved text did not explicitly mention released trained weights, but the available option set requires one of the listed labels; code availability is clearly affirmative.
section5_comments: The target was cellular cardiac allograft rejection on endomyocardial biopsy, which fits Acute Rejection. In cross-validation, the binary rejection yes/no AUROC was 0.849. External AUROCs were 0.734, 0.729, and 0.716. For multiclass ISHLT grades, the cross-validated AUROCs were 0.835 for 0R, 0.633 for 1R, and 0.905 for 2/3R. Although the methods mention calculation of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, I did not see explicit numeric values for these in the retrieved text, so I leave them NR. Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_comments: This was a multicentre retrospective series with external validation, which is a strength, but cohort sizes were still modest and selected from archived biopsies with available ISHLT grading.
qa_predictors_comments: Predictors were routine H&E pathology whole-slide images from endomyocardial biopsies, processed in a standardized digital workflow.

qa_analysis_comments: Strengths include repeated three-fold cross-validation, three external validation cohorts, comparison with CRANE, bootstrapped confidence intervals, and code availability. Remaining limitations are mainly sample size and reduced external performance, not major analytic flaws.

Race/ethnicity was reported, and multiple clinical factors were included, such as diagnosis group, 6-minute walk distance, respiratory support, pulmonary arterial pressure, oxygen use, creatinine, BMI, bilirubin, insurance, and education. A single overall mean age for the full analytic cohorts was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The study compared seven models for each outcome: current LAS/CAS Cox models, updated Cox models, nonlinear spline-enhanced Cox models, random survival forests, logistic models, linear discriminant analysis, and gradient-boosted trees. The main comparators were the current LAS/CAS survival models, which are linear risk-score models. The data were “randomly partitioned into 10 training and test samples for cross-validation.” Predictors came from SRTR candidate/recipient tabular data available at allocation. The retrieved text did not report SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or explicit hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: The Methods state that the authors used “multiple imputation to account for missing predictor data,” and inverse probability-of-censoring weighting to address informative censoring due to transplant. They also describe reconciliation of relisted patients and construction of residual cohorts. The study used repeated cross-validation folds rather than one fixed train/test split, so exact training and test counts are NR. Code availability was not reported in the retrieved text. Class-imbalance handling was not described.
section5_comments: The primary outcomes were waitlist death or removal as too sick, and post-transplant death or retransplantation. Figure 1 shows subgroup AUC patterns, especially worse variability among Medicaid patients. Because the paper centers on AUC/C-statistic-style discrimination across many models and time horizons rather than a single deployed model, and because the prompt asks for held-out test/validation metrics, I leave the single numeric AUC field as NR rather than choose one arbitrary value. Calibration and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used large national SRTR cohorts of waitlist candidates and transplant recipients in the United States, which reduces center-level selection bias, although exclusions for missing key variables were applied.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were derived from SRTR variables available at allocation or cohort time points, consistent with the clinical use case for LAS/CAS modeling.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcomes were clearly defined as time from waitlist placement to death or removal as too sick, and time from transplant to death or retransplantation.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include TRIPOD-aligned internal validation, 10-fold cross-validation, multiple imputation, inverse probability-of-censoring weighting, and comparison of several model classes; however, only internal validation was performed and post-transplant discrimination remained poor across all models.
qa_applicability_quotes: This article directly evaluates machine-learning and alternative modeling approaches for lung transplant allocation-related prediction, making it highly relevant to the review question.

qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include multiple model comparisons, kNN imputation, 5-fold cross-validation, and explainability analyses, but uncertainty remains because hyperparameter tuning, calibration, and exact split sizes were not reported.
qa_applicability_quotes: This study directly addresses AI/ML for heart transplant PGD prediction using donor-recipient variables and is closely aligned with the review question.

I did not identify an explicit funding or conflict-of-interest statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The Results state: “Of the 41 patients referred to the multimodal rehabilitation program (mean age of 55.8 [SD 9.7] years; 22 men).” This implies 19 women, or 46.3%. Table 1 reports comorbidity and clinical-history-related variables including Charlson Comorbidity Index, transplant indication, malnutrition, sarcopenia, muscle strength, exercise capacity, and quality of life. Race/ethnicity was not reported.
section3_comments: The paper explicitly states this was a “prospective observational study” and that “an ANN and regression analysis were used.” The ANN was implemented in R using the nnet package, with “30 neurons, a decay of 0.001, ‘tanh’ activator, and linear output relationships,” so architecture details were reported. Garson’s algorithm was used to quantify variable contribution and select variables with relative importance >0.5 for subsequent regression, which supports both explainability and automated feature selection. No explicit train/validation/test split or cross-validation was reported.
section4_comments: The primary analysis used “23 common baseline variables that were complete (with no missing data points) for all participants,” which is best classified as complete case analysis. Data preprocessing was described: variables were defined by type, attrition classes were encoded as 1/2/3, numeric and ordinal variables were rescaled between −1 and +1, and categorical variables were dummy coded. I found no mention of class-imbalance handling and no released code repository; only function names and package details were provided. Because a separate training/test split was not reported, training and test sample sizes are NR.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was attrition rate in the rehabilitation program, classified as low (<5% missing data), medium (5–10%), or high (>10%), so the closest allowed category is Other. The article reports significance of factors associated with attrition rather than conventional predictive metrics such as AUC or accuracy. Table 2 shows significant variables: low age-dependent BMI (p = 7.08 × 10−5), end-stage respiratory disease requiring LT (p = 0.000111), EQ-5D VAS (p = 0.0009078), low handgrip strength by Mediterranean reference values (p = 0.0230351), and low handgrip strength by EWGSOP2 cutoffs (p = 0.0455796). No calibration or DCA was reported.
qa_participants_quotes: The study included only 41 patients from a single center, all referred to one rehabilitation program, which limits representativeness and creates substantial selection risk.
qa_predictors_quotes: Baseline predictors were clinically relevant, but only the 23 variables with no missing data were analyzed in the ANN, so potentially important factors were excluded.
qa_outcome_quotes: Attrition was explicitly defined using the percentage of missing data per participant and then categorized into low, medium, or high attrition.
qa_analysis_quotes: The ANN was trained on a very small sample without a reported holdout validation set, and the authors note that including all variables in regression led to overfitting and/or multicollinearity.
qa_applicability_quotes: This article directly concerns AI use in lung-transplant recipient care, specifically rehabilitation-program attrition after transplantation.

algorithm_name: Machine learning decision tree model / multivariate decision tree analysis
section1_comments: The study was conducted “at our center” at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center and included ACHD patients “evaluated for heart or heart + additional organ transplant between 2004 and 2014.” Funding is explicitly listed from the National Institutes of Health and the American Heart Association, plus HeartFest. I did not find a visible COI statement in the retrieved text.

Race was reported as 91.4% White, 3.4% Black, and 5.2% Asian. Table 1 also includes multiple comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, pulmonary hypertension, portal hypertension, chronic renal insufficiency, and tobacco history.
section3_comments: The Methods describe “a retrospective chart review” and state that “a machine learning decision tree model was used to evaluate multiple clinical parameters correlating with 1- and 10-year survival.” Input data were clinical, hemodynamic, laboratory, and CPET variables from chart review. The model was “verified… using K-fold cross validation.” The variables entered into multivariate analysis were those previously significant on univariate analysis, which is best categorized as manual/clinical feature selection. No hyperparameter tuning or explainability method was reported.
section4_comments: Of 71 identified patients, “58 patients had all relevant data… available for evaluation and were included in the study,” which is most consistent with complete-case analysis. The paper mentions K-fold cross-validation but does not report fold sizes, explicit train/test counts, imbalance handling, code availability, or preprocessing/normalization steps typical of ML pipelines.
section5_comments: The paper evaluates both 1-year and 10-year survival. Figure 1 and the text report clinically interpretable decision rules rather than AUC-style performance. For 1-year outcomes, transplanted patients with SVP <14 mmHg had 100% survival, and non-transplanted patients with PCWP <15 mmHg had 100% survival. For 10-year outcomes, all waitlisted/declined patients with PCWP ≥17 mmHg died, and all transplanted/deferred patients with SVP <10 mmHg were alive. Kaplan–Meier curves in Figure 2 show 1-year survival of 100% for deferred, 85.7% for transplanted, 42.1% for waitlisted, and 54.5% for declined patients. No AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA were reported.

qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors included clinically relevant pre-listing hemodynamic, laboratory, and functional variables collected during transplant evaluation, especially catheter-based measurements such as PCWP, SVP, and EDP.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcomes were clearly defined as 1- and 10-year survival after transplant evaluation/decision, and the paper reports group-specific survival at multiple time points via Kaplan–Meier analysis.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include use of univariate analysis, multivariate decision-tree analysis, and K-fold cross-validation, but the small sample size, complete-case inclusion, and lack of standard predictive performance metrics limit robustness.
qa_applicability_quotes: The paper directly studies machine-learning-assisted outcome prediction in heart transplant evaluation, albeit in a congenital heart disease subgroup rather than a general thoracic transplant population.

algorithm_name: AI-ECG deep-learning model
section1_comments: The study included heart transplant recipients “at three Mayo Clinic US sites” and retrospectively identified patients “between January 1988 and April 2021.” The paper states support from NIH in the article end matter and includes an explicit disclosures/conflict statement section, so COI declaration was present. Figure 2 describes the architecture, and the paper states the best model was chosen after “a randomized hyperparameter search over optimizer, learning rates, class weights, batch size, and regularization.” The comparator was not a single clinical rule or human reader; the paper compares against standard ECG variables alone, which had inferior AUC 0.579.
section4_comments: Missing-data handling was not described for model inputs. Class imbalance was addressed at least in part because the hyperparameter search included “class weights.” Preprocessing was described: ECGs were digital 12-lead recordings at 500 Hz, and the model input was a “12 by 5000 array,” with random noise and translation layers. The paper does not report code release. The training and test sets contained “6074/758 unique ECG-biopsy pairs,” respectively.
section5_comments: Allograft rejection was defined as “moderate or severe acute cellular rejection (ACR).” On the held-out test set, the AI-ECG achieved “AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.78–0.90),” sensitivity 95%, specificity 52.6%, PPV 5.1%, and NPV 99.7% using threshold 0.4. The prospective proof-of-concept study showed AUC 0.78 and sensitivity 100%, but the prompt asks for held-out test/validation-set metrics, so the primary extracted model performance is from the retrospective test set. qa_participants_quotes: This was a retrospective study from “three Mayo Clinic US sites,” and patients were restricted to those with digital ECGs and EMBs within 30 days, which may limit representativeness and introduce selection bias.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were standardized 12-lead ECG waveforms acquired at 500 Hz and recorded before EMB, so the predictor measurement process was objective and clinically plausible.
qa_outcome_quotes: ACR was defined using ISHLT criteria, and the final classification groups were “reviewed and approved by a cardiovascular pathologist and transplant cardiologist.”
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include patient-level partitioning, held-out testing, and hyperparameter search, but uncertainty remains because missing-data handling for clinical variables was not described, clustering was simplified by assuming repeated EMB independence, and no calibration analysis was reported.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly addresses AI-based detection of heart transplant rejection using a non-invasive model in transplant recipients, which is closely aligned with the review question.

section1_comments: The cohort included bilateral lung transplant recipients “at our center between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2019,” which makes this a U.S. single-center study. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The final cohort “consisted of 576 patients.” Table 1 reports recipient sex as 237 female of 576 total recipients, or 41.15%. Recipient age was reported as median 59 years rather than mean, so mean age is NR. Race, BMI, diagnosis, LAS, ICU status, ventilation, ECMO, donor variables, and pulmonary artery pressure were reported.
section3_comments: The study used donor and recipient pretransplant structured data from UNOS, UNet, and the local EHR. Four prediction algorithms were trained: LR, KNN, XGB, and SVC. Feature reduction was done with lasso regression, and hyperparameters were optimized using 5-fold cross-validation with random grid search. Feature importance was assessed using SHAP. The cohort was split 75%/25% into train/test sets.
section4_comments: The paper states that “missing data were median imputed for continuous data and mode imputed for binary data,” which is simple imputation. Preprocessing included binary encoding of categorical variables and MinMax scaling fit on the training data and applied to the test data. The population was divided into a 75%/25% train-test split, which corresponds to about 432 training and 144 test patients from 576 total. I did not see explicit class-imbalance mitigation. The model was deployed on a secure website, but no source-code release was stated, so code availability is best classified as Other.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “PGD grade 3 at any time within 72 hours of transplantation,” which maps to PGD. The abstract states that the final selected KNN model had “an area under the receiver operating characteristics curve of 0.65.” Table 3 shows KNN among the better-performing models, and Table 4/Figure 4 show explicit calibration assessment using Cox intercepts, slopes, and calibration curves before and after sigmoid calibration. The retrieved text does not provide clear final held-out PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1 values for the selected final KNN model, so I leave those as NR. DCA was not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: This was a retrospective single-center study of 576 recipients from one institution, which limits representativeness despite a decent sample size.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were donor and recipient variables “known at the time of donor offer acceptance,” making them appropriately timed and clinically relevant for prediction.

study_id: 15_Glass-2024-A machine learning algorithm improv
study_metadata:

algorithm_name: ResNet50 convolutional neural network with transfer learning
section1_comments: The biopsies were “previously as pAMR2 as part of routine standard of clinical care between 2018 and 2021 from Duke University Medical Center Department of Pathology,” so the data source was single-center in the USA. The paper includes a “Declaration of competing interest” stating “None.” I did not identify a funding statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study used “300 hematoxylin and eosin slides” from cardiac transplant endomyocardial biopsies. It did not report recipient mean age, sex distribution, race/ethnicity, or baseline comorbidity data in the retrieved text. The unit of model development was annotated biopsy regions rather than a clinical cohort table.
section3_comments: The study used annotated H&E pathology image patches and a “convolutional neural network approach utilizing transfer learning.” The ResNet50 model was initialized with pretrained weights and fine-tuned. The model was compared against blinded human pathologist review in a separate curated set of slides. Regions of interest were manually annotated by experts, which functions as manual/clinical feature selection at the region level. Training settings including Adam optimizer, learning rate 0.0001, cross-entropy loss, and stopping on validation-loss plateau were reported.
section4_comments: The dataset contained 4,212 annotations split 70%/10%/20% into training, validation, and testing. That corresponds to approximately 2,948 training annotations and 842 test annotations. The four classes were balanced at 1,053 regions each, so explicit class-imbalance correction was not reported and was likely unnecessary. Preprocessing was described through de-identification, whole-slide scanning at 40X, annotation, extraction of non-overlapping 224×224 windows, and train/validation/test splitting. Code availability was not reported. Missing-data handling was not relevant to image patches and was not described.
section5_comments: The task was histologic diagnosis of pAMR-H in cardiac transplant biopsies. The closest category in the allowed list is Acute Rejection. The algorithm achieved “98% overall validation accuracy.” Figure 3 shows multiclass AUROC 0.982 and binary AUCs of 0.995 for pAMR-H vs normal endomyocardium, 0.992 for pAMR-H vs healing injury, and 0.992 for pAMR-H vs ACR. The paper also reports pAMR-H classification accuracies of 99.5%, 99.2%, and 99.2% against those three categories, respectively. PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1-score, calibration, and DCA were not reported. I used the highest explicitly reported AUC value for the single AUC field.
qa_participants_quotes: The training material came from previously diagnosed Duke cases from 2018–2021, so this was a retrospective single-center pathology dataset and not a broad clinical recipient sample.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were standardized digital H&E pathology image patches scanned at 40X, with expert consensus used to define ground truth and expert annotation of regions of interest.
qa_outcome_quotes: Ground truth for pAMR-H was based on expert consensus plus cases confirmed as pAMR2 with immunologic evidence such as “>50% positive C4d immunofluorescence and/or >10% CD68 positive intravascular macrophages.”
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include balanced classes, predefined train/validation/test splitting, transfer learning, ROC/AUC reporting, and human-reader comparison. Limitations acknowledged by the authors include patch-level rather than whole-slide development and single-institution staining/scanning, with ongoing external verification still needed.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly applies AI to heart-transplant pathology and rejection diagnosis, which is clearly within thoracic organ transplantation AI.

Because the paper spans multiple organs and mixed datasets, “Other” is the closest fit for organ focus and dataset source.

It frames the problem as donor-recipient allocation across liver, heart, and lung transplantation datasets rather than a single patient cohort.
section3_comments: The paper proposes an “MCNN-HELM based prediction model” and states that a “prairie dog optimizer (PDO)” is used to improve matching-pair performance. It compares the proposed method against MINLP, IGBFS-NB, SVM, and FO, and evaluates policy scenarios such as Real, FCFS, UF, and BF. The retrieved text describes preprocessing and training/testing flowcharts, but it does not clearly state a conventional clinical study design such as retrospective cohort with a well-defined patient cohort, so “Other” is the most accurate label. Hyperparameter configuration is explicitly mentioned in the conclusion.
section4_comments: The paper states that “missing values and inaccurate data present in real-time datasets are removed via pre-processing,” and separately notes that “some records and attributes are eliminated,” which is most consistent with complete-case style exclusion rather than imputation. Preprocessing is described, but explicit training and test sample counts are not visible in the retrieved text. I found no public code-availability statement. Class-imbalance handling is not described.
section5_comments: The paper’s main task is donor-recipient allocation and suitable donor identification with minimized waiting time, so “Donor acceptance” is the closest restricted outcome label. Table 5 reports training accuracy 97.5%, computational time 2.2 s, PEFO 16.3582, PEPO 16.1401, and ABDT 0.6784. For the lung dataset (UNOS-LU), Table 3 shows that the BF policy had death rate 0.13, average benefit 275.43, and average survival 1290.48, compared with Real 0.15, 221.48, and 1175.42. The paper does not report AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA. Because only training accuracy is explicitly reported, I am not inferring a held-out test accuracy.
qa_participants_quotes: The paper uses three “real-time datasets” across liver, heart, and lung transplantation, but the retrieved text does not provide a transparent lung-specific cohort derivation or sample description.
qa_predictors_quotes: The framework uses donor and recipient transplantation details and geolocation/resource considerations, but the exact lung-specific predictor set is not clearly enumerated in the retrieved text.
qa_outcome_quotes: The paper targets “suitable donor” selection, minimized waiting time, and high-risk prioritization, but the exact formal outcome definition for the lung subset is not clearly specified in the retrieved excerpts.
qa_analysis_quotes: The paper reports strong training accuracy and simulation metrics, but the retrieved text does not show a clear held-out clinical validation framework, standard external validation, or conventional discrimination/calibration metrics for lung transplantation specifically.
qa_applicability_quotes: Although the article includes a lung dataset, it is a broad multi-organ allocation systems paper rather than a lung-only thoracic transplant prediction study with a clearly defined transplant cohort.

algorithm_name: Taelcore (topological autoencoder with best linear combination for optimal reduction of embeddings)
section1_comments: The authors are based in France and Spain, and the paper states they “recycle the dataset from ‘Personalised Risk Predictor for Acute Cellular Rejection in Lung Transplant Using Soluble CD31’” for a lung-transplant ACR study, but the retrieved text does not provide an explicit funding statement, COI statement, or recruitment years. The clinical dataset appears to be a single clinical cohort rather than a registry.
section2_comments: The Methods state: “We analysed a clinical dataset of 40 patients who underwent lung transplantation surgery,” and “seven (17.5%) experienced acute cellular rejection within one year of the operation.” The retrieved text does not report age, sex, race/ethnicity, or comorbidity tables for these 40 patients.
section3_comments: The paper proposes “Taelcore,” combining autoencoders, multilayer perceptron (MLP), and topological data analysis tools. It compares Taelcore-enhanced performance against AE, PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, RF, KNN, and GNB. The nine measured clinical variables from the first 72 hours after transplant were used as input features. The evaluation is based on success percentages and dimensionality-reduction quality metrics rather than a conventional held-out train/test clinical validation framework, so “Other” is the most accurate validation label. The retrieved text does not describe SHAP/LIME or hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: Figure 1 and the text describe preprocessing including standardisation, box-plot outlier detection, denoising using the sCD31–ACR relationship, Rips filtration, persistence diagrams, and entropy vectorisation. The lung cohort is imbalanced (7 ACR vs 33 non-ACR), but the retrieved text does not describe reweighting, oversampling, or other imbalance handling. Missing-data handling is not reported. The paper states: “The code associated with this study is publicly available,” which supports Other rather than “algorithm weights available.” Exact train/test sample sizes are not given in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The target was ACR within 1 year after lung transplantation. Table 1 reports percentage success before and after topological improvement: RF 50%→80%, MLP 80%→90%, KNN 50%→50%, and GNB 90%→90%. The discussion explicitly states “an accuracy achieved of 90%” for Taelcore in predicting ACR after lung transplantation. No AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA were reported. Because the paper presents “percentage of success” rather than a richer held-out metric set, I report 90% as the model accuracy figure and leave the others NR.
qa_participants_quotes: The clinical lung-transplant dataset included only 40 patients, with 7 ACR cases, which creates substantial risk of selection instability and limited generalisability.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were clearly defined early post-transplant clinical measurements collected at 24, 48, and 72 hours, including sCD31, PaO2/FiO2, and SOFA respiratory scores.
qa_outcome_quotes: The paper clearly targets “acute cellular rejection,” but the retrieved excerpts do not provide the operational diagnostic definition or biopsy/grading criteria used to label ACR.
qa_analysis_quotes: The study is methodologically innovative, but it relies on a very small dataset, reports “percentage of success” rather than a full clinical validation framework, and does not provide exact train/test sizes or standard clinical performance metrics such as AUC and calibration.
qa_applicability_quotes: The paper directly addresses AI-based prediction of acute rejection after lung transplantation, which is strongly aligned with the review question.

study_id: 20_Hsich-2020-Heart Transplantation_ An In-Depth

RSF was used to determine “importance of mortality risk factors and their interactions.” Inputs were recipient and donor tabular variables from SRTR. The paper does not frame this against a human or guideline comparator. Variable screening in the sex-focused parametric models used “machine learning variable selection,” which is best categorized as automated. Explicit hyperparameter tuning was not reported.
section4_comments: Missing data were handled with “multiple imputation by chained equations for parametric survival models” and “missForest for the random forest analysis,” so this fits best as Other. The paper describes exclusions, missingness rates, and imputation. No class-imbalance method or code release was reported. Exact training/test sizes were not given because the analyses were not based on a simple fixed split in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The primary endpoint was “all-cause mortality assessed as time from heart transplantation to death or end of follow-up,” so the closest restricted category is Other. The study focused on hazard phases, variable importance, and interactions rather than reporting AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, or F1-score. Figure 1 showed 1-month survival 96%, 1-year survival 89%, and 12-year survival 50%, but these are cohort survival estimates rather than model discrimination metrics. Calibration and DCA were not reported.

qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were recorded at the time of transplantation and included clinically relevant recipient and donor variables, including hemodynamics, labs, support devices, donor cause of death, and ischemic time.
qa_outcome_quotes: The primary outcome was clearly defined as all-cause mortality from transplantation to death or end of follow-up, with mortality verified through the Social Security Death Master File.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include national scope, complementary parametric and RSF analyses, interaction assessment at multiple time points, and imputation for missingness. Uncertainty remains because conventional predictive performance metrics for a deployable model were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly studies AI/statistical risk modeling for post-heart-transplant survival using a national transplant registry, which is highly relevant to the review question.

section2_comments: The final SRTR lung-transplant dataset included “33,244 patients,” with 984 PTLD cases and 32,260 non-cases. The extracted text does not provide a main baseline table with overall age or sex percentages for the lung cohort in the main results section I could verify. The features included demographics, immunosuppression, viral infections, and HLA variables, so clinical history was included.
section3_comments: The study used gradient-boosted decision trees, specifically XGBoost and LightGBM, trained with focal loss and then calibrated using the “Ψγ transformation.” It also compared against standard XGBoost, logistic regression, Platt scaling, and isotonic regression. The lung-transplant task used 54 tabular SRTR features. Evaluation used repeated 10-fold cross-validation experiments, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization was explicitly described. I did not find SHAP/LIME or a separate feature-selection step beyond using the defined feature set.
section4_comments: The lung-transplant datasets were described as “high degree of class-imbalance,” and the focal-loss strategy was explicitly motivated as a way to handle imbalanced or skewed class distributions. Preprocessing/exclusion steps were described in Figure 2 and Section 4.1.1. However, I did not find a clear statement on missing-data imputation for the SRTR lung dataset, nor explicit fixed training/test sample counts because the study relied on repeated 10-fold cross-validation rather than a single holdout split. I also did not identify a code-availability statement in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The lung-transplant outcome was PTLD, which is not one of the preset transplant-outcome categories, so the closest allowed choice is Other. The abstract states that the calibrated focal-aware XGBoost achieved “AUROC, Brier score, and calibration slope of 0.700, 0.128, and 0.968 for predicting the 10-year cancer risk.” The paper also reports that for 1-year PTLD prediction, “XGBoost-Focal calibrated using the Ψγ transformation achieved the best sensitivity (0.631).” Calibration plots, calibration slopes/intercepts, and Brier scores were central to the paper; DCA was not reported. I did not infer PPV, specificity, or NPV because they were not clearly stated in the retrieved excerpts.
qa_participants_quotes: The lung-transplant analysis used a large national SRTR cohort and applied transparent exclusion criteria, reducing single-center selection bias.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were structured SRTR variables available in the registry, including demographics, immunosuppression, viral infection history, and HLA data.
qa_outcome_quotes: The binary outcome was explicitly defined as PTLD, derived from the SRTR malignancy file, with time-to-PTLD calculated from transplant date to diagnosis date.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include repeated 10-fold cross-validation, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, and detailed calibration assessment. Remaining uncertainty comes from the lack of a fully independent external validation cohort and the absence, in the retrieved text, of a clear missing-data strategy for the SRTR lung dataset.
qa_applicability_quotes: This article directly addresses AI-based clinical risk prediction in lung transplant recipients using SRTR data and is highly relevant to the review question.

Visual interpretation techniques were used to reveal disease-relevant image regions, which counts as interpretability, although not specifically SHAP/LIME. I did not find explicit hyperparameter-tuning details in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The study excluded scans with large pixel size, too few slices, and scans of patients with extensive infiltrates, which is most consistent with complete-case/exclusion-based handling rather than imputation. Class imbalance was addressed in the design and evaluation by patient-level five-fold splitting and weighted ROC analysis to avoid bias from patients with more scans, but no oversampling was described. Data preprocessing and acquisition details were described in depth, including scan inclusion/exclusion, reconstruction type, and late-fusion slice handling. Because the study used five-fold cross-validation at the patient level, fixed training/test N were not reported. Code availability was not reported in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: BOS is the obstructive phenotype of chronic lung allograft dysfunction, so the closest restricted category is CLAD. qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were chest CT scans processed with a defined DNN pipeline, and CT acquisition/reconstruction details were explicitly described.
qa_outcome_quotes: BOS was defined according to “current diagnostic guidelines,” with onset defined when FEV1 consistently fell below 80% of best FEV1.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include patient-level five-fold cross-validation, bootstrapped confidence intervals, stage-specific evaluation, and at-risk detection analysis. Uncertainty remains because this is a low-data, single-center study without external validation.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly addresses AI-based BOS detection after lung transplantation using CT imaging and is highly relevant to the review question.
