The retrieved text reports 1,690 patient biopsies in the U.S. cohort, 585 patients in Turkey, and 123 patients in Switzerland, totaling 2,398 patients/biopsies across cohorts used for development and external testing. I did not find a cohort-wide mean age, sex percentage, race/ethnicity, or comorbidity summary in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: CRANE is a deep-learning system operating on H&E-stained whole-slide biopsy images using a pretrained CNN encoder plus attention-based multiple instance learning. It was compared with expert pathologist assessment in a reader study, and it was externally evaluated on Turkish and Swiss cohorts, which makes external geographic validation the strongest validation label. The system also generated attention heatmaps for interpretation. Hyperparameters and architecture details are described in Methods.
section4_comments: The internal U.S. cohort was split into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% hold-out testing. Since the U.S. dataset contained 5,054 WSIs, this corresponds to about 3,548 training WSIs and about 1,011 hold-out WSIs; adding the external Turkish and Swiss test cohorts gives 1,717 + 123 + 1,011 = about 2,851 total test WSIs, but for the strict held-out internal test field I report the internal U.S. holdout only as 1,011 if only internal is desired. However, because the prompt asks for test/validation size and the paper emphasizes rigorous external testing, I instead used the clearly reported external test cohorts separately in the narrative and note this ambiguity. Tissue segmentation, patching, transfer learning, and multi-magnification fusion were clearly described. Class imbalance was handled partly by balanced cohort partitioning rather than conventional reweighting; hence “Other.” Missing-data handling and code availability were not reported in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: On the U.S. hold-out set, the model detected overall rejection with AUC 0.962 and accuracy 0.899. It detected cellular rejection with AUC 0.958 and accuracy 0.893, antibody-mediated rejection with AUC 0.874 and accuracy 0.899, Quilty B lesions with AUC 0.939 and accuracy 0.920, and low-grade versus high-grade rejection with AUC 0.833 and accuracy 0.818. No PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, calibration, or DCA were reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used a large internal U.S. dataset plus two independent external international cohorts from Turkey and Switzerland, reducing single-center selection bias.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were standardized H&E whole-slide biopsy images, and the workflow for segmentation, patching, and model inference was clearly defined.
qa_outcome_quotes: EMB labels included rejection presence, subtype, grade, and Quilty B lesions, and all AMR cases were confirmed with C4d immunohistochemistry.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include a large internal development set, hold-out testing, two external geographic validation cohorts, multiple tasks, interpretability heatmaps, and a reader study. Remaining uncertainty is minor compared with most studies in this review.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly addresses AI-based assessment of rejection after heart transplantation using biopsy pathology, which is highly relevant to the review question.

algorithm_name: Partial Response Network (PRN-Lasso); benchmarked against IHTSA deep learning model, IMPACT, and Explainable Boosting Machine
section1_comments: The study used UNOS cohorts from 1997–2018 and an external Scandinavian cohort from 1997–2018, so the data origin is multinational and best classified as international registry data rather than a single-country registry alone. I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The UNOS cohorts included derivation n = 31,315, test n = 6,120, and blinded external validation n = 4,750, totaling 42,185 UNOS recipients; the Scandinavian cohort added 2,293 recipients, for 44,478 total across all cohorts described. Female sex was 26% in the external validation cohort and 24% in the derivation cohort; I report 26% because the primary external-validation cohort is the main focus of performance reporting. Race and multiple comorbidities/clinical variables were reported, including diabetes, dialysis, infection, ECMO, IABP, VAD, ventilator use, bilirubin, creatinine, and diagnosis. A single overall mean age across all cohorts was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The paper developed a self-explaining neural network, the Partial Response Network, and benchmarked it against the previously published deep learning IHTSA model, IMPACT, and EBM. Inputs were tabular recipient and donor variables. The main study design was a temporal derivation/tuning/validation framework: 1997–2013 for training, 2014–2016 for testing/hyperparameter optimization, and 2017–2018 as blinded external validation. Explainability was intrinsic to the PRN design through explicit partial-response functions rather than SHAP/LIME, but it still meets the user’s category of explainability used.
section4_comments: The Scandinavian external dataset had missing values imputed using the median for each column, which fits best under simple imputation. The model-development workflow clearly described derivation, test, and external validation cohorts and standardization around medians for partial responses. I did not find any resampling or class-weighting approach for class imbalance, nor a code-release statement. The derivation cohort size was 31,315 and the primary blinded external validation cohort size was 4,750.
section5_comments: The modeled outcome was 1-year mortality after heart transplantation, which maps to 1-year survival in this extraction framework. In the blinded external UNOS 2017–2018 cohort, PRN-Lasso achieved AUROC 0.628 [0.602, 0.654], compared with 0.635 [0.609, 0.662] for IHTSA; calibration for PRN was good with Hosmer–Lemeshow chi-square 15.01, p = 0.135. In the Scandinavian cohort, AUROC was 0.626 with imputed data and 0.634 with observed-only data. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used large registry-based cohorts from UNOS plus an external Scandinavian dataset, with clear temporal separation for derivation, testing, and blinded validation, which reduces major selection bias.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were clinically relevant recipient and donor variables commonly used for 1-year mortality prediction, including age, creatinine, ischemic time, ventilator status, diagnosis, infection, and transplant year.
qa_outcome_quotes: The paper explicitly modeled 1-year mortality after heart transplantation and reported event rates and AUROCs consistently across cohorts.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include temporal external validation, comparison with multiple benchmarks, calibration assessment, and additional external validation in Scandinavia. Remaining uncertainty is limited compared with many studies in this review.
qa_applicability_quotes: This study directly addresses explainable AI for prediction of 1-year mortality after heart transplantation and is highly relevant to the review question.

section1_comments: The study “utilized the UNOS registry” and identified candidates “listed between 2018 and 2022 as UNOS Status 2,” making this a U.S. national registry study. I did not identify an explicit funding or competing-interest declaration in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The cohort included “4,178 patients listed as Status 2.” From Table 1, mean age was 52.3 in failures and 54.3 in non-failures; weighted overall mean is about 54.1 years. Female sex was 96/504 in failures and 885/3674 in non-failures, for an overall 981/4178 = 23.5%. Race, diabetes, ventilation, dialysis, cardiomyopathy type, hemodynamics, biochemistry, medications, and region were all reported.
section3_comments: The authors “used the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm” and developed one comprehensive model plus region-specific models. Inputs were structured UNOS tabular clinical features. Model interpretation used SHAP. Predictors were chosen from clinically different features between groups and then reduced to 19 inputs after removing highly correlated variables and creating missingness indicators. Validation used 5 × 5 nested cross-validation with grid search.
section4_comments: The study explicitly compared several imputation methods, including “XGBoost’s built-in imputation mechanism,” and Supplementary Table S1 determined the best strategy per model; among the restricted categories, “algorithm handles natively” fits best. Class imbalance was addressed by testing under-sampling, SMOTE, and increased class weights. Preprocessing included removal of correlated features, creation of PAPi, missingness indicators, and categorical encoding. Fixed train/test counts were not reported because evaluation used nested cross-validation folds. Code availability was not stated.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was failure to bridge to transplant, defined as “death while on the waiting list, being too sick to transplant, being listed as an inactive patient due to a high risk of transplantation (Status 7) or upgrading to UNOS status 1.” Within the restricted outcome labels, Waitlist mortality is the closest fit, though the actual endpoint is broader than mortality alone. The overall model achieved AUC 0.71 ± 0.03, accuracy 0.72 ± 0.02, sensitivity 0.54 ± 0.04, and specificity 0.75 ± 0.02. PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_quotes: This was a contemporary UNOS national registry cohort of 4,178 Status 2 candidates with explicit inclusion criteria, which reduces single-center selection bias.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were clinically relevant pre-listing/support variables measured near MCS initiation, including hemodynamics, labs, support devices, medications, and demographics.
qa_outcome_quotes: The primary outcome was clearly defined as Status 2 failure, including death, too sick for transplant, Status 7 inactivation due to high transplant risk, or upgrade to Status 1.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include nested cross-validation, grid search, SHAP-based interpretation, and explicit handling of missingness and imbalance. Uncertainty remains because performance was only moderate and varied substantially across regions.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly studies machine-learning prediction in heart transplant candidates awaiting transplantation and is clearly relevant to the review question.

qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly evaluates machine learning for outcome prediction after heart transplantation using a national transplant registry and is clearly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 39_Ozcan et al. - 2022 - Artificial intelligence-derived cardiac ageing is associated with cardiac events post-heart transpla

algorithm_name: AI-ECG age algorithm / ECG-age convolutional neural network
section1_comments: The study was performed “at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, MN” and included “564 consecutive cardiac transplant patients who underwent HTx in our institution between 1990 and 2018,” so this is a U.S. single-center cohort. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: “A total of 540 patients with available pre- and post-transplantation ECG data were included.” Table 1 reports recipient age 49 ± 14 years and recipient sex male in 366/540, implying 32% female. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text. Clinical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, ischemic cardiomyopathy, lipid measures, ischemic time, immunosuppression, rejection, CAV grade, and pacemaker implantation.

The model was applied without additional training to this transplant cohort. No SHAP/LIME-type explainability or hyperparameter-tuning process for this study cohort was reported. Validation here is best marked as not reported because this paper is primarily an application/prognostic study of a previously developed model rather than a new derivation-validation paper.
section4_comments: The analysis included only patients “with available pre- and post-transplantation ECG data,” which is most consistent with complete-case inclusion. The ECG-age algorithm had been previously trained on 774,783 subjects outside this study, but this paper did not retrain or provide study-specific train/test counts for the transplant cohort. Data handling was described, including averaging ECG ages from ECGs obtained within 1 year before and after HTx and excluding ECGs used in the original training/validation sets. section5_comments: The study outcome was MACE, defined as “any incident of coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, re-transplantation, and all-cause mortality,” so the closest allowed category is Adverse Events. During median follow-up of 8.8 years, 307 patients experienced MACE. The main reported performance/result metric was association strength rather than discrimination: ΔECG age ≥ 0 was associated with MACE in multivariable Cox analysis, HR 1.58 (95% CI 1.18–2.10, P = 0.002). qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were standardized 12-lead ECGs processed by a previously developed CNN, and the study clearly defined pre- and post-transplant ECG age windows.
qa_outcome_quotes: MACE was explicitly defined as coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, re-transplantation, and all-cause mortality, with events collected by detailed chart review.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include multivariable Cox models, competing-risk analysis, and long follow-up. Uncertainty remains because this was a prognostic application of an existing AI tool rather than a full derivation/validation study within the transplant cohort, and no discrimination/calibration metrics were reported.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly applies AI to post-heart-transplant risk stratification and cardiac events, which is clearly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 03_Ahady Dolatsara-2020-A two-stage machine learn
study_metadata:
A two-stage machine learning framework to predict heart transplantation survival probabilities over time with a monotonic probability constraint
Ahady Dolatsara, Hamidreza et al.
Decision Support Systems / 2020
algorithm_name: Two-stage framework with Stage I ML models and Stage II isotonic regression; selected implementation reported in main results: UP-LASSO-logistic regression
section1_comments: The paper states, “Our UNOS dataset covered 103,570 heart transplant events up to and including September 30, 2016,” and the registry/process described are explicitly U.S.-based through UNOS. Funding was supported “in part by the Ohio Supercomputer Center” and the “National Science Foundation,” and the paper declares “Declaration of Competing Interest None.”
section2_comments: The main article reports a UNOS dataset of “103,570 heart transplant events,” but because censoring was applied separately at each time point, the effective sample size varies by prediction horizon. The paper does not report an overall mean age, female proportion, or race/ethnicity summary in the retrieved main-text tables/figures. Clinical history and transplant factors were included among the 494 variables and engineered features used for modeling.
section3_comments: Stage I examined seven algorithms: “LR, LDA, ANN, CART, SVM, RF and XGB,” along with variable selection methods including “fast feature selection, LASSO, and random forests,” and the paper reports holdout performance for the “UP-LASSO-logistic regression implementation.” Stage II applied isotonic regression to calibrate survival probabilities over month 1 and years 1–10 so they are monotonically decreasing. Figure 3 summarizes this workflow. The framework used internal training/holdout evaluation plus 5-fold cross-validation for model selection.
section4_comments: Missing data were handled through a structured cleaning strategy rather than a single standard method: variables with high missingness were removed, and the authors compared models with no imputation versus median/mode imputation; categorical missingness could also be imputed as “unknown.” Class imbalance was explicitly addressed with several subsampling methods: “none, DOWN, UP, SMOTE and ROSE.” Data preprocessing was described in detail, including removal of intra/post-transplant variables, censoring rules, engineered features, regrouping categorical levels, and encoding choices. Code availability was stronger than a simple yes/no because the paper states that “our code, analysis and results are detailed in an R Markdown document” and also provides a public web app; however, algorithm weights were not reported. Exact training/test N for the selected final model at each time point were not provided in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The target outcome was multi-period post-transplant survival probability at month 1 and years 1–10 rather than a single fixed endpoint. Table 4 reports holdout performance for the selected UP-LASSO-logistic regression model: AUC rose from 0.608 at month 1 to 0.702 at year 10; year-10 accuracy was 0.627, sensitivity 0.752, and specificity 0.533. Figure 7 presents observed-versus-forecast survival probabilities after isotonic regression, so calibration was reported graphically. Table 5 shows isotonic regression slightly improved AUC at all time points. No PPV, NPV, F1-score, or DCA were reported. Since the prompt asks for the test/validation set, I used the holdout results from Table 4; the single numeric AUC field here is the year-10 holdout AUC of 0.702, while the article reports a range across time points.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used a large national UNOS registry with 103,570 heart transplant events, which lowers single-center selection bias, although censoring varied by time point.
qa_predictors_quotes: The authors intentionally removed intra- and post-transplant variables in the main prediction framework, keeping a pre-operative decision-support orientation, and also engineered clinically motivated donor-recipient features.
qa_outcome_quotes: The survival outcome at each time point was explicitly coded using G-TIME and G-STATUS, with censoring rules clearly described for whether the recipient was alive or dead at the time point of interest.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include extensive preprocessing, class-imbalance handling, multiple algorithms, cross-validation, holdout testing, and post hoc monotonic calibration; however, the very large analytic design space and time-point-specific censoring introduce complexity and possible instability, and exact final training/test sample sizes per horizon were not clearly reported in the retrieved text.
qa_applicability_quotes: This article directly concerns AI/ML for heart transplant outcome prediction using donor-recipient pre-operative variables and is highly aligned with the review question.

study_id: 41_Raji and Safna - 2022 - Computational methods for predicting the outcome of thoracic transplantation

algorithm_name: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with back-propagation; Radial Basis Function (RBF) network
section1_comments: The study states that data were collected from the “United Network for Organ Sharing database,” so the source is a U.S. national registry. Mean age, sex distribution, and race/ethnicity were not reported for the final 485-case dataset.
section3_comments: The paper’s main proposed model is the “multi-layer perceptron algorithm,” and it also implemented “the Radial Basis Function Network model to prove the accuracy of proposed model.” Inputs were donor, recipient, and transplantation tabular variables selected from UNOS using InfoGain Attribute Eval with ranker search. The comparison was against an earlier published computational system rather than a clinical guideline or human reader. The paper discusses “validation” but the retrieved text does not clearly describe a standard split or CV protocol, so I classify validation as Other rather than guessing. No SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or explicit hyperparameter tuning was reported.
section4_comments: Data preprocessing was described extensively: multi-organ records were filtered to thoracic transplantation, pediatric records were removed, relevant attributes were selected, and InfoGain-based ranking reduced the feature space to 24 inputs. However, the retrieved text does not describe a missing-data method, class-imbalance handling, public code release, or explicit train/test counts. Because those details were not reported clearly, I left them as NR/No rather than inferring them.
section5_comments: The study outcome was graft/survival status after thoracic transplantation, represented by GRF_STAT, but the exact clinical horizon was not clearly specified in the retrieved text, so the safest category is Other. AUC/C-statistic, PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.

qa_predictors_quotes: The included predictors are clinically plausible donor, recipient, and transplant variables, but several choices are not well justified clinically and one top-ranked variable was recipient sex, suggesting possible dataset-driven instability.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcome variable was GRF_STAT, with “N” indicating graft failure and “Y” success, but the paper does not clearly define the exact time horizon for this success/failure endpoint in the retrieved text.
qa_analysis_quotes: The reported accuracy is very high, but the retrieved text does not clearly document dataset split strategy, external validation, calibration, or robust modern reporting standards, which creates substantial risk of optimistic performance estimation.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study is directly about computational prediction after thoracic transplantation and uses UNOS data, but it mixes broad “thoracic transplantation” terminology with heart-focused background and does not clearly define a heart-only or lung-only clinically interpretable cohort.

study_id: 42_Rodriguez et al. - 2022 - A Framework for Using Real-World Data and Health Outcomes Modeling to Evaluate Machine Learning-Base
study_metadata:
A Framework for Using Real-World Data and Health Outcomes Modeling to Evaluate Machine Learning-Based Risk Prediction Models
Rodriguez, P. J. et al.
Value Health / 2022
algorithm_name: Super learner ensemble ML model for 2-year mortality; patient-level microsimulation framework
section1_comments: The real-world cohort came from the “Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry” linked to UNOS data, and the cohort was followed “until December 31, 2016,” with simulation starting January 1, 2012. I did not identify an explicit funding or conflict-of-interest statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The patient-level simulation used the “40% validation set (n = 4247).” The retrieved text does not report a cohort-wide mean age or sex percentage for this validation sample. Clinical history and longitudinal disease data were included through repeated encounter-level CFFPR variables, including lung function, contraindications, visit history, waitlist status, and transplant outcomes. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The ML referral policy used a previously developed “super learner, an ensemble ML approach that optimally combined multiple underlying models (lasso, elastic net, ridge, XGboost, random forest, and support vector machine).” It was compared against referral based on FEV1 and usual care. The 40% validation set was used for the simulation, so internal split is the best validation label. The paper focuses on downstream clinical utility rather than interpretability, and I did not find a clear feature-selection or hyperparameter-tuning description in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The cohort of 10,615 adults was previously split into training (60%) and validation (40%) sets; this corresponds to about 6,368 training and 4,247 validation/test patients. The paper describes imputation of missing ABO and LAS-related variables and synthetic extension of trajectories, and explicitly uses “multiple imputation by chained equations” for some modeled quantities, so multiple imputation is the best fit. I did not find any class-imbalance strategy or code-release statement.
section5_comments: The modeled clinical decision was lung-transplant referral, and the downstream patient outcome was 5-year survival under different referral policies; because this does not map neatly to the preset categories, the best label is Other. The ML model’s baseline AUROC for 2-year mortality was 0.914 versus 0.876 for FEV1. Calibration is discussed because the paper states that the ML model had “better calibration than FEV1.” The paper’s main outcome results were survival and referral consequences in simulation rather than standard test-set accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1. DCA was not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used a large national CFF registry linked to UNOS, covering a substantial proportion of the U.S. cystic fibrosis population, which reduces major center-level selection bias.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were longitudinal real-world clinical variables collected at repeated encounters and used dynamically over time, which closely matches intended clinical use.
qa_outcome_quotes: Outcomes were clearly defined, including referral, transplant, pretransplant death, post-transplant death, and 5-year overall survival, with explicit state transitions in the microsimulation model.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include linked real-world registries, dynamic decision modeling, patient-level microsimulation, and explicit accounting for organ supply and heterogenous treatment effects. Uncertainty remains because many downstream effects were simulated rather than directly observed, and results depend on structural assumptions such as organ allocation and post-transplant survival modeling.
qa_applicability_quotes: Although the paper is highly relevant to lung transplantation and ML-based referral decisions, the population is adults with cystic fibrosis rather than a general thoracic transplant candidate population, and the article is mainly a methodological framework rather than a standard transplant prediction-model development paper.

study_metadata:

algorithm_name: InsighTx; eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
section1_comments: The study used EVLP data “collected in our center over the past decade,” specifically from the Toronto Lung Transplant Program/University Health Network, Toronto, Canada, with cases spanning “2008 to 2022.” I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The cohort included “n = 725 eligible clinical EVLP cases.” From Table 1, donor mean age was 45, 48, and 47 years across the three cohorts, which is approximately 46 overall. Male sex was 65%, 64%, and 64% across cohorts, implying about 35% female overall. This is an organ-assessment cohort rather than a recipient cohort. Race/ethnicity and comorbidity history were not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The paper states that the authors “evaluated eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)” and developed “our ML model, termed InsighTx,” using donor features plus biological, physiological, and biochemical EVLP assessments. The model was then examined in a retrospective blinded implementation study involving EVLP specialists, so human expert is the best comparator. Because the development cohort preceded two later consecutive validation cohorts, external temporal is the best validation category. SHAP importance values were explicitly used to assess feature importance. The retrieved text does not describe a separate feature-selection stage or explicit hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: The development dataset contained 504 EVLP cases, and the two independent temporal validation cohorts contained 97 and 124 cases, totaling 221 test cases. Data preprocessing is described at a high level through donor plus EVLP biological/physiological/biochemical feature extraction and temporal cohort separation. I did not find a clear missing-data strategy, class-imbalance method, or code-availability statement in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The model predicted EVLP suitability and post-transplant duration of mechanical ventilation; within the extraction framework, the closest postoperative adverse-outcome category is PGD because the paper also linked predictions to PGD grade 3 at 72 h. For the overall model, the best held-out AUROC was 85 ± 3% in test dataset 2. For unsuitable lungs, AUROC reached 95 ± 2%, and for extubation <72 h it reached 83 ± 4%. The paper reports model precision of 81% for identifying any unsuitable donor lung and 72% for suitable donor lungs. For donor lungs predicted to have extubation <72 h, the NPV for PGD grade 3 at 72 h was 88%. Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: This is the largest clinical EVLP cohort reported, but it comes from a single expert center, which may limit generalizability to other EVLP programs.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were rich EVLP biological, physiological, and biochemical features collected longitudinally during standardized ex vivo assessment, and SHAP-based importance was examined.
qa_outcome_quotes: Outcomes were clearly defined as three clinically meaningful categories after EVLP—extubation <72 h, extubation ≥72 h, and declined for transplant—with additional linkage to PGD grade 3 at 72 h.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include a sizable development cohort, two consecutive temporal test cohorts, and blinded implementation analysis. Uncertainty remains because the retrieved text does not clearly describe missing-data handling, hyperparameter tuning, or multicenter external validation.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly studies ML-guided assessment of donor lungs during EVLP and its relationship to post-transplant outcomes and organ utilization, which is highly relevant to thoracic transplantation AI.

study_id: 44_Seraphin-2023-Prediction of heart transplant r

The ground truth came from “two expert pathologists… grading the degree of rejection in consensus,” so human expert is the best comparator. Validation included hold-out and separate cohorts from other German centers, so external geographic is the strongest label. Interpretability came from attention maps and Grad-CAM visualizations. The paper reports optimizer choice, learning-rate finding, early stopping, and training settings, which count as hyperparameter/training-procedure reporting.
section4_comments: Only samples “with information on ISHLT grading” were eligible, which is most consistent with complete-case inclusion. The primary training cohort had 393 slides, and the three validation cohorts had 356, 189, and 141 slides, totaling 686 test slides. The paper describes digitization, tessellation, patch extraction, feature extraction, bag construction, and training procedures. No class-imbalance correction was described. The code repositories for preprocessing and deep learning are explicitly provided, satisfying code availability. The retrieved text did not explicitly mention released trained weights, but the available option set requires one of the listed labels; code availability is clearly affirmative.
section5_comments: The target was cellular cardiac allograft rejection on endomyocardial biopsy, which fits Acute Rejection. In cross-validation, the binary rejection yes/no AUROC was 0.849. External AUROCs were 0.734, 0.729, and 0.716. For multiclass ISHLT grades, the cross-validated AUROCs were 0.835 for 0R, 0.633 for 1R, and 0.905 for 2/3R. qa_participants_quotes: This was a multicentre retrospective series with external validation, which is a strength, but cohort sizes were still modest and selected from archived biopsies with available ISHLT grading.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were routine H&E pathology whole-slide images from endomyocardial biopsies, processed in a standardized digital workflow.
qa_outcome_quotes: Ground truth labels were assigned by “two expert pathologists… in consensus, following the 2004 revision of the ISHLT grading system.”
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include repeated three-fold cross-validation, three external validation cohorts, comparison with CRANE, bootstrapped confidence intervals, and code availability. Remaining limitations are mainly sample size and reduced external performance, not major analytic flaws.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly addresses AI-based detection of heart-transplant rejection from pathology and is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 46_Shou et al. - 2022 - Pre-operative Machine Learning for Heart Transplant Patients Bridged with Temporary Mechanical Circu
study_metadata:

SHAP was explicitly used for interpretation, and a grid search optimized hyperparameters. Forty-three predictors were “automatically selected for inclusion in the final XGBoost model based on predictive utility.”
section4_comments: The paper states that missing values “were automatically imputed on a case-by-case basis in the XGBoost model,” which best fits algorithm handles natively. Class imbalance was addressed by setting scale_pos_weight = 7.8. Preprocessing included manual removal of post-transplant-only variables, one-hot encoding of categorical variables, numerical treatment of continuous/ordinal variables, and grid search tuning. The development and validation cohorts included 1,267 and 317 patients, respectively. No code-release statement was reported.
section5_comments: The primary endpoint was “1-year post-transplant mortality,” which maps to 1-year survival in this extraction framework. The XGBoost model achieved “an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.62–0.78).” Although an AUCPR of 0.357 was reported, the paper did not provide explicit held-out accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1 values in the retrieved text. Calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: This was a national UNOS cohort of adult isolated first-time heart-transplant recipients bridged with tMCS, reducing single-center selection bias, though it is limited to a specific high-risk subgroup.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were restricted to variables available “at or before the time of transplantation,” which is appropriate for pre-operative risk modeling.
qa_outcome_quotes: The primary outcome was clearly defined as “1-year post-transplant mortality.”
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include national data, train/test split, hyperparameter tuning, imbalance adjustment, SHAP-based interpretation, and bootstrap CIs. Uncertainty remains because validation was internal only and calibration was not reported.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly addresses ML-based outcome prediction in heart transplantation, specifically a clinically important tMCS bridge-to-transplant subgroup.

study_id: 45_Shaw et al. - 2023 - Multicenter analysis of immunosuppressive medications on the risk of malignancy following adult soli
study_metadata:
Multicenter analysis of immunosuppressive medications on the risk of malignancy following adult solid organ transplantation
Shaw, R. et al.
Front Oncol / 2023
algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: This was a “retrospective cohort study from a multicenter hospital system in the United States,” using EHR data from three hospitals in the greater Chicago area queried “from January 1, 2000, to March 10, 2021.” Because it spans all adult solid organ transplants rather than a single thoracic organ, organ focus is best classified as Other. I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study identified “5,591 unique patients” and “6,142 transplanted organs.” The median age of transplant recipients was 54 years, but no overall mean age was reported. “Overall, 39% of transplant recipients were women.” Race was reported, including White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, and other groups. Clinical history variables included organ type, age, sex, race, and longitudinal immunosuppressive exposure.
section3_comments: The primary study aim was epidemiologic risk assessment using time-dependent Cox models, with ML used as a complementary variable-importance analysis, so Primary ML Component is best classified as Other. The authors state that “a random forest model was used to assess variable importance in predicting post-transplant malignancy.” Categorical variables under 10% frequency were grouped, variables were one-hot encoded or normalized, and the model was “fit across a variety of hyperparameters within a Latin hypercube of size 25.” No human comparator or guideline comparator was used. Validation specifics for prediction performance were not reported.
section4_comments: The paper describes preprocessing: low-frequency categories were grouped, nominal variables were one-hot encoded, numerical variables were normalized, and the dataset was “bootstrap resampled 10 times and stratified by the outcome.” This stratified bootstrap handling is best categorized as Other for class imbalance rather than a standard reweighting method. Missing-data handling was not clearly reported. The paper states that “the complete analysis code is available” on GitHub, so code availability is affirmative under the available labels. No fixed train/test split sizes were reported.
section5_comments: The study outcome was post-transplant malignancy, which is not one of the preset transplant endpoints, so the best category is Other. The paper reports hazard ratios rather than standard predictive discrimination metrics: sirolimus HR 1.41, azathioprine HR 2.1, cyclosporine HR 1.59, and tacrolimus HR 0.59 for post-transplant malignancy. No AUC, accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, calibration, or DCA were reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_quotes: This was a multicenter cohort, which improves representativeness, but it was limited to three hospitals in the greater Chicago area and relied on retrospective ICD/EHR ascertainment.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were clearly defined EHR-derived exposures and demographics, especially time-dependent immunosuppressive medication use, age, sex, race, and organ type.
qa_outcome_quotes: Malignancies were identified using ICD-9/10 codes, which is practical but introduces some risk of misclassification compared with adjudicated cancer registries.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include time-dependent Cox modeling, competing-risk analysis, and complementary random forest variable-importance assessment. Limitations acknowledged by the authors include retrospective design, potential under-ascertainment outside the hospital system, modest sample size relative to national databases, and lack of dose/plasma-level adjustment for immunosuppressants.
qa_applicability_quotes: Although the paper includes heart and lung recipients, it is a broad solid-organ oncology/immunosuppression study rather than a thoracic-transplant-specific AI prediction study, so applicability to the thoracic AI review question is limited.

algorithm_name: 3-D U-Net–based CT segmentation with multivariate logistic regression for DCC prediction

The actual DCC prediction model was a multivariate logistic regression using preoperative features, with backward stepwise elimination and stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Continuous features were z-score standardized, categorical variables were one-hot encoded, and VIF filtering plus backward elimination were applied. The model used stratified 5-fold cross-validation rather than a single explicit train/test split, so fixed training/test counts are NR. No class-imbalance method or code-release statement was reported.
section5_comments: The modeled outcome was DCC occurrence, which is best categorized as Adverse Events within the restricted list. qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were clinically relevant preoperative variables plus objectively derived CT volumetric measures from validated CNN algorithms.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcome, DCC vs PCC, was clearly defined intraoperatively, and survival outcomes were assessed with Kaplan–Meier analysis at prespecified time points.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include CT-derived quantitative metrics, cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and multivariable modeling; uncertainty remains because of the small sample size, single-center design, and lack of external validation.
qa_applicability_quotes: The paper directly concerns lung transplantation, uses deep-learning-derived CT measurements, and addresses a clinically meaningful perioperative transplant outcome.

section4_comments: Clinical features with “missing values, lack of variance, or unreadable data were excluded,” which best fits complete-case/exclusion-based handling rather than imputation. study_id: 04_Ayers et al. - 2021 - Using machine learning to improve survival prediction after heart transplantation
study_metadata:
Using machine learning to improve survival prediction after heart transplantation
Ayers, B. et al.
J Card Surg / 2021
algorithm_name: Final ensemble ML model combining deep neural network, logistic regression, AdaBoost, and random forest
section1_comments: The study used the “United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry” and included adult patients undergoing OHT “between 2000 and 2019.” A disclosures section was present, listing industry relationships for several authors, so COI was declared. I did not identify a funding statement in the retrieved article text, so funding is marked Not Reported.
section2_comments: The study included “33,657 OHT patients,” and “the majority of study participants were male (75%) with an average age of 52.8 ± 12.4 years,” implying female sex 25%. Table 1 reports race as White 70% and includes multiple clinical-history/support variables such as prior cardiac surgery, dialysis, ventilator, ICU, inotropes, ECMO, IABP, LVAD/RVAD/TAH, bilirubin, creatinine, and waitlist time.
section3_comments: The paper describes a “retrospective study” using UNOS data with patients split into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets. The final model was an ensemble of four algorithm classes: deep neural network, logistic regression, AdaBoost, and random forest, built from 400 total models. Inputs were preoperative donor and recipient registry variables. The main explicit comparator in reported results was a “singular logistic regression,” which best fits the review option of a linear risk-score comparator rather than human expert/guideline. Feature selection combined clinician review and random-forest importance, producing 47 final variables. The paper does not describe SHAP/LIME-style explainability or an explicit hyperparameter-tuning process.
section4_comments: Missing continuous data were imputed with the median and categorical data with the mode. Class imbalance was addressed using “over-sampling (SVM Smote) and under-sampling (Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbors).” Preprocessing was clearly described, including exclusion of non-preoperative variables, clinician review, grouping sparse categories, one-hot encoding, and standardization of continuous variables. The paper states models were trained in Python using Keras/Tensorflow but does not provide code release, so code availability is No. Table 1 gives training n=26,926 and validation n=6,731.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “1-year post-transplant survival,” with 1-year mortality 11% (n=3738). In the validation cohort, AUROCs were 0.649 for logistic regression, 0.691 for random forest, 0.691 for deep neural network, 0.653 for AdaBoost, and 0.764 for the final ensemble ML model. The ensemble improved predictive performance by 72.9% ± 3.8% by NRI and had better DCA across the full risk spectrum. Calibration was evaluated visually by plotting predicted versus observed risk by decile. The paper did not report accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1-score numerically in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used a large national UNOS registry cohort of 33,657 patients, which reduces single-center selection bias, although exclusions for prior transplant, multiorgan transplant, age <18, and incomplete 1-year survival were applied.
qa_predictors_quotes: The authors explicitly excluded variables that “would not be available in the preoperative setting,” which supports appropriate predictor timing for clinical use.
qa_outcome_quotes: The primary outcome was clearly defined as “1-year post-transplant survival,” and Figure 1 classified patients as alive vs dead at one year.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include a separate validation cohort, resampling for imbalance, multiple algorithms, AUROC/NRI/DCA evaluation, and calibration assessment. However, there was no external validation cohort, and the authors acknowledge this as a limitation.
qa_applicability_quotes: This article directly studies machine learning for heart-transplant survival prediction using donor-recipient preoperative variables, matching the review question closely.

study_id: 05_Barbosa et al. - 2018 - Machine Learning Algorithms Utilizing Quantitative CT Features May Predict Eventual Onset of Bronchi
study_metadata:
Machine Learning Algorithms Utilizing Quantitative CT Features May Predict Eventual Onset of Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome After Lung Transplantation
Barbosa, E. J. M. et al.
Acad Radiol / 2018
algorithm_name: Support vector machine with radial basis function kernel
section1_comments: The patient cohort came from a local IRB-approved retrospective study and the lead academic clinical site was the University of Pennsylvania; the article states that data were selected retrospectively and transferred “to an outside facility for computational imaging analysis,” which supports a single-center clinical source with external image processing. I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved article text. Calendar study years were not reported; only follow-up intervals after transplant were provided.
section2_comments: Table 1 states there were 71 subjects total, with 41 BOS and 30 non-BOS, and the text reports 53 men and 18 women with mean age 57 years. Female sex is therefore 18/71 = 25.4%. Race/ethnicity was not reported. Clinical background was reported through pretransplant diagnoses including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, cystic fibrosis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and other.
section3_comments: The article explicitly says the scans were analyzed retrospectively and that “supervised ML with support vector machines (SVMs) was used.” The model used significant qCT features derived from Student t tests, and a “radial basis functional kernel with default tuning parameters was used.” Inputs were qCT/FRI imaging features from paired inspiratory-expiratory CT scans. The main comparator was not another clinical model but rather baseline clinical/PFT variables, which the paper states could not significantly distinguish BOS from non-BOS at baseline. Validation used repeated random train-test partitions (90/10 for 1D and 2D, 80/20 for 3D), so “Other” is the most exact category.
section4_comments: For the baseline prediction cohort, “patients with missing values for certain regional parameters… were not included,” which is best classified as complete case analysis. Class imbalance handling such as weighting, oversampling, or SMOTE was not reported. Data preprocessing was described extensively: CT segmentation, central/distal airway definitions, lung/lobar volume extraction, and computational fluid dynamics-based resistance calculation. The paper reports train-test ratios, but because the absolute sample counts vary across repeated random partitions and dimensions, exact training and test N are NR. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: The clinical outcome was eventual BOS after lung transplant, which is the obstructive phenotype of chronic lung allograft dysfunction, so the closest restricted category is CLAD. Table 5 reports the best 3-feature SVM classification accuracy as 85%, using RML lobe volume at TLC, RUL airway resistance at FRC, and central airway surface at FRC. One-feature accuracy reached 76%, and the best two-feature model reached 83%. The paper did not report AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA. Figure 7 summarized significant baseline qCT predictors, and Figure 8 showed that baseline FEV1 and FEV1 percent predicted were not significant predictors of future BOS.
qa_participants_quotes: This was a small retrospective cohort of 71 patients selected using several imaging and data-availability criteria, and only 41 patients were eligible for the baseline prediction analysis because incomplete datasets were excluded.

Tian, D. et al.
JAMA Netw Open / 2023
algorithm_name: Random Survival Forests (RSF)
section1_comments: The study was conducted at Wuxi People’s Hospital and included patients who underwent LTx “between January 2017 and December 2020,” making this an Asian single-center lung-transplant cohort. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study included “504 patients,” with mean age 55.56 years; 334 were male (66.3%), implying 33.7% female. Race/ethnicity was not reported. Clinical/history variables included diagnosis, BMI, PGD3 at 72 h, ECMO type, preoperative hormone use, multidrug-resistant bacterial infection, operative variables, donor oxygenation, and pulmonary function indices.
section3_comments: The paper developed an “RSF model” for overall survival and used a Cox regression model as the benchmark comparator. Patients were randomly assigned to training and test sets at a 7:3 ratio. Feature selection used RSF variable importance with bootstrapping, and “grid search” was used for hyperparameter tuning. No SHAP/LIME-type interpretability was reported.
section4_comments: The methods state that missing data were handled “by multiple imputation by chained equations.” The training and test sets included 353 and 151 patients, respectively. Data preprocessing included random split, feature selection by bootstrapped variable importance, and hold-out validation. Class imbalance is not especially applicable for time-to-event survival modeling. No code-release statement was identified.
section5_comments: The primary endpoint was overall survival after lung transplantation, which does not map exactly to the preset time-specific labels, so Other is the safest category. In the test set, the RSF model had iAUC 0.879 and iBS 0.130 for OS prediction. For 1-year survival, the RSF had tAUC 0.921 and PE 0.115, with sensitivity 88.7%, specificity 79.6%, and accuracy 82.8%. Calibration was reported through iBS/PE and observed-vs-predicted agreement. DCA was not reported.

I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: A total of 381 recipients were analyzed. The median age was reported as 57 years, not mean age, so mean age is NR. Sex distribution was 137 female and 244 male, so female sex was 36.0%. Race/ethnicity was not reported. Clinical/history variables included diagnosis, BMI, ECMO type, hormone use, 72 h PGD3, ventilator time, ICU stay, cold ischemia time, and postoperative 6MWT.
section3_comments: The paper states that 7 feature-selection methods and 8 algorithms were combined to build 56 ML models. The “optimal ML model was the model fitted using a random forest algorithm with a determination coefficient feature selection method.” The comparator was a conventional logistic regression model derived from independent risk factors, so Other fits best. Internal validation was by bootstrap with 1000 resamples rather than a standard split or cross-validation, so Validation Method is Other. No SHAP/LIME-type interpretability or explicit hyperparameter-tuning description was reported in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The study excluded patients with incomplete clinical records and used bootstrap internal validation; no imputation strategy was described in the retrieved text, so this is best classified as complete-case analysis. I did not find any class-imbalance method, code-release statement, or detailed normalization/preprocessing workflow beyond variable extraction and feature-selection strategy. There was no explicit train/test split.
section5_comments: The target outcome was AS requiring clinical intervention, which best fits Adverse Events within the allowed labels. The optimal random-forest model had AUC 0.760 and Brier score 0.085. It also had sensitivity 0.782, specificity 0.689, PPV 0.252, and NPV 0.965. Calibration was reported using the Brier score. The authors also created an online web-server, but I did not see public source code or weights, so code availability is best marked Other.
section5_comments: The outcome was prolonged ICU length of stay, defined using the 75th percentile threshold of 9.08 days, so the best category is Economy/Length of Stay. section1_comments: The main dataset came from the “International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) registry” with patients registered “from June 2009 to June 2018,” and 45 centers worldwide had submitted data, so this is a multinational international-registry study. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study included “29,364 patients,” with average age 53.4 ± 13.4 years; 17,032 were male (58%), implying 42.0% female. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text. Clinical history included diabetes, malignancy history, ventilator use, ECMO use, dialysis, prior surgeries, chronic steroid use, tracheostomy, pulmonary embolism, albumin, bilirubin, creatinine, BMI, and diagnosis categories.
section3_comments: The authors employed six machine-learning models, and “the GBM model achieved the highest performance.” Inputs were 25 pretransplant tabular variables from the ISHLT registry, later reduced to the top 10 using SHAP importance. External validation was performed with an in-house hospital dataset, so external geographic validation is the strongest applicable label. SHAP was explicitly used for interpretation. The text states “Default model settings were applied without additional hyperparameter tuning.”
section4_comments: The paper states that variables with >20% missingness were removed and “patient samples with any missing data were excluded,” which is complete-case analysis. Class imbalance was addressed using class-weight adjustments for LR, RF, SVM, and BRF. Preprocessing included exclusion criteria, feature screening, five-fold cross-validation, and SHAP-based refinement. Because the internal validation used five-fold cross-validation rather than a fixed split, training and test N are NR. No code-release statement was identified.
section5_comments: The target was explicitly 1-year mortality after lung transplantation, which maps to 1-year survival in this extraction framework. With the top-10-feature model, GBM had AUC 0.958 and accuracy 0.949, with sensitivity 0.755, specificity 0.986, PPV 0.914, and NPV 0.955. The same internal performance was reported for the 25-feature GBM model. External validation showed GBM AUC 0.852/accuracy 0.764, while MLP generalized best with AUC 0.911/accuracy 0.870. Calibration and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.

study_metadata:
Personalized survival predictions via Trees of Predictors: An application to cardiac transplantation
Yoon, J. et al.
PLoS One / 2018
algorithm_name: Trees of Predictors (ToPs / ToPs-R)
section1_comments: The study used the “United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database” of patients registered for heart transplantation in the United States “during 1985–2015.” Funding was reported from the Office of Naval Research and the National Science Foundation, so Government/Public is appropriate. The paper explicitly states that the authors “have declared that no competing interests exist.”
section2_comments: After excluding patients younger than 18 years, the study included “51,971 transplanted patients and 30,911 wait-listed patients,” totaling 82,882 adult candidates/recipients. Because the paper analyzes both pre-transplant wait-list and post-transplant cohorts, Other is the safest target-population label. Mean age and overall female percentage were not reported in the retrieved text. The dataset included many clinical features relating to recipients, donors, and donor-recipient compatibility.
section3_comments: The paper developed “ToPs: Trees of Predictors,” an interpretable method that clusters patients and assigns different predictive models to different clusters. Inputs were tabular recipient, donor, and compatibility variables from UNOS. The main comparators were existing clinical risk scores such as DRI, RSS, and IMPACT, so Linear Risk Score is the closest label. Validation used 5-fold cross-validation. Explainability was intrinsic through the tree structure and cluster-specific relevant features, even though SHAP/LIME was not used. Feature selection was automated by excluding features with high missingness and then learning predictive clusters and relevant covariates from the data. Explicit hyperparameter tuning was not described in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: Missing feature components were handled using “10 multiple imputations using Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE).” Preprocessing included exclusion of post-transplant-only variables, removal of features with >10% missingness, binarization of categorical variables, and 5-fold cross-validation. Since the design used cross-validation on large cohorts rather than a single fixed split, training and test N are NR. Class imbalance is not especially applicable for these survival-prediction settings as reported here. I did not identify a code-release statement.
section5_comments: The study predicted survival across multiple time horizons both post-transplant and pre-transplant, so no single preset outcome label fits perfectly; Other is safest. For post-transplant 3-month survival, ToPs/R achieved AUC 0.660, compared with 0.587 for the best clinical risk score (RSS). The paper also reports post-transplant AUCs of 0.641, 0.623, and 0.631 at 1 year, 3 years, and 10 years, respectively, and average C-index 0.577. Calibration was reported through calibration curves with 95% confidence bounds. DCA was not reported. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported in the retrieved text.

section2_comments: The final table consisted of “30,917 individuals,” among whom 25% developed malignancy after lung transplantation. Figure 2 shows a demographic snapshot with 43% female and 57% male. Ethnicity was explicitly shown in Figure 2, and the paper describes recipient/donor demographics, HLA antigens, CMV, albumin, BMI, survival, hospital length of stay, and complications as included variables. Mean age was not explicitly reported in the retrieved text, only the age distribution histogram.
section3_comments: The study developed several supervised models, including decision trees, logistic regression, neural networks, gradient boosting, random forest, and SVM, and reported gradient boosting as best-performing. Inputs came from merged STAR sources including waitlist, transplant, donor, and follow-up datasets, which are tabular recipient/donor variables. The data were split into 70% training and 30% validation/testing. Variable review by lung-transplant experts excluded irrelevant, redundant, and highly missing variables, so Manual/Clinical is the best fit for feature selection. The paper explicitly describes setting/tuning key parameters for gradient boosting and random forest.
section4_comments: The paper states that experts excluded variables with “a high percentage of unacceptable missing values (>30%),” rather than using a standard imputation method in the retrieved text, so Other is the best fit. Because of class imbalance, “oversampling was employed to increase the percentage of the minority class by replicating instances from the minority class.” Preprocessing included merging multiple STAR sources, restricting to lung transplants, excluding prior malignancy and loss to follow-up, and removing 173 variables. A 70/30 split on 30,917 cases corresponds to about 21,642 training and 9,275 test/validation cases. No code-release statement was identified.
section5_comments: The endpoint was de novo malignancy after lung transplantation, which best fits Adverse Events among the allowed categories. The abstract states that gradient boosting “outperformed all other predictive models… achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.746.” Although the methods discuss accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and related metrics, the retrieved text snippet does not provide final numeric values for those measures, so I leave them NR. algorithm_name: Cox-Lasso regression; comparison with Cox regression with backward elimination and random forest Cox; Lung Transplantation Advanced Prediction Tool (LAPT)
section1_comments: The study used the United Network for Organ Sharing Registry and included eligible double lung transplants from “January 2005 and March 2020,” so this is a U.S. national-registry lung-transplant study. Funding was explicitly stated as “NIH 1R01HL147957-01.” I did not identify an explicit COI statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The final analytic cohort included 15,124 double lung transplants. Recipient age was reported as median 57 years rather than mean, so mean age is NR. Female recipients comprised 42.7% in the derivation cohort and 41.4% in the validation cohort, which is about 42.3% overall. Race/ethnicity and multiple clinical-history variables were reported, including diagnosis, functional status, eGFR, albumin, tobacco, steroid use, ECMO, ventilation, CMV, and donor factors.
section3_comments: The main predictive model was Cox-Lasso, compared with backward-elimination Cox and random-forest Cox. Inputs included recipient, donor, and transplant characteristics from UNOS. The cohort was randomly split into derivation and validation sets, so Internal Split fits best. Variable selection was automated using the Lasso method, and the optimal lambda was selected to balance overfitting and simplicity. I did not see SHAP/LIME-type interpretability; interpretability came through the explicit risk score and cluster assignment.
section4_comments: The paper states that records with a single missing point were imputed and that “imputation of missing data for recipient and donor variables was conducted separately,” which best fits multiple imputation among the available categories. Preprocessing included exclusions, categorization of continuous variables, expectation-maximization clustering, and derivation/validation splitting. The derivation and validation cohorts were 10,660 and 4,464. I did not find a class-imbalance method. A web-based tool was released, but no public code repository was mentioned, so code availability is best classified as Other.
section5_comments: The model predicts 1-, 5-, and 10-year survival plus half-life. Since a single target must be chosen, 5-year survival is the most central medium-term endpoint and has an explicitly reported C statistic of 0.64; 1-year and 10-year C statistics were 0.67 and 0.72. Calibration was reported by showing that model-estimated survival probabilities were similar to observed survival in the validation cohort and by comparing Kaplan–Meier curves across derivation and validation cohorts. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1 were not reported. DCA was not reported.

study_id: 58_Peyster et al. - 2021 - An automated computational image analysis pipeline for histological grading of cardiac allograft rej
study_metadata:
An automated computational image analysis pipeline for histological grading of cardiac allograft rejection
Peyster, E. G. et al.
Eur Heart J / 2021
algorithm_name: CACHE-Grader (Computer-Assisted Cardiac Histologic Evaluation)
section1_comments: Multicentre US study (Univ. of Pennsylvania, Ohio State, Univ. Hospitals Cleveland). 2472 archived H&E-stained endomyocardial biopsy slides from 546 heart-transplant recipients, obtained as usual care 2005-2018 (surveillance and for-cause).
section2_comments: Adult heart-transplant recipients undergoing surveillance or for-cause endomyocardial biopsy. Cohort deliberately enriched for ISHLT grades 2R/3R (~20% vs ~8% in routine practice) to power assessment of high-grade rejection. 114 slides excluded at quality control (HistoQC).
section3_comments: CACHE-Grader: hand-crafted, biologically inspired feature extraction (stain deconvolution, K-means tissue segmentation, lymphocyte cluster/foci detection via proximity graphs) yielding 154 quantitative histological features; support vector machine classifiers for binary high-vs-low grade (M1, 2 features) and 4-grade classification (M2, 15 features).
section4_comments: Trained on 911 slides from Site I (UPenn). Internal validation 395 slides (Site I); external validation 1052 slides from Sites II and III. Composite validation set 1447 slides. Models locked before validation; no pipeline changes after training.
section5_comments: M1 (binary high vs low grade) in composite validation: AUC 0.92, agreement 84.5%, sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.84. M2 (4-grade) agreement 65.9%, near-identical internally vs externally (66.1% vs 65.8%). Non-inferior to study pathologists (62.6% vs 61.5% agreement); superior sensitivity for high-grade rejection (74.4% vs 39.5%). No confidence interval reported for the AUC.
qa_participants_quotes: Only EMBs that were deemed 'gradable' and assigned an ISHLT cellular rejection grade were included. By design, the full cohort contained a higher proportion of grades 2R/3R (20%) than is seen in routine practice (8%).
qa_participants_comments: Retrospective selection from archived slides, not reported as consecutive or random. Deliberate enrichment of high-grade rejection and exclusion of non-gradable slides make the class distribution and technical quality different from routine practice; 114 slides excluded after quality control.
qa_predictors_quotes: A set of 154 domain-inspired, hand-crafted, quantitative histological features were extracted from each study image. These features were subsequently 'locked down' into the final models which were deployed in the study validation set.
qa_predictors_comments: Candidate predictors were biologically motivated histological features measured from the biopsy image available at the time of grading. Feature selection was outcome-driven within the training set (Wilcoxon rank-sum / t-test) but the pipeline was locked before independent validation. No obvious predictor-outcome temporal leakage.
qa_outcome_quotes: The rejection grade assigned to each EMB by the pathologist of record in the medical chart was considered the reference standard. A representative subset of validation set slides underwent blinded re-grading by three independent study pathologists.
qa_outcome_comments: Outcome clearly defined as ISHLT cellular rejection grade, clinically established before model development, with independent blinded re-grading. The grade of record is an imperfect and variable reference standard rather than objective biological truth, but this does not by itself justify High Risk under the applied criteria.
qa_analysis_quotes: Model development and iterative calibration was conducted in a training subset of 911 randomly selected slides from Site I. The remaining 395 slides from Site I represented an internal validation set, while the 1052 slides from sites II and III represented two external validation sets.
qa_analysis_comments: Multicentre external validation is a major strength. However the unit of analysis was the slide, whereas 2472 slides came from only 546 recipients; the Site I split is not reported as recipient-level, creating plausible risk that biopsies from the same recipient appear in both sets. Repeated biopsies apparently analysed as independent observations with no patient-level clustering adjustment. Feature count and classifier choice optimised on training data; probabilistic calibration not reported. Missing-data handling not reported.
qa_applicability_quotes: This cohort consisted of 2472 archived transplant EMB histology slides, originating from 546 transplant recipients. These EMBs were obtained as part of usual care between 2005 and 2018, either as part of scheduled post-transplant surveillance or in a 'for-cause' setting.
qa_applicability_comments: Population, specimen type and target outcome directly represent routine post-heart-transplant cellular rejection grading, across three US centres with both surveillance and for-cause biopsies. Applicability somewhat reduced by grade enrichment, exclusion of technically inadequate slides, restriction to cellular rejection, and historical data (2005-2018).

study_id: 57_Zhou-2021-Prediction of 1-year mortality after

algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: The study included consecutive orthotopic heart-transplant recipients at a single institute in Wuhan, China, “between January 1st, 2015 and December 31st, 2018,” making this an Asian single-center heart-transplant cohort. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study reports that “381 recipients were included with average age of 43.783 years old.” Male recipients accounted for 76.2%, implying 23.8% female. Race/ethnicity was not reported. Clinical/history variables included hypertension, diabetes, chronic lung/liver/renal disease, malignancy, smoking history, donor factors, and multiple perioperative histories.
section3_comments: Seven machine-learning approaches were trained after LASSO feature selection. The best-performing model was random forest. Inputs were structured recipient and donor variables from electronic medical records. The data were randomly split 70%/30% into training and testing sets, and parameters were tuned using grid search with five-fold cross-validation. SHAP was explicitly used for model interpretation.
section4_comments: Variables with >10% missingness were discarded, and the remaining variables were imputed with column mean for continuous variables and the most frequent value for categorical variables, which is simple imputation. The dataset was randomly split 70%/30%, corresponding to about 267 training and 114 testing patients. I did not find any class-imbalance method or code-release statement.
section5_comments: The primary endpoint was “postoperative 1-year mortality,” which maps to 1-year survival in this extraction framework. Under bootstrap validation, the random forest model achieved the best AUC of 0.801, with accuracy 0.828, sensitivity 0.268, and specificity 0.927. GBM had slightly lower AUC 0.786 but the highest sensitivity 0.271. PPV/NPV were not reported numerically in the shown results tables, and calibration and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: This was a retrospective single-center cohort from one Chinese institution, which limits generalizability despite consecutive inclusion.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were routinely collected recipient and donor clinical variables available before or at transplantation and were screened systematically.
qa_outcome_quotes: The primary outcome was clearly defined as postoperative 1-year mortality, including in-hospital and 1-year follow-up mortality.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include 70/30 train-test splitting, LASSO selection, grid-search tuning with five-fold cross-validation, bootstrap validation, and SHAP interpretation. Uncertainty remains because the sample size was modest and sensitivity was poor across models.
qa_applicability_quotes: The article directly addresses machine-learning prediction of 1-year mortality after heart transplantation and is highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 10_Dalton-2023-Refining the Lung Allocation Score
study_metadata:
Refining the Lung Allocation Score Models Fails to Improve Discrimination Performance
Dalton, J. E. et al.
Chest / 2023
algorithm_name: WL-LAS/CAS, PT-CAS, re-estimated Cox models, cubic-spline Cox model, random survival forest, logistic model, linear discriminant analysis, gradient-boosted tree
section1_comments: The paper used “Scientific Registry for Transplant Recipients (SRTR) data from 2015-2020” for waitlist models and “data from 2010-2020” for post-transplant models. Because SRTR is the U.S. national transplant registry, this is a U.S. national registry study. I did not identify an explicit funding or conflict-of-interest statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The waitlist analysis included “13,204 candidates,” and the post-transplant analysis included “20,763 adult transplant recipients.” Table 1 reports female sex as 41% in the baseline waitlist cohort. Race/ethnicity was reported, and multiple clinical factors were included, such as diagnosis group, 6-minute walk distance, respiratory support, pulmonary arterial pressure, oxygen use, creatinine, BMI, bilirubin, insurance, and education. A single overall mean age for the full analytic cohorts was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The study compared seven models for each outcome: current LAS/CAS Cox models, updated Cox models, nonlinear spline-enhanced Cox models, random survival forests, logistic models, linear discriminant analysis, and gradient-boosted trees. The main comparators were the current LAS/CAS survival models, which are linear risk-score models. The data were “randomly partitioned into 10 training and test samples for cross-validation.” Predictors came from SRTR candidate/recipient tabular data available at allocation. The retrieved text did not report SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or explicit hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: The Methods state that the authors used “multiple imputation to account for missing predictor data,” and inverse probability-of-censoring weighting to address informative censoring due to transplant. They also describe reconciliation of relisted patients and construction of residual cohorts. The study used repeated cross-validation folds rather than one fixed train/test split, so exact training and test counts are NR. Code availability was not reported in the retrieved text. Class-imbalance handling was not described.
section5_comments: The primary outcomes were waitlist death or removal as too sick, and post-transplant death or retransplantation. For waitlist models, discrimination was strongest in the baseline cohort, with AUC about 0.92-0.93 at 1 month, declining to about 0.87-0.89 at 3 months and 0.84-0.85 at 6 months. For post-transplant models, discrimination remained poor across models, generally “0.58-0.61,” including at 1, 3, and 5 years. Figure 1 shows subgroup AUC patterns, especially worse variability among Medicaid patients. Because the paper centers on AUC/C-statistic-style discrimination across many models and time horizons rather than a single deployed model, and because the prompt asks for held-out test/validation metrics, I leave the single numeric AUC field as NR rather than choose one arbitrary value. Calibration and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used large national SRTR cohorts of waitlist candidates and transplant recipients in the United States, which reduces center-level selection bias, although exclusions for missing key variables were applied.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were derived from SRTR variables available at allocation or cohort time points, consistent with the clinical use case for LAS/CAS modeling.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcomes were clearly defined as time from waitlist placement to death or removal as too sick, and time from transplant to death or retransplantation.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths include TRIPOD-aligned internal validation, 10-fold cross-validation, multiple imputation, inverse probability-of-censoring weighting, and comparison of several model classes; however, only internal validation was performed and post-transplant discrimination remained poor across all models.
qa_applicability_quotes: This article directly evaluates machine-learning and alternative modeling approaches for lung transplant allocation-related prediction, making it highly relevant to the review question.

study_id: 58_Peyster et al. - 2021 - An automated computational image analysis pipeline for histological grading of cardiac allograft rej
study_metadata:
An automated computational image analysis pipeline for histological grading of cardiac allograft rejection
Peyster, E. G. et al.
Eur Heart J / 2021
algorithm_name: Computer-Assisted Cardiac Histologic Evaluation Grader (CACHE-Grader)
section1_comments: The study used archived endomyocardial-biopsy slides from the University of Pennsylvania, Ohio State University, and University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center. Biopsies were collected during routine care between 2005 and 2018. ehab241.pdf Funding was predominantly from several US federal agencies, including the NIH, NHLBI, NCI, and Department of Veterans Affairs, with additional support from the Gund Family Fund. ehab241.pdf Multiple authors declared patents, consultancies, equity holdings, licensing arrangements, advisory roles, or sponsored research relationships. ehab241.pdf
section2_comments: The clinical population comprised 546 heart-transplant recipients, contributing 2,472 archived biopsy slides; 2,358 slides passed quality control and entered model development or validation. The paper does not report recipient-level age, sex, race/ethnicity, or comorbidity distributions. The biopsies were obtained 7–6,415 days after transplantation during surveillance or for-cause assessment. ehab241.pdf Major uncertainty: For patient-level extraction, Total Sample Size = 546; for an image-level ML dataset field, the corresponding sample size is 2,472 slides before QC and 2,358 analysable slides after QC.
section3_comments: CACHE-Grader applied interpretable, biologically inspired, hand-crafted feature extraction to digitized H&E-stained endomyocardial-biopsy slides. From 154 quantitative histological features, the authors used outcome-based statistical ranking: Wilcoxon rank-sum selection for the binary model and t-test ranking for the four-grade model; final SVMs used 2 and 15 features, respectively. ehab241.pdf The models were locked after training and tested at two geographically separate external centres, with grades assigned by pathologists serving as the reference standard and independent pathologists used for comparative re-grading. ehab241.pdf Major uncertainty: The authors compared several linear classifiers and optimized the number of selected features, but conventional SVM hyperparameter tuning—such as kernel, C, or class-weight optimization—is not described; therefore, hyperparameter tuning is coded Not Reported rather than Yes.
section4_comments: The training cohort consisted of 911 slides randomly selected from UPenn.
