The complete held-out validation cohort contained 1,447 slides, comprising 395 internal-validation slides and 1,052 external-validation slides from OSU and UH. ehab241.pdf The investigators deliberately enriched the cohort with 2R/3R biopsies—approximately 20% versus 8% in routine practice—to provide adequate representation of clinically important high-grade rejection. ehab241.pdf Preprocessing included stain deconvolution, K-means tissue segmentation, focus detection, automated HistoQC assessment, and normalization of some features by tissue-compartment size. Source code was made publicly available. ehab241.pdf Major uncertainties: Class imbalance was addressed through dataset-level enrichment, not through reported SMOTE, weighted loss, cost-sensitive SVM training, or resampling within the training algorithm. The paper does not describe conventional missing-value imputation. Slides failing technical quality control were excluded, which is a QC-exclusion procedure rather than missing-data imputation. Test Size = 1447 refers to the composite held-out validation set. The strictly geographically external subset was 1,052 slides.
section5_comments: For the binary M1 classifier distinguishing low-grade rejection, 0R/1R, from high-grade rejection, 2R/3R, the composite held-out validation set produced an AUC of 0.92, accuracy/agreement of 84.5%, sensitivity of 85%, and specificity of 84%. ehab241.pdf The four-grade M2 classifier achieved 65.9% agreement overall, including 65.8% in the geographically external centres. ehab241.pdf Major uncertainties: The target is histological acute cellular rejection grade, not a patient-level future rejection event. PPV and NPV can be calculated from the published confusion matrix, but they were not explicitly reported as performance metrics and are therefore entered as NR. “Iterative calibration” in the methods describes iterative model/pipeline development; it is not evidence of statistical calibration assessment. No calibration curve, calibration slope/intercept, Brier score, or DCA was reported.
qa_participants_quotes: Only biopsies considered gradable and already assigned an ISHLT grade were included, and the cohort was deliberately enriched with 2R/3R rejection beyond routine prevalence. This creates a selected spectrum that differs from unfiltered clinical practice.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were biologically motivated, quantitatively defined image features available from the biopsy at the time of grading. Although feature ranking was outcome-driven in the training set, the selected features and final models were locked before independent internal and geographic external validation.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcome was clearly defined according to the established ISHLT cellular-rejection grading system, and a random validation subset was blindly re-graded by independent study pathologists. ehab241.pdf The reference grade was nevertheless imperfect because the grade of record reflects substantial inter-pathologist variability. ehab241.pdf
qa_analysis_quotes: The study had large held-out internal and external validation sets, but the analysis unit was the biopsy slide while 2,472 slides originated from only 546 recipients. The paper does not state that training and internal validation were separated at recipient level or that repeated biopsies were handled with clustered analysis, creating potential patient-level leakage and underestimated uncertainty. Statistical calibration was also not evaluated. ehab241.pdf
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly examined a clinical AI model applied to routine post-operative heart-transplant biopsies from three transplant centres, including both surveillance and for-cause biopsies. ehab241.pdf Applicability is reduced somewhat by deliberate high-grade enrichment, exclusion of technically inadequate slides, and restriction to cellular rather than antibody-mediated rejection.

study_id: 60_Ayer A et al. - 2026 - A Novel Model to Predict Progression to Death After Withdrawal of Care in Potential Donation-After-C
study_metadata:
A Novel Model to Predict Progression to Death After Withdrawal of Care in Potential Donation-After-Circulatory-Death Heart Donors.
Ayer, A. et al.
J Card Fail / 2026
algorithm_name: Multivariate logistic regression
section1_comments: Development data comprised consecutive DCD heart offers made to adult patients at the University of California San Diego from January 1 to June 30, 2023; donor data were obtained from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS). External validation used consecutive offers at New York University from April 2023 to October 2025. The paper states, “There are no funding sources for this work.” A disclosure section reports industry relationships for one author, while all other authors reported no industry relationships.
section2_comments: The primary complete-case analysis included 234 potential DCD heart-donor offers in the development cohort and 53 in the external-validation cohort. A pooled overall age and female percentage were not reported; development-cohort mean age was 37.4 years and 31.6% were female, while validation-cohort mean age was 34.8 years and 71.7% were male. Race was reported, and clinical-history variables included previous cardiac arrest, cause of neurological injury, neurological examination findings, brain imaging, haemodynamic and ventilator variables, laboratory values, and sedative/analgesic use.
section3_comments: The study compared multivariate logistic regression with random forest, decision tree, radial-basis-function SVM, and Gaussian naïve Bayes. Candidate predictors were first identified by significant univariate logistic-regression associations, followed by backward elimination for the multivariable logistic model. Five-fold stratified cross-validation was used for candidate-model comparison, after which the selected logistic-regression model was trained on the full development cohort and externally validated at New York University. Interpretability was explicit: the authors preferred logistic regression partly because of its “greater interpretability,” and Table 4 provides model coefficients. No hyperparameter-search procedure was reported for the four machine-learning algorithms.
section4_comments: Regression imputation was used for missing development data. The primary external validation excluded offers with unavailable model inputs, while a sensitivity analysis used fivefold multiple imputation in an expanded validation cohort of 86 offers; therefore, missing-data handling was mixed. Outcome proportions were preserved using five-fold stratified cross-validation, although no resampling or class weighting was reported. Source code was not reported, but the full logistic-regression coefficients and intercept are provided in Table 4 and an online calculator is available. No predictor normalization or standardization procedure was described.
section5_comments: The outcome was progression to circulatory death after withdrawal of care among potential DCD heart donors. In the primary external-validation cohort of 53 offers, the final multivariate logistic-regression model achieved AUC 0.88 (95% CI 0.78–0.97), sensitivity 1.00, specificity 0.50, PPV 64%, and NPV 100%. Accuracy and F1-score were not explicitly reported. Calibration was evaluated using intercept, slope, and Brier score; external validation showed an intercept of −1.55, slope of 1.51, and Brier score of 0.19, indicating systematic overprediction. Decision-curve analysis was not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: Consecutive offers were used, but only 53 of 110 offers assessed for primary external validation had all model inputs and were included. The authors acknowledge that “the exclusion of offers with incomplete data may have skewed the cohort composition,” creating substantial selection-bias risk in the primary validation analysis.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were measured before withdrawal of care and were available at the intended prediction time, which is appropriate. However, the authors describe “delimited, incomplete, and nonstandardized reporting of donor data in UNOS,” and retrospective clinical measurements and protocols were not standardized across donor hospitals.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcome depended on whether circulatory death occurred before procurement was abandoned. Procurement was “generally abandoned 120 minutes after withdrawal of care,” but this period was occasionally shortened at the procurement team’s discretion, and elapsed time before abandonment was inconsistently documented; thus, outcome ascertainment was not standardized.
qa_analysis_quotes: Predictors were screened using univariate significance and backward elimination, several neurological predictors were potentially collinear, and the VIS coefficient was acknowledged to be unstable. Primary external validation used complete cases only, the external sample was small, and no internal optimism correction or hyperparameter-tuning strategy for the machine-learning comparators was reported, despite calibration and external validation being performed.
qa_applicability_quotes: The population, predictors, and outcome directly concern prediction modelling in potential DCD heart donors and are therefore directly applicable to AI and prediction-model research in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 61_Dag et al. - 2026 - A data-guided analytical framework for assessing the value of additional variables in heart transpla
study_metadata:
A data-guided analytical framework for assessing the value of additional variables in heart transplant decision making
Dag, A. et al.
Decis. Anal. J. / 2026
algorithm_name: Support Vector Machine with Random Under-Sampling (SVM_RUS; old-variable model)
section1_comments: The study used the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) heart transplant database. The source dataset covered October 1, 1987 to December 31, 2012, but transplantations before June 30, 2004 were excluded, giving an analysed period from 2004 through 2012. The authors declared no relevant competing interests. The work was supported in part by Health Resources and Services Administration contract 234-2005-370011C.
section2_comments: After data cleaning, the dataset contained 25,512 heart transplant cases and 161 variables. For the 1-year analysis, 19,704 observations were classified as survival, 2,693 as failure, and 3,115 were censored, resulting in 22,397 evaluable observations. Overall mean age, female proportion, and cohort race/ethnicity distributions were not reported. The predictor set included donor and recipient demographics, clinical history, haemodynamic and laboratory variables, life support, prior cardiac surgery, functional status, and procedural characteristics.
section3_comments: The authors compared Tree-Augmented Naïve Bayes, logistic regression, SVM, decision tree, and random forest models using five-fold cross-validation. SVM models were reported to outperform the other algorithms across the three time horizons; the selected balanced 1-year model was SVM_RUS using 33 old variables. Automated feature selection combined information-gain fast feature selection, LASSO, and Cox regression, supplemented by predictors identified from the literature. Feature selection was repeated within each training fold to reduce leakage. Interpretability was addressed through normalized sensitivity analysis, ranked variable-importance plots, and a TAN-derived directed acyclic graph. No explicit hyperparameter-tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Missing numerical values were imputed using the median, while missing categorical observations were assigned an “UNKNOWN” category. Invariant variables, outliers, identifiers, and variables considered unrelated to survival were checked and removed. Class imbalance was addressed using random under-sampling and cost-sensitive models; RUS was applied only to each training fold, leaving the corresponding test fold at its natural class distribution. Exact per-fold training and test counts were not reported, and neither source code nor trained model weights were reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for the highest-AUC balanced 1-year model presented in Table 6: SVM_RUS using the old-variable set. Across five-fold cross-validation, this model achieved AUC 0.6342, sensitivity 0.6263, specificity 0.5490, and accuracy 0.6167. The corresponding combined-variable SVM_RUS model achieved AUC 0.6285, indicating no improvement after adding the six selected post-2004 variables. AUC confidence intervals, PPV, NPV, F1-score, formal calibration assessment, and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used a large national UNOS cohort and excluded transplantations before June 30, 2004 in accordance with the research objective. However, a detailed participant-flow diagram and counts for exclusions during cleaning were not provided, and the authors acknowledge “potential biases or incompleteness inherent to registry-based data.”
qa_predictors_quotes: The source dataset included pre-operative, procedural, and post-operative variables, including examples such as acute rejection and hospital length of stay. The intended prediction time was not clearly fixed, creating a risk that variables unavailable at the intended clinical decision point, or variables occurring after transplantation, could enter model development.
qa_outcome_quotes: The study describes survival prediction but selected “gstatus,” defined as graft survival or failure, rather than patient survival status. The authors state that gstatus was chosen to focus on patients who “solely died due to heart-transplantation related reasons,” but graft failure is not equivalent to patient death, creating ambiguity and potential outcome misclassification.
qa_analysis_quotes: Nested feature selection and fold-specific under-sampling were methodological strengths, but 450 model combinations were evaluated without an independent external validation cohort. Hyperparameter tuning was not described, no AUC confidence intervals or calibration metrics were reported, and the final model was chosen from the same cross-validation framework used for performance estimation. The authors explicitly acknowledge that the “absence of external validation limits” generalizability.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates machine-learning models using heart transplant recipient and donor registry variables to predict post-transplant outcomes. Although the selected target was graft status rather than pure patient mortality, it remains directly relevant to AI applications in heart transplantation.

study_id: 62_Ding Q et al. - 2026 - Machine learning-based prediction of high hospital charges after lung transplantation in chronic obs
study_metadata:
Machine learning-based prediction of high hospital charges after lung transplantation in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease patients.
Ding, Q. et al.
BMC Health Serv Res / 2026
algorithm_name: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
section1_comments: Data were obtained from the US Nationwide Inpatient Sample, part of the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project, and covered January 2005 through December 2014. The paper states “Funding: None” and “The authors declare no competing interests.”
section2_comments: The initial cohort contained 1,177 adult hospital admissions identified using ICD-9-CM lung-transplant procedure codes; 12 admissions with missing charge data were excluded, and 1,159 were included in the final analysis. Overall mean age and female percentage were not explicitly reported. Table 1 provides sex and race distributions by cost group and includes extensive clinical variables such as heart failure, coagulopathy, pulmonary vascular disease, acute kidney injury, sepsis, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, respiratory failure, and transplanted-lung complications.
section3_comments: The primary GBM was compared with logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM. Patients were divided into training and test cohorts in a 7:3 ratio, and ten-fold cross-validation was used within training to optimize hyperparameters. Feature selection used a two-stage automated process consisting of Pearson-correlation assessment followed by Random-Forest-based Recursive Feature Elimination, leaving 27 predictors. SHAP global and local analyses were used to interpret the selected GBM.
section4_comments: Missing Race and Zip-Code Income Quartile values were imputed using Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations with a Gradient Boosting Classifier for multiclass categorical imputation. Seven post-discharge or manually coded variables were excluded to reduce information leakage, and feature selection reduced the model to 27 variables. High-cost cases represented approximately 20% of the cohort, but no resampling, class weighting, or other explicit imbalance treatment was reported. The exact training count was not stated; the GBM test confusion matrix contains 348 observations. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The outcome was high-cost hospitalization, defined as total hospital charges at or above the cohort’s 80th percentile ($600,223.40). On the held-out test set, GBM achieved AUC 0.8078, accuracy 0.8164, precision 0.6944, recall 0.6657, and F1-score 0.6773. No AUC confidence interval, explicitly reported specificity, or NPV was provided. Calibration curves were presented, and GBM had a Brier score of 0.1360. Decision-curve analysis was not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: The stated target population was lung-transplant recipients with COPD, but the Methods describe identifying adult admissions solely through lung-transplant procedure codes and do not report a COPD-specific diagnostic inclusion criterion. “Chronic pulmonary disease” was instead retained as a predictor and was present in only a subset of the cohort, creating uncertainty about whether the analysed participants represent the stated COPD population.
qa_predictors_quotes: Although seven overt post-discharge variables were removed, several retained predictors were contemporaneous or postoperative events, including acute kidney injury, sepsis, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, respiratory failure, and complications of the transplanted lung. The prediction time was not clearly defined, so some predictors may only become available after substantial hospital charges have already accumulated.
qa_outcome_quotes: Total hospital charges were obtained from the same administrative database for all admissions, and high cost was defined consistently as charges “greater than or equal to” the explicit 80th-percentile threshold of $600,223.40. The outcome was therefore objective and uniformly defined, although it represents charges rather than true economic costs.
qa_analysis_quotes: The study used an internal test split and hyperparameter tuning, but there was no external validation and no AUC confidence interval. The paper does not state that MICE imputation, the 80th-percentile outcome threshold, and RFE feature selection were confined to the training data, creating potential leakage. The 20:80 outcome imbalance was not explicitly addressed, and calibration was presented graphically without calibration intercept or slope.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates machine-learning prediction in lung-transplant hospitalizations and addresses a prespecified transplantation-related healthcare-utilization outcome. Despite uncertainty regarding the COPD-specific cohort definition, it remains applicable to a review of AI models in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 63_Fessler J et al. - 2025 - Machine Learning for Predicting Pulmonary Graft Dysfunction After Double-Lung Transplantation A Sin
study_metadata:
Machine Learning for Predicting Pulmonary Graft Dysfunction After Double-Lung Transplantation: A Single-Center Study Using Donor, Recipient, and Intraoperative Variables.
Fessler, J. et al.
Transpl Int / 2025
algorithm_name: eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
section1_comments: The study included all eligible double-lung transplant recipients treated at Hôpital Foch, France, from January 2012 through December 2019. Funding was provided by Hôpital Foch, with additional support acknowledged from the association “Vaincre la Mucoviscidose.” The authors declared that the research was conducted “in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.”
section2_comments: Of 510 double-lung transplant recipients, 477 met the inclusion criteria; 83 developed PGD3-T72 and 394 did not. Age was reported as median and interquartile range rather than an overall mean, and an overall female percentage was not explicitly stated. Clinical variables included primary lung disease, BMI, pulmonary hypertension, diabetes, prior thoracic surgery, waiting-list and ICU status, mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, laboratory values, Lung Allocation Score, donor characteristics, ECMO, and sequential intraoperative measurements.
section3_comments: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
section4_comments: Numerical variables were not transformed, categorical variables were one-hot encoded, and missing values were not imputed because “XGBoost treats missing data as a specific modality.” PGD3-T72 occurred in 83 of 477 recipients, but no class weighting, over-sampling, under-sampling, or other explicit imbalance method was reported. The primary XGBoost train/test split proportion and corresponding counts were not stated. The authors report that their “full codebase has been made publicly available.”
section5_comments: The primary outcome was grade 3 primary graft dysfunction at 72 hours according to the 2016 ISHLT definition. The optimal six-feature XGBoost model was evaluated at step 8, immediately after second graft implantation, and achieved a median AUROC of 0.84 with an IQR of 0.065; the abstract reports sensitivity 0.81 and specificity 0.68. Although bootstrap confidence intervals were said to have been generated, numeric lower and upper 95% CI limits were not reported. Accuracy, PPV, NPV, and F1-score were not provided in the main paper. The authors qualitatively described superior or well-calibrated risk estimates, but no calibration intercept, slope, Brier score, or calibration plot was reported. DCA was not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: The study included “all DLT recipients” at the center during the defined period, with explicit exclusions for multiorgan transplantation, cardiopulmonary bypass, and duplicate retransplantation records. The flowchart accounts for 477 of 510 recipients, supporting a clearly defined cohort.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictor data were prospectively collected in real time from electronic health records and organized into prespecified chronological surgical steps. The selected step-8 variables were available by the intended intraoperative prediction time, and categorical encoding and missing-value handling were described.
qa_outcome_quotes: PGD3-T72 was assessed using the 2016 ISHLT definition and “graded by consensus by a board-certified panel including an intensivist, a pulmonologist, and an anesthesiologist.” Postoperative ECMO for hypoxemia was explicitly classified as grade 3.
qa_analysis_quotes: The authors explicitly state that “feature selection was not nested within a formal cross-validation loop” and that performance “may be modestly optimistic due to the potential for information leakage.” Additional concerns include 500 repeated internal random splits without external validation, moderate sample size with 83 outcome events, no explicit handling of class imbalance, and absence of numeric calibration results or AUC confidence-interval bounds.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates an interpretable machine-learning model for predicting a clinically important early outcome in double-lung transplant recipients using donor, recipient, and intraoperative data. It is therefore directly applicable to AI prediction research in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 64_Kim DD et al. - 2026 - An integrated clinical-histopathologic prediction model for cardiac allograft rejection Translating
study_metadata:
An integrated clinical-histopathologic prediction model for cardiac allograft rejection: Translating machine learning into clinical risk frameworks.
Kim, D. D. et al.
J Heart Lung Transplant / 2026
algorithm_name: eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
section1_comments: The cohort was derived from adult heart transplant recipients at the University of Pennsylvania using four previously published digitized-biopsy datasets. Calendar years for patient inclusion were not reported. The study was supported by National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute grants K08HL159344, R01HL170152, and R01HL158071. The disclosure statement reads, “None to state.”
section2_comments: The final cohort comprised 484 recipients and 1,188 outpatient EMB-associated encounters. Mean recipient age was 52.6 years; 77.1% were male, but female percentage was not explicitly reported. Race was reported as White 70.7%, Black 19.2%, and Other 10.1%. Clinical history included BMI, retransplantation, CMV status, renal function, LVAD history, coronary disease, ischemic cardiomyopathy, diabetes, pulmonary hypertension, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, CKD, cPRA, medications, laboratory trends, and donor characteristics.
section3_comments: The primary model integrated structured EHR variables with quantitative pathology features extracted from digitized H&E-stained EMB slides. Data were split 80:20 by patient identifier, with 10-fold cross-validation during training and performance assessed exclusively on the held-out test set. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, clinical-only, morphology-only, and integrated configurations were compared. SHAP rankings were used to identify influential features and derive the Integrated Rejection Risk Index; no explicit hyperparameter-search or tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Patients were required to have at least 90% completeness of routinely collected clinical variables, and residual missingness was handled using multiple imputation by chained equations. The cohort was deliberately enriched for future-rejection patients, 26.9% versus a 15.1% institutional incidence, “to mitigate class imbalance.” Longitudinal predictors were constructed using time bins, change-from-baseline, change-from-prior-encounter, and rate-of-change features. Figure 2 reports 954 training encounters and 234 held-out test encounters; all splitting was performed at patient level. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: The primary feasibility outcome was future cardiac allograft rejection occurring more than 7 days and no more than 42 days after a CAR-free outpatient encounter. CAR included ISHLT cellular rejection greater than 1R, pAMR greater than 0, or clinically evident rejection. On the held-out test set of 234 encounters, the integrated longitudinal clinical-morphologic XGBoost model achieved AUROC 0.86, AUPRC 0.74, macro F1 0.83, sensitivity 0.72, specificity 0.94, PPV 0.74, and NPV 0.94. Numeric 95% confidence bounds for AUROC and accuracy were not reported. Formal calibration analysis and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: Inclusion required at least two digitized biopsies, sufficient linked EHR data, and at least 90% data completeness. The authors state that “not all clinically performed biopsies were digitized or available” and that digitized biopsies were preferentially available at selected early time points. The cohort was also enriched for future rejection, resulting in a selected sample that differs from routine practice.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were extracted from routinely collected clinical data and digitized biopsies obtained before the prediction window. Quantitative morphology used previously validated automated pipelines, longitudinal feature definitions were described, and patient-level splitting prevented encounters from the same patient appearing in both training and test sets.
qa_outcome_quotes: Future CAR was defined using established transplant criteria: ISHLT cellular rejection greater than 1R, pathologic AMR greater than 0, or previously defined clinically evident rejection. The outcome window was prespecified as greater than 7 and no more than 42 days after a CAR-free encounter.
qa_analysis_quotes: The model used 1,361 candidate variables, while the training cohort contained 387 patients and only 45 training patients with rejection within 6 weeks, creating substantial overfitting risk. Although patient-level splitting and held-out testing were strengths, external validation, explicit hyperparameter tuning, calibration assessment, and AUC confidence intervals were absent. The event-enriched cohort also affects prevalence-dependent performance measures.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates machine-learning prediction of future cardiac allograft rejection in post-transplant heart recipients using routine clinical and biopsy-pathology data, making it directly relevant to AI applications in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 65_Koritsánszky KB et al. - 2025 - Shifting Determinants of Mortality Risk After Orthotopic Heart Transplantation Identified by Machine
study_metadata:
Shifting Determinants of Mortality Risk After Orthotopic Heart Transplantation Identified by Machine Learning.
Koritsánszky, K. B. et al.
J Cardiovasc Dev Dis / 2025
algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: The study used the institutional database of the Heart and Vascular Center, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary, and included OHT recipients treated from 30 January 2012 to 23 December 2024. Funding was provided through a European Union-supported project, the Hungarian Ministry for Culture and Innovation/National Research, Development and Innovation Fund, and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. Conflicts were declared for two authors, including compensated work as Chief Medical Officer of Argus Cognitive, Inc. and advisory-board membership at GE Healthcare, both stated to be unrelated to the manuscript.
section2_comments: The cohort comprised 581 adolescent and adult OHT recipients; overall age was 50.7 ± 10.9 years and 155 patients (26.67%) were female. Race or ethnicity was not reported. The dataset included demographics, heart-failure diagnosis, comorbidities, functional status, mechanical circulatory support, right-heart catheterization, laboratory values, donor variables, medications, postoperative organ dysfunction, circulatory support, transfusion, ICU and ventilation duration, and postoperative complications.
section3_comments: Random Forest
section4_comments: Features with more than 40% missingness were excluded. Remaining continuous values were imputed using the mean, categorical values using the mode, and continuous predictors were standardized with z-score normalization. All preprocessing was fitted only within the training portion of the nested cross-validation. SMOTE was applied exclusively to training data within each fold. Exact outer-fold training and hold-out counts were not explicitly reported, and source code or trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for the 1-year random forest model using all preoperative and postoperative variables, evaluated across the outer hold-out folds of nested five-fold cross-validation. The model achieved AUC 0.86 (95% CI 0.80–0.92) and Brier score 0.10. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. The preoperative-only 1-year model achieved AUC 0.67 (95% CI 0.56–0.78; Brier score 0.15). Formal calibration plots, calibration intercept or slope, and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: The study included the institutional cohort of 581 adolescent and adult patients who underwent OHT during a clearly specified period, and mortality status and date of death were obtained for all patients from Hungary’s National Health Insurance Database. No major selective exclusions were reported.
qa_predictors_quotes: The primary high-performing models included postoperative maximum or minimum laboratory values, ICU and ventilation duration, total transfusions, postoperative complications, and duration of circulatory support. A fixed prediction time for these variables was not defined, and some predictors may occur after substantial follow-up or be directly affected by impending death, creating temporal leakage and reverse-causation risk.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcomes were objectively defined 30-day and 1-year all-cause mortality. Vital status and date of death were obtained for all patients through the national insurance database, supporting consistent and complete outcome ascertainment.
qa_analysis_quotes: Nested cross-validation, fold-specific preprocessing, and training-only SMOTE were important strengths. However, performance was internally validated only, there was no external or temporal validation, the cohort contained relatively few deaths, and the all-feature models incorporated postoperative variables with unclear availability at the intended prediction time. These issues may produce optimistic performance despite the rigorous cross-validation pipeline.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates explainable machine-learning models for 30-day and 1-year mortality after heart transplantation using recipient, donor, and perioperative data. It is directly relevant to AI prediction research in thoracic organ transplantation, although the all-feature model is applicable only after postoperative information has accrued.

study_id: 66_Luo L et al. - 2026 - In silico perturbations provide multivariate interpretability in predicting post-lung transplant out
study_metadata:
In silico perturbations provide multivariate interpretability in predicting post-lung transplant outcomes.
Luo, L. et al.
Sci Rep / 2026
algorithm_name: EHRFormer
section1_comments: The study used de-identified United Network for Organ Sharing Standard Transplant Analysis and Research File data, described as SRTR/OPTN data, from US lung transplant recipients. Transplants before 8 November 2022 were included, and the abstract describes the period as 1987–2022. The authors stated, “This research received no funding” and declared no competing interests.
section2_comments: The abstract reports 43,869 first-time lung transplant recipients, although the Results also describe an exploratory cohort of 47,864 recipients and Figure 1 reports 37,369 observations in the all-years modeling dataset. The study was restricted to first-time recipients older than 18 years. Overall mean age and female percentage were not reported. Recipient and donor ethnicity, transplant indication, functional status, infection, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, renal function, hemodynamics, lung function, and other clinical-history variables were included.
section3_comments: EHRFormer was a tabular BERT model with three transformer layers, 64-dimensional embeddings, an intermediate layer size of 128, and four attention heads. It was compared with XGBoost. Features were automatically filtered to those with less than 10% missingness within each era, producing 140–152 variables. The models used an 80:20 train/test split, five-fold cross-validation within training, and held-out test evaluation. EHRFormer hyperparameters were optimized with Optuna, while XGBoost used Bayesian optimization. Interpretability included SHAP for XGBoost and single- or multivariable in silico perturbations for EHRFormer.
section4_comments: Numerical variables were mean-imputed and categorical variables were mode-imputed. Categorical predictors were ordinal- or one-hot encoded, and EHRFormer numerical inputs were quantile-binned. The majority class was randomly downsampled to a 1:1 ratio separately in both training and test sets. Exact post-downsampling training and test counts were not explicitly reported. The authors provided a GitHub repository containing the underlying code; the UNOS-derived training and validation datasets were not publicly available.
section5_comments: Values were extracted for the best all-years held-out test model for 1-year mortality, EHRFormer. It achieved AUC 0.64 (95% CI 0.61–0.66), accuracy 0.60, F1-score 0.64, precision 0.58, recall 0.70, and specificity 0.49. NPV was not reported. The XGBoost comparator achieved AUC 0.63 (95% CI 0.60–0.67). Calibration assessment and DCA were not reported. Patients who died during or within 90 days of the index hospitalization were excluded from the mortality-prediction task.
qa_participants_quotes: The analysis excluded patients who died during or within 90 days of the index stay and required predictors to have at least 90% completeness. The authors also downsampled the majority class in the test set to a 1:1 ratio, producing a selected evaluation population that does not represent the natural post-transplant mortality spectrum.
qa_predictors_quotes: The highest-performing model included index-hospitalization variables such as length of stay, acute rejection, dialysis, ECMO, intubation, and ventilation duration. The authors acknowledge that index-stay features are unavailable when listing decisions are made, and the intended clinical prediction time was not fixed clearly.
qa_outcome_quotes: Mortality labels were derived from recorded death date, transplant date, patient status, and status date. One-, three-, and five-year survival windows were explicitly calculated, providing an objective and consistently defined outcome.
qa_analysis_quotes: The study used held-out testing, cross-validation, hyperparameter optimization, and bootstrap confidence intervals, but preprocessing was not explicitly stated to be fitted only within training data. Random splitting across a 35-year period did not provide temporal or external validation, and downsampling the test set altered outcome prevalence and limits interpretation of accuracy, precision, and F1-score. Calibration was not assessed.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates modern machine-learning models for post-transplant survival and lung-function outcomes in adult lung transplant recipients using a national thoracic-transplant registry. It is directly relevant to AI applications in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 59_Allehyani B et al. - 2025 - Machine learning approach to predict 1-year mortality after heart transplantation a single-centre s
study_metadata:
Machine learning approach to predict 1-year mortality after heart transplantation: a single-centre study.
Allehyani, B. et al.
Eur Heart J Imaging Methods Pract / 2025
algorithm_name: Support Vector Machine
section1_comments: The study used data from King Faisal Specialist Hospital & Research Centre in Saudi Arabia and included all heart transplant cases recorded between January 2007 and December 2022. The authors stated, “Conflict of interest: None declared” and “No funding received for this research.”
section2_comments: The cohort included 419 heart transplant recipients with a mean age of 33.61 ± 18.94 years; 305 patients, or 72.7%, were male, but an exact female percentage was not explicitly reported. Clinical variables included cardiomyopathy type, diabetes, blood type, mechanical-support devices, LVEF, immunosuppressive therapy, BMI, and ischaemia time. Race/ethnicity was not reported for the current cohort; references to race/ethnicity in Tables 1 and 2 concerned variables used in previous studies.
section3_comments: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
section4_comments: Preprocessing included “cleaning the data to remove any inconsistencies or missing values, normalizing the data for uniformity, and encoding categorical variables.” No imputation was described, so removal of records or observations with missing data was classified as complete-case analysis. No oversampling, undersampling, class weighting, SMOTE, or other class-imbalance method was reported. The training-set count was not explicitly stated; the test confusion matrices contain 84 observations. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: The extracted performance corresponds to the SVM on the held-out test set. The paper reports accuracy 0.952381, precision 0.90, recall 0.75, F1 score 0.818182, and ROC-AUC 0.868056; no 95% confidence interval for AUC was provided. Specificity, NPV, calibration assessment, and DCA were not reported. The LR comparator achieved an AUC of 0.875 and accuracy of 96.43%. The orientation or labels of the displayed confusion matrices appear inconsistent with the reported precision and recall values, so the explicitly tabulated performance values were extracted.
qa_participants_quotes: The authors stated that “all patients who underwent orthotropic heart transplantation recorded between January 2007 and December 2022 were included.” Although retrospective and single-centre, the use of all eligible transplant recipients reduces evidence of selective participant inclusion.
qa_predictors_quotes: The feature-importance figures appear to include “Status,” explicitly defined as patient death during 1-year follow-up, and “cause OF DEATH during 1 year” among the model features. Inclusion of the outcome or a direct consequence of the outcome as an input would constitute substantial target leakage. The timing and availability of other variables, including immunosuppressive therapy, were also insufficiently specified.
qa_outcome_quotes: One-year mortality is an objective outcome, and the paper defines class 1 as mortality within one year. However, the ascertainment method was not described, six participants had unknown survival status in Table 3, and the handling of these unknown outcomes in model development was not reported.
qa_analysis_quotes: The test set was small and contained few mortality events, class imbalance was not addressed, the training/test split and k-fold procedure were inadequately specified, and no confidence intervals or calibration analyses were reported. Potential outcome leakage and inconsistencies between the confusion-matrix orientation and reported precision/recall further increase the risk of biased performance estimates.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly concerns ML-based prediction of 1-year mortality among post-operative heart transplant recipients and is therefore directly applicable to a review of AI models in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 67_Mete M et al. - 2026 - Predicting Simultaneous Heart Kidney Allocation and Posttransplant Adverse Kidney Outcomes
study_metadata:
Predicting Simultaneous Heart Kidney Allocation and Posttransplant Adverse Kidney Outcomes.
Mete, M. et al.
Kidney Int Rep / 2026
algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: The study used United Network for Organ Sharing Standard Transplant Analysis and Research files from the OPTN national registry. Model development used transplants from 18 October 2018 through 31 December 2020; temporal external validation used January–June 2021 and September 2023–March 2024 cohorts. The work was supported in part by a Health Resources and Services Administration contract. The disclosure states, “All authors declared no competing interests.”
section2_comments: The model was developed in 6,579 adult heart transplant recipients and evaluated in two external cohorts of 1,567 and 1,853 recipients, giving 9,999 participants across development and validation. The intended use was decision support at heart-transplant waitlisting. Age was reported as a median of 57 years rather than a mean, and 72.5% were male; an explicit female percentage was not reported. Race and clinical history were reported, including diabetes, heart-failure diagnosis, previous transplantation, dialysis, mechanical support, renal function, biomarkers, and right-heart catheterization measurements.
section3_comments: An expert panel initially selected 44 clinically relevant variables from 531 registry variables. Random-forest Gini importance was then used to select the final 15 predictors. Hyperparameters were exhaustively searched across numbers of trees, maximum depth, maximum features, positive-class weights, and random seeds. Internal five-fold cross-validation was followed by validation in two later temporal cohorts. Interpretability was provided through feature-importance distributions and a patient-level web calculator.
section4_comments: Missing predictor values were imputed with a K-nearest-neighbors imputer using K = 50, primarily for right-heart catheterization measurements, BNP, and blood urea nitrogen. Class imbalance was addressed through positive-sample class-weight tuning from 3 to 10, and precision-recall performance was reported for the 13.4% adverse-outcome prevalence. The primary temporal external test cohort contained 1,567 recipients; a second external cohort contained 1,853. Study code or trained model weights were not reported, although the model was implemented as an online calculator.
section5_comments: The composite adverse outcome comprised receipt of simultaneous heart-kidney transplantation or, after heart transplantation alone, chronic dialysis, eGFR below 20 ml/min per 1.73 m², or kidney-transplant listing/transplantation within 1 year. In the first temporal external-validation cohort of 1,567 recipients, the random forest achieved c-statistic 0.899, sensitivity 0.680, specificity 0.941, PPV 0.680, NPV 0.941, and F1-score 0.680. A 95% confidence interval for the c-statistic and model accuracy were not reported. Calibration and DCA were not reported. The second postpolicy validation cohort achieved a c-statistic of 0.874.
qa_participants_quotes: The intended population was heart-transplant candidates at waitlisting, but model development included only candidates who ultimately underwent heart transplantation or simultaneous heart-kidney transplantation. Patients with missing creatinine or dialysis status were excluded, and nontransplanted candidates were not represented, creating selection and verification bias for the intended waitlist use.
qa_predictors_quotes: Most predictors were measured at listing, but eGFR and dialysis status were also obtained immediately before transplantation, approximately 35–40 days later. These later measurements are not available at the initial waitlisting decision and introduce temporal mismatch when the model is described as a tool “at the time of heart transplant listing.”
qa_outcome_quotes: The composite outcome combined an actual clinical allocation decision—receipt of SHKT—with objective posttransplant kidney outcomes. SHKT receipt depends on center practice, clinician judgment, and policy rather than confirming irreversible kidney disease, creating incorporation and treatment-decision bias.
qa_analysis_quotes: The large cohort, hyperparameter search, five-fold cross-validation, and two temporal external validations were strengths. However, calibration was not assessed, confidence intervals were not reported, and it was not clearly stated whether KNN imputation and feature selection were fitted separately within each cross-validation fold. The model and decision threshold were selected through an extensive search, increasing optimism risk.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates a machine-learning model intended to guide allocation decisions in heart-transplant candidates and predicts clinically relevant posttransplant kidney outcomes. It is directly applicable to AI research in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 69_Peyster et al. - 2021 - An automated computational image analysis pipeline for histological grading of cardiac allograft rej
study_metadata:
An automated computational image analysis pipeline for histological grading of cardiac allograft rejection
Peyster, E. G. et al.
Eur Heart J / 2021
algorithm_name: Computer-Assisted Cardiac Histologic Evaluation-Grader (CACHE-Grader)
section1_comments: Archived biopsy slides were obtained from the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, and Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center during usual care between 2005 and 2018. Funding was predominantly from US public agencies, including the NIH, Department of Veterans Affairs, and Department of Defense, with additional foundation and institutional support. Multiple authors declared consultancy, equity, patent, licensing, advisory-board, or sponsored-research interests.
section2_comments: The analytic units were 2,472 archived H&E-stained endomyocardial-biopsy slides originating from 546 heart transplant recipients. Biopsies were obtained 7–6,415 days after transplantation during scheduled surveillance or for-cause assessment. Recipient-level age, sex, race/ethnicity, and comorbidity distributions were not reported.
section3_comments: The pipeline extracted 154 biologically inspired, hand-crafted histologic features describing lymphocyte foci, tissue compartments, densities, and spatial interactions. Support vector machine classifiers were selected for binary low- versus high-grade rejection (M1) and four-grade rejection classification (M2). Features were ranked using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test for M1 and a t-test for M2, resulting in models with 2 and 15 features, respectively. Validation included 395 held-out slides from the development center and 1,052 geographically external slides from two other centers; no explicit SVM hyperparameter-search procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Slides underwent automated HistoQC assessment, stain deconvolution, tiling, K-means tissue segmentation, lymphocyte-cluster detection, and feature normalization relative to tissue-compartment size. The authors deliberately enriched the cohort for grades 2R/3R to approximately 20%, compared with approximately 8% in routine practice, to ensure sufficient high-grade cases; this addressed imbalance through cohort construction rather than algorithmic weighting or resampling. The training set contained 911 slides, and the composite validation set contained 1,447 slides: 395 internal and 1,052 external. Missing-feature imputation was not described. Source code was publicly available through the CACHE-Grader repository.
section5_comments: Values refer to the binary M1 classifier for low-grade 0R/1R versus high-grade 2R/3R rejection in the composite independent validation set. It achieved 84.5% agreement with the grade of record, AUC 0.92, sensitivity 0.85, and specificity 0.84; no AUC confidence interval was reported. The four-grade M2 classifier achieved 65.9% agreement (95% CI 63.4–68.3%), with similar internal and external agreement of 66.1% and 65.8%. Numeric PPV, NPV, F1-score, formal probabilistic calibration metrics, and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: The cohort was retrospectively selected, included only biopsies considered gradable and assigned an ISHLT grade, and was deliberately enriched for 2R/3R rejection to approximately 20% rather than the approximately 8% prevalence in routine practice. This nonconsecutive spectrum enrichment may affect representativeness and prevalence-dependent performance measures.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictors were objectively derived from digitized H&E slides using a prespecified workflow involving quality control, stain deconvolution, tissue segmentation, lymphocyte detection, and quantitatively defined morphological features. The final feature sets and models were locked before validation.
qa_outcome_quotes: The reference outcome was the clinical “grade of record” assigned by a pathologist rather than an objective gold standard. The authors explicitly acknowledge poor interpathologist reliability and state that true diagnostic accuracy is difficult to define; independent regrading was performed only in a subset of 166 slides.
qa_analysis_quotes: The study used multiple biopsies from 546 recipients but randomly divided slides rather than explicitly separating recipients, and no adjustment for within-recipient clustering was reported. The external-site validation reduces leakage concerns for the geographically external component, but incomplete reporting of SVM hyperparameter tuning, exclusion after image-quality control, and reliance on an imperfect reference standard remain important analytical limitations.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates an ML-based pathology model in post-transplant heart recipients for automated grading of cardiac allograft cellular rejection, which is directly relevant to AI applications in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 70_Sharma G et al. - 2025 - Development and Validation of a Hybrid Machine Learning Model to Predict Lung Transplant Outcomes
study_metadata:
Development and Validation of a Hybrid Machine Learning Model to Predict Lung Transplant Outcomes.
Sharma, G. et al.
JAMA Netw Open / 2025
algorithm_name: AutoScore-Survival
section1_comments: The study used the United Network for Organ Sharing–Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network registry and included US lung transplants performed between October 16, 1987, and March 26, 2025. Dr Sharma was supported by three American Heart Association awards. The article states, “Conflict of Interest Disclosures: None reported.”
section2_comments: The cohort comprised 51,933 adults undergoing their first lung transplant. Age was reported as a median of 59 years rather than a mean; 22,028 recipients (42.4%) were women. Race and ethnicity were reported. Candidate predictors included recipient demographics, functional status, prior cardiac surgery, laboratory measures, donor characteristics, transplant type, ischemic time, inotropic support, hospital length of stay, and posttransplant ventilation support.
section3_comments: AutoScore-Survival is a hybrid framework that used a random survival forest to rank 61 candidate variables and Cox proportional hazards regression to generate an interpretable integer-based score. A parsimony plot in the development validation cohort selected nine predictors. The cohort was temporally split into development and contemporary testing periods; the development cohort was further divided into training and validation sets for model selection and hyperparameter tuning. Interpretability was provided through a nine-variable point score, hazard ratios, risk groups, and a web calculator.
section4_comments: Missing values were retained as an “unknown” or “not reported” category rather than imputed. Continuous predictors were categorized to generate the point-based score, and the model-development workflow and temporal allocation were described. The development cohort contained 24,014 training recipients and 2,668 validation recipients; the temporal testing cohort contained 25,251 recipients. Class imbalance treatment was not applicable to the time-to-event survival framework, which incorporated censoring and had an overall event rate of 61.4%. Source code or trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The outcome was time from lung transplantation to death or retransplantation, evaluated at 1, 5, and 10 years. In the temporal testing cohort, the 1-year time-dependent AUC was 0.61 (95% CI 0.52–0.70). The testing-set integrated AUC was 0.61 (95% CI 0.60–0.63) and C-index was 0.64 (95% CI 0.63–0.64). Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. Calibration was assessed using plots, calibration slope, observed-to-expected ratios, and Brier scores; decision-curve analysis showed net benefit across clinically relevant thresholds.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used a large national registry and transparently identified all adult first-time lung transplant recipients during the specified period. Exclusions for duplicates, age younger than 18 years, unknown follow-up, and index-hospitalization death or retransplantation were explicitly reported in the participant flowchart and were broadly consistent with the stated postdischarge prediction setting.
qa_predictors_quotes: The model included hospital length of stay and posttransplant ventilation support while survival time was measured from the date of transplantation. These predictors accrue after time zero and can reflect early complications or impending death; the authors note that very short stays may represent “early, catastrophic events,” creating temporal leakage, reverse causation, and potential immortal-time bias.
qa_outcome_quotes: Death or retransplantation is an objective time-to-event outcome recorded consistently in the national registry, and the 1-, 5-, and 10-year horizons were prespecified. Index-hospitalization events were excluded to align the model with postdischarge use.
qa_analysis_quotes: The large sample, prespecified temporal split, validation cohort, automated variable selection, confidence intervals, calibration, and DCA were strengths. However, the “final model was obtained via recalibration-in-the-large on the 2015 to 2025 cohort,” and calibration and clinical-utility performance were then reported in that same testing cohort. This means the temporal test set was not fully independent for all reported performance measures and may yield optimistic calibration and DCA estimates.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates an interpretable machine-learning–assisted model for death or retransplantation after lung transplantation using national registry data. It is directly applicable to AI prediction research in thoracic organ transplantation, although its intended use is postdischarge rather than pretransplant candidate selection.

study_id: 71_Tran-Dinh A et al. - 2026 - Early identification of high-risk individuals for mortality after lung transplantation A retrospect
study_metadata:
Early identification of high-risk individuals for mortality after lung transplantation: A retrospective cohort study with topological feature engineering.
Tran-Dinh, A. et al.
PLOS Digit Health / 2026
algorithm_name: Topological Attention Multilayer Perceptron
section1_comments: The study included consecutive lung transplant recipients at Bichat-Claude Bernard Hospital in Paris, France, between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2020. Funding included the French Agence Nationale de la Recherche and regional Spanish public/FEDER funding, with Institute Mutualiste Montsouris covering article-processing charges. The authors declared that no competing interests existed.
section2_comments: Of 287 consecutive recipients screened, 24 were excluded for more than 20% missing key variables and 11 for insufficient follow-up without documented death, leaving 252 patients: 189 survivors and 63 non-survivors at 1 year. Overall mean age and female percentage were not explicitly reported in the article text. Clinical variables included diabetes, ischemic heart disease, primary lung disease, pulmonary arterial pressure, BMI, CMV mismatch, preoperative and intraoperative ECMO, transplant type, ICU severity scores, postoperative organ support, infections, primary graft dysfunction, renal failure, and rejection.
section3_comments: The primary classifier was a regularized MLP using 49 clinical variables and 27 topological features generated from persistent-homology representations. It was compared with the Lung Transplant Risk Index, Charlson Comorbidity Index, FEV1, clinical-only MLP, random forest, gradient boosting, logistic regression, and other classifiers. Validation used nested stratified cross-validation with five outer folds for performance estimation and three inner folds for hyperparameter tuning. Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation was performed within each training fold, retaining a mean of 34 ± 6 features. SHAP, partial-dependence plots, effect sizes, and an interpretable risk score were used for explanation.
section4_comments: Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations with ten iterations and five imputed datasets, using predictive mean matching for continuous variables and logistic regression for binary variables. Scaling, imputation, topological extraction, and feature selection were fitted exclusively within training folds. Class imbalance was addressed with inverse-frequency class weights of 1 for survivors and 3 for non-survivors; SMOTE was evaluated in sensitivity analysis. Exact per-fold training and test counts were referenced in Supplementary Table S2 but were not stated numerically in the article text. The data, code, and split manifest were made publicly available in the TopoAttention repository.
section5_comments: The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality within 365 days after transplantation. Table 2 reports AUC 0.87 (95% CI 0.81–0.93), accuracy 0.90 (95% CI 0.85–0.95), sensitivity 0.84, specificity 0.90, PPV 0.82, NPV 0.91, F1-score 0.83, and PR-AUC 0.71 for the Topological Attention model. The abstract separately reports 87.4% accuracy, 84.1% sensitivity, and 89.6% specificity on the test dataset, indicating minor inconsistency or different rounding/evaluation summaries. Calibration was evaluated with curves, Expected Calibration Error 0.08, Brier score 0.12, calibration slope 0.91, and intercept −0.15. DCA showed positive net benefit across thresholds from 0.1 to 0.5 and benefit relative to treat-all and treat-none strategies above approximately 0.15.
qa_participants_quotes: The cohort comprised consecutive adult first lung transplant recipients with explicit eligibility criteria, which reduces selective recruitment. However, 24 of 287 screened patients were excluded because more than 20% of key variables were missing and 11 were excluded for incomplete follow-up, without a reported comparison of included and excluded patients; the effect of these exclusions is therefore unclear.
qa_predictors_quotes: The high-performing model included postoperative variables such as total ICU length of stay, mechanical-ventilation duration, ECMO duration, acute renal failure, and antibody-mediated rejection “within one year.” Several of these variables occur well after the stated sequential prediction points at transplantation, ICU admission, and ICU day 7, creating substantial temporal leakage and incorporation of future clinical course into mortality prediction.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcome was objectively defined as all-cause mortality within 365 days. Survival status was obtained from hospital records and national death-registry data, and the authors reported no loss to follow-up before the endpoint among included patients.
qa_analysis_quotes: Nested cross-validation, fold-specific preprocessing, automated feature selection, class weighting, confidence intervals, calibration, and DCA were important strengths. Nevertheless, only 63 events were available for an initially 76-feature neural-network model, no independent external validation was performed, training accuracy reached 1.00, and postoperative predictors with unclear or outcome-proximal timing create severe optimism and leakage risk. The discrepancy between abstract accuracy and Table 2 also reduces analytical clarity.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates an explainable machine-learning model for 1-year mortality after lung transplantation using recipient, operative, and postoperative data. It is directly relevant to AI applications in thoracic organ transplantation, although applicability depends on the clinical time point at which predictions are intended to be made.

study_id: 68_Noh et al. - 2025 - Machine Learning for 1-Year Graft Failure Prediction in Lung Transplant Recipients The Korean Organ
study_metadata:
Machine Learning for 1-Year Graft Failure Prediction in Lung Transplant Recipients: The Korean Organ Transplantation Registry
Noh, Dasom et al.
CLINICAL TRANSPLANTATION / 2025
algorithm_name: Multilayer Perceptron
section1_comments: Data were obtained from the Korean Organ Transplantation Registry, described as a prospective multicenter cohort registry in South Korea, with lung transplant recipients registered from March 2015 through December 2021. Funding was provided by National Institutes of Health research projects and a South Korean government-funded IITP grant. The authors stated, “The authors declare no conflicts of interest.”
section2_comments: Of 303 initially enrolled recipients, patients who withdrew, underwent heart-lung transplantation, were lost to follow-up, or had incomplete data were excluded, leaving 240 recipients. Mean age was 56.1 ± 9.5 years and 65.8% were male; an explicit female percentage was not reported. Clinical variables included transplant indication, diabetes, hypertension, CKD, malignancy, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease, infection, steroid exposure, pulmonary function, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, laboratory values, HLA crossmatch, donor-specific antibodies, and panel-reactive antibodies.
section3_comments: The primary MLP was compared with logistic regression, SVM, random forest, gradient boosting machine, and balanced random forest. Twenty-five preoperative variables associated with graft failure in univariate analyses were ranked using averaged logistic-regression coefficients across repeated 5-fold cross-validation, and the top nine variables with normalized absolute coefficients above 0.25 were retained. Grid-search hyperparameter optimization was reported. The MLP contained two 60-unit ReLU dense layers with dropout of 0.7 and a sigmoid output. SHAP DeepExplainer was used for interpretation.
section4_comments: Only patients with complete data for all selected preoperative variables were analysed, and no imputation was performed. Class imbalance was addressed using balanced class weights for several models and a balanced-random-forest implementation; the exact imbalance method used for the final MLP was not explicitly specified. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation preserved the graft-failure proportion in each fold. Exact fold-specific training and validation counts were not reported. Feature-selection and model-preparation procedures were described, but predictor scaling or normalization before MLP training was not explicitly reported. Source code and model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The outcome was 1-year graft failure, defined as death or retransplantation due to graft failure within 1 year; retransplantation date was treated as equivalent to the date of death. Across stratified 5-fold cross-validation, the MLP achieved AUC 0.780, accuracy 0.733, sensitivity 0.673, specificity 0.751, PPV 0.449, NPV 0.886, and F1-score 0.537. No 95% confidence interval for AUC was reported. Calibration analysis and DCA were not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: Sixty-three of 303 enrolled recipients were excluded because of withdrawal, heart-lung transplantation, loss to follow-up, or incomplete data, but the numbers attributable to each exclusion were not reported. Complete-case inclusion of only 240 recipients may have produced a selected cohort and biased the event distribution.
qa_predictors_quotes: The final model used only pretransplant variables, and the authors explicitly excluded intraoperative and early postoperative outcomes. Clinical definitions and measurement timing were described, with laboratory values taken from the measurement closest to transplantation.
qa_outcome_quotes: One-year graft failure was objectively defined as death or retransplantation due to graft failure within 1 year. Retransplantation was consistently treated as graft failure by assigning the retransplantation date as the equivalent event date.
qa_analysis_quotes: The cohort contained only 55 graft-failure events, yet 25 candidate predictors and six algorithms were evaluated. Feature selection appears to have been performed using the same dataset used for cross-validated performance estimation rather than within a fully nested validation procedure, increasing leakage and optimism risk. There was no independent external validation, no AUC confidence interval, and no calibration assessment.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates machine-learning prediction of a clinically relevant 1-year outcome in lung transplant recipients using pretransplant variables. It is directly applicable to AI research in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 72_Weigt SS et al. - 2025 - Development and validation of a bronchoalveolar lavage genomic classifier for acute cellular rejecti
study_metadata:
Development and validation of a bronchoalveolar lavage genomic classifier for acute cellular rejection.
Weigt, S. S. et al.
EBioMedicine / 2025
algorithm_name: 31-gene bronchoalveolar-lavage cell-pellet genomic ACR Random Forest classifier
section1_comments: CTOT-20 was a prospective observational cohort enrolling adult lung transplant recipients at five North American centres: Duke University, UCLA, University of Toronto, Johns Hopkins, and Cleveland Clinic. Participants were transplanted between December 2015 and August 2018; the consecutively sampled study subset was transplanted from August 2016 to April 2017, with follow-up through July 2021. Funding included National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases awards, with additional Cystic Fibrosis Foundation and Saul and Joyce Brandman Foundation support. Multiple author conflicts were declared, including research grants, consulting, honoraria, advisory roles, and a provisional patent related to allograft injury or rejection.
section2_comments: The primary CTOT-20 analytic cohort contained 181 recipients contributing 806 pre-CLAD BAL-cell-pellet samples that passed RNA quality control. Mean age was 55.2 years and 80 of 181 recipients (44.2%) were female. Race and ethnicity, native lung-disease category, transplant type, Lung Allocation Score, HLA mismatch, induction therapy, and grade 3 primary graft dysfunction were reported. The independent UCLA cohort contained 219 recipients, although external diagnostic validation was performed in 78 samples meeting the clinically significant ACR or stable-control phenotype definitions.
section3_comments: RNA-seq-derived gene-expression features were used to classify clinically significant ACR versus stable controls defined by bronchoscopy, microbiology, donor-specific antibodies, and pathologist-assigned transbronchial-biopsy grades. Logistic regression, Elastic-Net, and Random Forest were evaluated; Random Forest was selected. Ten-fold cross-validation tuned mtry from 1–15 and ntree from 100–5000. Boruta automated all-relevant feature selection reduced 62 differentially expressed genes to a locked 31-gene model. Interpretability was provided through individual gene-importance rankings and biologic pathway analysis. Validation included a held-out internal test set and an independent geographically separate UCLA cohort.
section4_comments: RNA quantity and integrity thresholds were prespecified; 185 of 991 pre-CLAD samples failed quality control, predominantly because of insufficient RNA quantity. Sequencing preprocessing included fastp read cleaning, quality metrics, STAR alignment, FeatureCounts quantification, RPKM calculation, low-expression filtering, and LIMMA-voom differential-expression analysis. No missing-predictor imputation was described. Clinically significant ACR was substantially less frequent than stable control in the model-development sample, but no class weighting, over-sampling, under-sampling, or other imbalance method was reported. The development split contained 150 training and 38 internal-test samples; the independent external validation analysis contained 78 samples. Gene-expression and clinical data were deposited in Mendeley Data, but source code or trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted from the independent UCLA validation cohort for distinguishing clinically significant ACR from stable controls. The 31-gene Random Forest classifier achieved AUC 0.90 (95% CI 0.83–0.96), accuracy 82.1%, sensitivity 73.3%, and specificity 87.5%. PPV, NPV, and F1-score were not reported for the external cohort. The internal held-out test set contained 38 samples and achieved AUC 0.72 (95% CI 0.53–0.88). Formal probability calibration and decision-curve analysis were not reported. As a secondary prognostic finding, late genomic ACR was associated with subsequent CLAD risk.
qa_participants_quotes: Although CTOT-20 was prospective and multicenter, the analysis used BAL samples from only 200 consecutively transplanted participants, excluded samples failing RNA quality control, and developed the diagnostic model using only 37 clinically significant ACR and 151 highly selected stable-control samples. This case-versus-stable-control spectrum does not represent the full range of routine post-transplant bronchoscopy findings.
qa_predictors_quotes: BAL-cell-pellet gene expression was measured using a standardized laboratory workflow with prespecified RNA quantity and integrity thresholds, read-quality filtering, reference-genome alignment, and quantitative expression processing. Predictor measurement was performed on the same BAL specimen obtained at the diagnostic assessment and did not depend on subsequent clinical outcomes.
qa_outcome_quotes: The reference diagnosis depended primarily on pathologist-assigned transbronchial-biopsy A-grade. The authors note that TBB is limited by sampling error, inadequate or suboptimal specimens, and poor interobserver agreement between expert pathologists. These limitations create substantial risk of reference-standard misclassification.
qa_analysis_quotes: Differential-expression screening appears to have identified the 62 candidate genes using the full clinically significant ACR and stable-control dataset before the 80:20 model split, creating potential information leakage. Repeated samples were explicitly treated as independent observations, and random sample-level splitting could place samples from the same recipient in both training and test sets. Additional concerns include only 37 positive samples, no reported class-imbalance handling, and no calibration analysis, despite hyperparameter tuning, Boruta selection, internal testing, and external validation.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates a machine-learning genomic classifier for acute cellular rejection in post-transplant lung recipients and compares it with the current biopsy-based diagnostic standard. It is directly applicable to AI and machine-learning applications in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 73_White JP et al. - 2026 - Predicting expiration among potential donation after circulatory death donors at 30- and 120-min pos
study_metadata:
Predicting expiration among potential donation after circulatory death donors at 30- and 120-min post extubation.
White, J. P. et al.
J Heart Lung Transplant / 2026
algorithm_name: Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), max variable model
section1_comments: Data were collected from three geographically distinct US organ procurement organizations: HonorBridge, Gift of Life Donor Program, and OneLegacy, covering January 2014 through June 2025. The study was supported by the Sam Malik Foundation. The authors included a conflict-of-interest declaration stating that they had no conflicts of interest.
section2_comments: The overall cohort contained 4,464 potential DCD donors for whom withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy was initiated with intent for organ donation. Median age was 46 years rather than a reported mean, and 37% were female. Race was reported, and clinical history included diabetes, hypertension, cause and mechanism of death, neurologic reflexes, ventilatory variables, hemodynamics, laboratory values, and whether a lung offer had been made.
section3_comments: Separate XGBoost models were developed for 30- and 120-minute expiration using a 14-variable max-sample cohort and a 61-variable max-variable cohort. Each dataset was randomly divided 80:20 into training and held-out test sets. Multivariable logistic regression served as the baseline comparator. Predictors contributing less than 5% of the importance of the highest-ranked variable were removed and the model was rerun. Feature-importance analysis and an interactive probability calculator supported interpretation, but a specific hyperparameter-search procedure was not reported.
section4_comments: Variables were required to have at least 85% completeness. Missing numerical values were imputed using medians and categorical values using the mode. The max-variable model used 2,092 donors and 61 predictors; the exact integer training and test counts resulting from the reported 80:20 random split were not stated. Expiration occurred in 59% and 82% of the max-variable cohort at 30 and 120 minutes, respectively, but no class weighting, resampling, or other explicit class-imbalance method was reported. A web application was provided, but source code or model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for the best held-out test model: the 61-variable XGBoost model predicting circulatory death within 120 minutes after extubation. It achieved ROC-AUC 0.89 and PR-AUC 0.97; no 95% confidence interval, accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1-score was reported. The corresponding 30-minute max-variable test model achieved ROC-AUC 0.76 and PR-AUC 0.80. Calibration curves and Brier scores were reported in supplementary figures, but decision-curve analysis was not reported.
qa_participants_quotes: All potential DCD donors with initiated withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy were eligible, and the total cohort was large and multicenter. However, the best-performing max-variable model was restricted to 2,092 donors from only two of the three OPOs to obtain 61 sufficiently complete variables, and the paper does not provide a detailed comparison of included versus unavailable cases for this model.
qa_predictors_quotes: Predictor collection was not standardized to a fixed time before the organ offer; the authors state that “a standardized datapoint prior to offer could not be defined” and acknowledge that inputs may not reflect exact values at the time of procurement offer. Measurements also varied across OPOs and may have been affected by unmeasured sedative or pharmacologic treatment.
qa_outcome_quotes: The endpoints—circulatory death within 30 and 120 minutes after extubation—were objective, clearly time-defined binary outcomes and were measured after withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy.
qa_analysis_quotes: Evaluation used only a random internal 80:20 split, despite data from multiple OPOs, and no prospective, geographic, or temporal external validation was performed. It was not stated whether median/mode imputation and importance-based feature elimination were fitted exclusively within the training set. Exact split counts, confidence intervals, detailed hyperparameter tuning, and threshold-specific classification metrics were not reported.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates machine-learning prediction in potential DCD donors to support heart and lung procurement decisions. The population, donor predictors, and clinically relevant expiration windows are directly applicable to AI research in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 74_Yim WY et al. - 2026 - Bridging machine learning and clinical practice a multicentre nomogram for 90-day graft failure ris
study_metadata:
Bridging machine learning and clinical practice: a multicentre nomogram for 90-day graft failure risk stratification in heart transplantation.
Yim, W. Y. et al.
Open Heart / 2026
algorithm_name: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
section1_comments: The primary derivation cohort came from the US UNOS/OPTN registry between 2008 and 2020, and geographic external validation was performed at Wuhan Union Hospital in China.
