The main Results section reports the WHUH period as 2015–2024, although the abstract reports 2018–2023 and Figure 1 reports 2015–2020; 2024 was retained as the latest explicitly stated year. Funding was provided by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Hubei Provincial Natural Science Foundation. The paper states, “Competing interests None declared.”
section2_comments: After inclusion, exclusion, and preprocessing, 25,200 UNOS recipients and 563 WHUH recipients were analysed, for a total of 25,763. Age was reported as median and IQR by outcome or risk group rather than as an overall mean, and an overall female percentage was not explicitly reported. Race mismatch was reported, and the candidate variables included donor and recipient age, sex, BMI, medical history, diagnosis, previous cardiac surgery, HLA mismatch, bilirubin, renal markers, mechanical support, donor medication use, centre volume, and cold ischaemia time.
section3_comments: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
section4_comments: Figure 1 lists missing baseline variables among the exclusions, supporting complete-case analysis, although detailed missing-data procedures were deferred to the online supplement. The main article states that missing-data handling and normalisation were performed but does not describe the exact normalisation method. The UNOS cohort was split 70:30, corresponding to 17,640 training and 7,560 internal test recipients; the final nomogram was additionally evaluated in 563 external-validation recipients. Graft failure occurred in 1,444 of 25,200 UNOS recipients, but no class weighting, resampling, or other explicit imbalance method was reported. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The target outcome was graft failure within 90 days after heart transplantation; the exact operational definition was deferred to the online supplemental methods and was not stated in the main article. Performance was extracted for the final eight-variable nomogram in the independent WHUH external-validation cohort: AUC 0.671 (95% CI 0.6025–0.7386). Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. Calibration was assessed and the nomogram had a reported Brier score of 0.0472 in development. DCA in the external cohort showed net benefit over treat-all and treat-none strategies across risk thresholds from 0.0 to 0.4.
qa_participants_quotes: The initial UNOS cohort contained 32,754 recipients, but only 25,200 remained after exclusions that included missing baseline variables. The article does not report a comparison of included and excluded recipients, so complete-case selection of approximately 23% of the original registry cohort may have introduced selection bias. The WHUH cohort was also a single-centre convenience validation sample.
qa_predictors_quotes: The final model intentionally used eight routinely available pretransplant donor, recipient, and procedural variables. The authors state that the predictors were available “at the time of donor acceptance,” reducing risk of temporal leakage from postoperative information.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcome was consistently described as 90-day graft failure, but its exact operational definition and ascertainment procedure were not provided in the main article and were deferred to online supplemental methods. It is therefore unclear whether outcome definitions were fully harmonised between UNOS and WHUH.
qa_analysis_quotes: Strengths included a large development cohort, five-fold hyperparameter optimisation, an internal split, geographic external validation, AUC confidence intervals, calibration assessment, and DCA. However, detailed missing-data and preprocessing procedures were not reported in the main article, class imbalance was not explicitly addressed, and Figure 1 appears to use the internal test set for “best model selection.” The exact fitting dataset for the final nomogram was also not clearly stated.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates an explainable machine-learning-informed prediction tool for early graft failure in adult heart transplant recipients using donor-recipient variables available before transplantation. It is directly applicable to AI and machine-learning research in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 75_Zadeh et al. - 2025 - Predictive analytics for de novo malignancies after lung transplantation
study_metadata:
Predictive analytics for de novo malignancies after lung transplantation
Zadeh, A. et al.
Intelligent Decision Technologies / 2025
algorithm_name: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
section1_comments: The study used the Standard Transplant Analysis and Research (STAR) data sources overseen by UNOS/OPTN and containing US transplantation records. The authors state that lung transplant recipient records from 1984 to 2021 were used, although the Methods also describe the STAR source as covering US transplants since 1987. The paper states that the authors received no financial support for the research and declared no potential conflicts of interest.
section2_comments: The investigators identified 66,590 lung transplant records, excluded recipients with a documented pretransplant malignancy, leaving 38,788, and then excluded those lost to follow-up, producing a final cohort of 30,917 recipients. Twenty-five percent developed a post-transplant malignancy. Figure 2 reports 43% female and presents ethnicity and age distributions, but an overall mean age was not reported. The registry variables included demographics, HLA/PRA, serology, donor characteristics, laboratory values, transplantation details, hospital course, rejection, survival, and other complications.
section3_comments: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
section4_comments: Variables with more than 30% missing data were removed during expert preprocessing, but the handling of residual missing values was not described; this was therefore classified as Other rather than imputation. Class imbalance was explicitly addressed by oversampling and replicating minority-class observations. Data cleaning, consolidation, variable filtering, and transformation were described, and SAS Enterprise Miner was used. The paper states a 70:30 split but does not report exact integer training and test counts. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The target was occurrence of de novo malignant cancer after lung transplantation among recipients with no prior malignancy. In the held-out test set, Gradient Boosting achieved AUC 0.746, accuracy 0.690, sensitivity 0.731, specificity 0.649, and precision 0.676. No AUC confidence interval, NPV, or F1-score was reported. The study did not report formal calibration assessment or decision-curve analysis.
qa_participants_quotes: Of 66,590 lung transplant records, only 30,917 remained after excluding recipients with prior malignancy and all individuals lost to follow-up. Exclusion of approximately 7,871 recipients after the no-prior-malignancy cohort was formed was not accompanied by a comparison of included and excluded patients, creating risk of informative selection.
qa_predictors_quotes: The model combined pretransplant, perioperative, and post-transplant variables, including hospital length of stay and treatment for rejection within 1 year. The intended prediction time was not defined, so predictors may have occurred during the same follow-up period in which malignancy developed, creating temporal leakage and limiting prospective use.
qa_outcome_quotes: De novo malignancy was identified from a malignancy follow-up data source, but no fixed prediction horizon, minimum follow-up duration, standardized malignancy definition, or time-to-event/censoring method was reported. Treating variable-duration follow-up as a binary classification outcome can misclassify recipients with insufficient observation time.
qa_analysis_quotes: The study used only a random internal split and no external or temporal validation. It is unclear whether expert variable filtering, correlation screening, and oversampling were performed exclusively within the training data. The paper also reports both a 70:30 dataset split and Gradient Boosting trained on 60% of observations without fully reconciling these procedures. Confidence intervals and calibration were not reported, and post-transplant predictors introduce substantial leakage risk.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates machine-learning models for predicting a clinically relevant complication in post-transplant lung recipients using a national thoracic-transplant registry. It is directly applicable to AI research in thoracic organ transplantation, although the unspecified prediction time limits clinical implementation.

study_id: 77_Zhu Y et al. - 2026 - Construction and validation of a machine learning-based prediction model for venous thromboembolism
study_metadata:
Construction and validation of a machine learning-based prediction model for venous thromboembolism in lung transplant recipients supported by ECMO.
Zhu, Y. et al.
Front Med (Lausanne) / 2026
algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: The study used electronic medical records from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine, China. The internal cohort covered May 2023–May 2024 and the temporal validation cohort covered June–November 2024. Funding was provided by the Health Commission of Zhejiang Province, China (No. 2025KY865). The authors declared no commercial or financial conflicts of interest.
section2_comments: The cohort included 189 elective lung transplant recipients receiving postoperative ECMO, comprising 117 patients with postoperative DVT and 72 without DVT. Age was reported only in categories of ≤60 and >60 years, so an overall mean was unavailable. There were 37 women (19.58%). Clinical variables included diagnosis, hypertension, diabetes, prior tumour, coronary disease, prior thrombosis, respiratory support, BMI, anticoagulant use, laboratory values, respiratory failure, and pulmonary-function measures.
section3_comments: Random Forest
section4_comments: Patients with incomplete case data were excluded, variables with more than 10% missingness were removed, and the remaining variables contained no missing values; no imputation was performed. Categorical variables were one-hot encoded. SMOTE oversampling was applied to the minority class in the training dataset. The article and Figure 1 refer to a 70:30 training-validation division, while the Methods describe calendar-based internal and temporal cohorts; exact integer split counts were not reported. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The target outcome was postoperative venous thrombosis, operationally assessed as lower-extremity DVT using serial colour Doppler ultrasonography. In the temporal validation set, the Random Forest model achieved AUC 0.895 (95% CI 0.788–1.000), accuracy 0.897, sensitivity 0.897, specificity 0.895, PPV 0.946, NPV 0.810, and F1-score 0.921. The abstract writes “PPV 0.946%,” but Table 3 reports 0.946, corresponding to 94.6%. Calibration curves were presented, and DCA indicated net clinical benefit over relevant threshold probabilities.
qa_participants_quotes: Inclusion required postoperative ECMO support and bilateral lower-limb Doppler examination before discharge, while patients with incomplete records, coagulation disorders, or severe ECMO contraindications were excluded. The study does not report consecutive recruitment or the number screened and excluded, creating substantial potential for selective inclusion in this small single-center cohort.
qa_predictors_quotes: Candidate predictors included postoperative laboratory results, respiratory failure, and anticoagulant administration. The model’s intended prediction time was not fixed, and anticoagulant therapy may be initiated because clinicians already perceive thrombosis risk or after evolving thrombotic findings, creating treatment-confounding and temporal-leakage risk.
qa_outcome_quotes: DVT ascertainment was rigorous, using bedside colour Doppler within 48 hours, repeat examinations when symptoms or D-dimer increased, and specialist confirmation. However, the paper labels the outcome as VTE while providing diagnostic criteria only for lower-extremity DVT and no explicit pulmonary-embolism definition, leaving the precise outcome construct unclear.
qa_analysis_quotes: The study included only 189 patients, and the RF AUC fell from 0.990 in training to 0.895 in validation, which the authors acknowledge as mild overfitting. It is not clearly stated that RFE was nested within training folds, the reported 70:30 split conflicts with the calendar-defined temporal cohorts, exact split counts are absent, and no geographically independent validation was performed. These limitations create substantial optimism and reproducibility concerns despite grid search, cross-validation, SMOTE, calibration, and DCA.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates an interpretable machine-learning model for a clinically important postoperative complication in ECMO-supported lung transplant recipients and is directly applicable to AI research in thoracic organ transplantation.

study_id: 76_Zhou X et al. - 2026 - Predicting heart transplant outcomes using explainable artificial intelligence a multicenter study
study_metadata: 76_Zhou X et al. - 2026 - Predicting heart transplant outcomes using explainable artificial intelligence a multicenter study.pdf
algorithm_name: Generalizable Interpretable Neural Network (GINN)
section1_comments: The primary dataset was the US UNOS registry from 1994–2024. Geographic external validation used Eurotransplant, Scandiatransplant, and a 14-patient Chinese cohort from Jiangxi Provincial People’s Hospital; the abstract reports Scandiatransplant data from 1997–2018, while study periods for Eurotransplant and External-CN were not explicitly stated. The authors declared that no financial support was received and that no commercial or financial conflicts of interest existed.
section2_comments: The analytic cohorts comprised 81,327 eligible UNOS recipients, 3,061 Eurotransplant recipients, 1,546 Scandiatransplant recipients, and 14 External-CN recipients, totalling 85,948. The UNOS cohort was divided into derivation (n=45,927), temporal test (n=20,200), and out-of-time validation (n=15,200) cohorts. Age and female sex were reported separately by UNOS era rather than as pooled overall values. Race and extensive donor-recipient clinical characteristics were reported, including diagnoses, prior surgery and transplantation, mechanical support, dialysis, donor hypertension and diabetes, creatinine, and ischemic time.
section3_comments: GINN used an additive Risk Response Network in which each of nine structured clinical variables was processed by a separate lightweight MLP and combined into a mortality-risk logit. The nine inputs were specified a priori from clinical relevance and established heart-transplant risk models; an embedded Lasso-style regularizer promoted sparsity but was not used as preliminary feature screening. Comparators included IMPACT, IHTSA, recalibrated IHTSA, and EBM. Interpretability was intrinsic through feature-specific partial-response curves and additive patient-level risk contributions. Temporal UNOS evaluation and geographic validation in Eurotransplant, Scandiatransplant, and External-CN were performed, but no explicit hyperparameter-search or tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Continuous variables were median-imputed, categorical variables were mode-imputed, and numerical variables were standardized using z-score normalization. Variable coding was harmonized across centers, and SMOTE was applied to the minority mortality class in the training set. The derivation cohort contained 45,927 recipients, an intermediate temporal test cohort contained 20,200, and the primary out-of-time validation cohort contained 15,200. The pipeline was implemented in Python/PyTorch using a fixed random seed. Data access procedures were described, but source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for GINN in the 15,200-recipient out-of-time UNOS validation cohort: AUROC 0.827 (95% CI 0.821–0.833), accuracy 0.80, reported precision 0.82, recall 0.80, and F1-score 0.81. Specificity and NPV were not explicitly reported. Calibration was assessed using calibration plots, slope, calibration-in-the-large, Brier score, and expected-to-observed ratio; Table 4 reports slope 1.02, CITL 0.02, Brier score 0.115, and E/O 1.01. DCA was not reported. The reported precision of 0.82 is not reconcilable with the death-class PPV implied by the displayed confusion matrix, and external-cohort AUROCs differ between the narrative/Figure 6 and Table 4.
qa_participants_quotes: The study used large national and international registries with prespecified temporal cohorts, but 63,136 of 144,979 UNOS records were excluded for recipient age below 18 years or donor age below 15 years, and 512 were excluded for follow-up below 1 year. Selection procedures and participant flow were not described for the Eurotransplant and Scandiatransplant cohorts, and External-CN contained only 14 patients.
qa_predictors_quotes: The nine predictors were specified a priori and consisted of donor, recipient, and perioperative variables available by the time of transplantation: recipient age, donor age, donor creatinine, preoperative ECMO, ventilator and inotropic support, NICM diagnosis, ischemic time, and donor hypertension. Measurement and encoding were harmonized across datasets, and no postoperative outcome-derived predictor was included.
qa_outcome_quotes: The outcome was one-year mortality after heart transplantation, an objective binary endpoint with a clearly specified time horizon. Registry follow-up was used, although the detailed method of death ascertainment was not described.
qa_analysis_quotes: Temporal and geographic validation, SMOTE restricted to training data, confidence intervals, calibration analysis, and ablation studies were strengths. However, hyperparameter tuning was not described, code was unavailable, and major internal inconsistencies reduce confidence: Eurotransplant, Scandiatransplant, and External-CN AUROCs differ between the main text/Figure 6 and Table 4; Figure 3 describes a 144,979-patient validation cohort despite only 81,327 eligible UNOS cases; and the reported precision is inconsistent with the displayed confusion matrix. These discrepancies make the performance estimates difficult to verify.
qa_applicability_quotes: The study directly evaluates an interpretable neural-network model for predicting one-year mortality after heart transplantation using donor-recipient clinical data and multiple international transplant registries. It is directly applicable to AI prediction research in thoracic organ transplantation.

section4_comments: Missingness was handled primarily by excluding variables with more than 50% missingness and filtering out patients missing survival/graft-failure time; blank categorical categories were recoded to “No” or equivalent, but no imputation was reported. Preprocessing steps were described, including exclusion filters, recoding, and near-zero-variance removal. study_id: 03_Ahady Dolatsara-2020-A two-stage machine learn

algorithm_name: Two-stage framework with Stage I ML models and Stage II isotonic regression; selected implementation reported in main results: UP-LASSO-logistic regression
section1_comments: The paper states, “Our UNOS dataset covered 103,570 heart transplant events up to and including September 30, 2016,” and the registry/process described are explicitly U.S.-based through UNOS. Funding was supported “in part by the Ohio Supercomputer Center” and the “National Science Foundation,” and the paper declares “Declaration of Competing Interest None.”
section2_comments: The main article reports a UNOS dataset of “103,570 heart transplant events,” but because censoring was applied separately at each time point, the effective sample size varies by prediction horizon. The paper does not report an overall mean age, female proportion, or race/ethnicity summary in the retrieved main-text tables/figures. Clinical history and transplant factors were included among the 494 variables and engineered features used for modeling.
section3_comments: Stage I examined seven algorithms: “LR, LDA, ANN, CART, SVM, RF and XGB,” along with variable selection methods including “fast feature selection, LASSO, and random forests,” and the paper reports holdout performance for the “UP-LASSO-logistic regression implementation.” Stage II applied isotonic regression to calibrate survival probabilities over month 1 and years 1–10 so they are monotonically decreasing. Figure 3 summarizes this workflow. The framework used internal training/holdout evaluation plus 5-fold cross-validation for model selection.
section4_comments: Missing data were handled through a structured cleaning strategy rather than a single standard method: variables with high missingness were removed, and the authors compared models with no imputation versus median/mode imputation; categorical missingness could also be imputed as “unknown.” Class imbalance was explicitly addressed with several subsampling methods: “none, DOWN, UP, SMOTE and ROSE.” Data preprocessing was described in detail, including removal of intra/post-transplant variables, censoring rules, engineered features, regrouping categorical levels, and encoding choices. Code availability was stronger than a simple yes/no because the paper states that “our code, analysis and results are detailed in an R Markdown document” and also provides a public web app; however, algorithm weights were not reported. Exact training/test N for the selected final model at each time point were not provided in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The target outcome was multi-period post-transplant survival probability at month 1 and years 1–10 rather than a single fixed endpoint. Table 4 reports holdout performance for the selected UP-LASSO-logistic regression model: AUC rose from 0.608 at month 1 to 0.702 at year 10; year-10 accuracy was 0.627, sensitivity 0.752, and specificity 0.533. Figure 7 presents observed-versus-forecast survival probabilities after isotonic regression, so calibration was reported graphically. Table 5 shows isotonic regression slightly improved AUC at all time points. No PPV, NPV, F1-score, or DCA were reported. Since the prompt asks for the test/validation set, I used the holdout results from Table 4; the single numeric AUC field here is the year-10 holdout AUC of 0.702, while the article reports a range across time points.

study_id: 04_Ayers et al. - 2021 - Using machine learning to improve survival prediction after heart transplantation
study_metadata:

J Card Surg / 2021
algorithm_name: Final ensemble ML model combining deep neural network, logistic regression, AdaBoost, and random forest
section1_comments: The study used the “United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry” and included adult patients undergoing OHT “between 2000 and 2019.” A disclosures section was present, listing industry relationships for several authors, so COI was declared. I did not identify a funding statement in the retrieved article text, so funding is marked Not Reported.
section2_comments: The study included “33,657 OHT patients,” and “the majority of study participants were male (75%) with an average age of 52.8 ± 12.4 years,” implying female sex 25%. Table 1 reports race as White 70% and includes multiple clinical-history/support variables such as prior cardiac surgery, dialysis, ventilator, ICU, inotropes, ECMO, IABP, LVAD/RVAD/TAH, bilirubin, creatinine, and waitlist time.
section3_comments: The paper describes a “retrospective study” using UNOS data with patients split into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets. The final model was an ensemble of four algorithm classes: deep neural network, logistic regression, AdaBoost, and random forest, built from 400 total models. Inputs were preoperative donor and recipient registry variables. The main explicit comparator in reported results was a “singular logistic regression,” which best fits the review option of a linear risk-score comparator rather than human expert/guideline. Feature selection combined clinician review and random-forest importance, producing 47 final variables. The paper does not describe SHAP/LIME-style explainability or an explicit hyperparameter-tuning process.
section4_comments: Missing continuous data were imputed with the median and categorical data with the mode. Class imbalance was addressed using “over-sampling (SVM Smote) and under-sampling (Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbors).” Preprocessing was clearly described, including exclusion of non-preoperative variables, clinician review, grouping sparse categories, one-hot encoding, and standardization of continuous variables. The paper states models were trained in Python using Keras/Tensorflow but does not provide code release, so code availability is No. Table 1 gives training n=26,926 and validation n=6,731.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “1-year post-transplant survival,” with 1-year mortality 11% (n=3738). In the validation cohort, AUROCs were 0.649 for logistic regression, 0.691 for random forest, 0.691 for deep neural network, 0.653 for AdaBoost, and 0.764 for the final ensemble ML model. The ensemble improved predictive performance by 72.9% ± 3.8% by NRI and had better DCA across the full risk spectrum. Calibration was evaluated visually by plotting predicted versus observed risk by decile. The paper did not report accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1-score numerically in the retrieved text.

algorithm_name: Support vector machine with radial basis function kernel

section1_comments: The patient cohort came from a local IRB-approved retrospective study and the lead academic clinical site was the University of Pennsylvania; the article states that data were selected retrospectively and transferred “to an outside facility for computational imaging analysis,” which supports a single-center clinical source with external image processing. I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved article text. Calendar study years were not reported; only follow-up intervals after transplant were provided.

Clinical background was reported through pretransplant diagnoses including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, cystic fibrosis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and other.
section3_comments: The article explicitly says the scans were analyzed retrospectively and that “supervised ML with support vector machines (SVMs) was used.” The model used significant qCT features derived from Student t tests, and a “radial basis functional kernel with default tuning parameters was used.” Inputs were qCT/FRI imaging features from paired inspiratory-expiratory CT scans. The main comparator was not another clinical model but rather baseline clinical/PFT variables, which the paper states could not significantly distinguish BOS from non-BOS at baseline. Validation used repeated random train-test partitions (90/10 for 1D and 2D, 80/20 for 3D), so “Other” is the most exact category.
section4_comments: For the baseline prediction cohort, “patients with missing values for certain regional parameters… were not included,” which is best classified as complete case analysis. Class imbalance handling such as weighting, oversampling, or SMOTE was not reported. Data preprocessing was described extensively: CT segmentation, central/distal airway definitions, lung/lobar volume extraction, and computational fluid dynamics-based resistance calculation. The paper reports train-test ratios, but because the absolute sample counts vary across repeated random partitions and dimensions, exact training and test N are NR. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: The clinical outcome was eventual BOS after lung transplant, which is the obstructive phenotype of chronic lung allograft dysfunction, so the closest restricted category is CLAD. Table 5 reports the best 3-feature SVM classification accuracy as 85%, using RML lobe volume at TLC, RUL airway resistance at FRC, and central airway surface at FRC. One-feature accuracy reached 76%, and the best two-feature model reached 83%. The paper did not report AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1-score, calibration, or DCA. Figure 7 summarized significant baseline qCT predictors, and Figure 8 showed that baseline FEV1 and FEV1 percent predicted were not significant predictors of future BOS.

study_id: 07_Chang-2025-Patterns of Left Ventricular Region

algorithm_name: k-means clustering
section1_comments: The study was the “Donor Heart Study,” coordinated at Stanford and “conducted at 8 organ procurement organizations across the United States,” so the data origin was U.S. multicenter rather than a registry. Funding was from the “National Institutes of Health (NIH)/National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (R01 HL125303),” and the authors stated that they had “no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.” Specific calendar start and end years for donor enrollment were not reported in the retrieved text.

section3_comments: The paper states that the Donor Heart Study was a “5-year multicenter observational prospective cohort study.” The machine-learning method was unsupervised “k-means clustering,” using all 17 segment-level wall motion scores from transthoracic echocardiography to identify RWMA phenotypes. The number of clusters was chosen using the cubic clustering criterion, but no held-out validation, SHAP/LIME-style interpretability method, or hyperparameter-tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: The analysis excluded donors without adequate initial TTE quality and then excluded 70 outliers after cluster analysis, which is most consistent with complete case analysis plus exclusions rather than imputation. Class imbalance handling was not relevant because this was unsupervised phenotyping rather than a binary classifier. Data preprocessing was described: only donors with RWMA on initial TTE entered clustering, 17 segment-specific WMS values were used, 8 preliminary clusters were generated and then consolidated into 4 clinically plausible phenotypes, and 70 outliers were excluded. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: This was not a supervised prediction model with held-out discrimination metrics. Instead, the clinically relevant outcomes associated with the RWMA phenotypes were donor-heart acceptance, changes in LVEF/WMSI on follow-up TTE, and recipient survival after transplantation. Table 1 reports donor-heart acceptance was highest in FBS (68.2%), and recipient 2-year survival among transplanted hearts was similar across phenotypes. study_id: 10_Dalton-2023-Refining the Lung Allocation Score

algorithm_name: WL-LAS/CAS, PT-CAS, re-estimated Cox models, cubic-spline Cox model, random survival forest, logistic model, linear discriminant analysis, gradient-boosted tree
section1_comments: The paper used “Scientific Registry for Transplant Recipients (SRTR) data from 2015-2020” for waitlist models and “data from 2010-2020” for post-transplant models. Because SRTR is the U.S. national transplant registry, this is a U.S. national registry study. I did not identify an explicit funding or conflict-of-interest statement in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The waitlist analysis included “13,204 candidates,” and the post-transplant analysis included “20,763 adult transplant recipients.” Table 1 reports female sex as 41% in the baseline waitlist cohort. Race/ethnicity was reported, and multiple clinical factors were included, such as diagnosis group, 6-minute walk distance, respiratory support, pulmonary arterial pressure, oxygen use, creatinine, BMI, bilirubin, insurance, and education. A single overall mean age for the full analytic cohorts was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The study compared seven models for each outcome: current LAS/CAS Cox models, updated Cox models, nonlinear spline-enhanced Cox models, random survival forests, logistic models, linear discriminant analysis, and gradient-boosted trees. The main comparators were the current LAS/CAS survival models, which are linear risk-score models. The study used repeated cross-validation folds rather than one fixed train/test split, so exact training and test counts are NR. Code availability was not reported in the retrieved text. Class-imbalance handling was not described.
section5_comments: The primary outcomes were waitlist death or removal as too sick, and post-transplant death or retransplantation. For waitlist models, discrimination was strongest in the baseline cohort, with AUC about 0.92-0.93 at 1 month, declining to about 0.87-0.89 at 3 months and 0.84-0.85 at 6 months. algorithm_name: CRANE (Cardiac Rejection Assessment Neural Estimator)
section1_comments: The study combined a U.S. cohort with external cohorts from Turkey and Switzerland, so it is multinational and multicenter. Figure 1 states the U.S. train cohort spanned 2004–2021, the Turkish cohort 2002–2020, and the Swiss cohort 2014–2020, making the overall time span 2002–2021. I did not identify funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study population comprised heart-transplant recipients undergoing EMB assessment. The retrieved text reports 1,690 patient biopsies in the U.S. cohort, 585 patients in Turkey, and 123 patients in Switzerland, totaling 2,398 patients/biopsies across cohorts used for development and external testing. I did not find a cohort-wide mean age, sex percentage, race/ethnicity, or comorbidity summary in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: CRANE is a deep-learning system operating on H&E-stained whole-slide biopsy images using a pretrained CNN encoder plus attention-based multiple instance learning. It was compared with expert pathologist assessment in a reader study, and it was externally evaluated on Turkish and Swiss cohorts, which makes external geographic validation the strongest validation label. The system also generated attention heatmaps for interpretation. Hyperparameters and architecture details are described in Methods.
section4_comments: The internal U.S. cohort was split into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% hold-out testing. Since the U.S. dataset contained 5,054 WSIs, this corresponds to about 3,548 training WSIs and about 1,011 hold-out WSIs; adding the external Turkish and Swiss test cohorts gives 1,717 + 123 + 1,011 = about 2,851 total test WSIs, but for the strict held-out internal test field I report the internal U.S. holdout only as 1,011 if only internal is desired. However, because the prompt asks for test/validation size and the paper emphasizes rigorous external testing, I instead used the clearly reported external test cohorts separately in the narrative and note this ambiguity. Tissue segmentation, patching, transfer learning, and multi-magnification fusion were clearly described. Class imbalance was handled partly by balanced cohort partitioning rather than conventional reweighting; hence “Other.” Missing-data handling and code availability were not reported in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: On the U.S. hold-out set, the model detected overall rejection with AUC 0.962 and accuracy 0.899. It detected cellular rejection with AUC 0.958 and accuracy 0.893, antibody-mediated rejection with AUC 0.874 and accuracy 0.899, Quilty B lesions with AUC 0.939 and accuracy 0.920, and low-grade versus high-grade rejection with AUC 0.833 and accuracy 0.818. No PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, calibration, or DCA were reported in the retrieved text.

The work is best characterized as imaging biomarker evaluation rather than conventional train/test ML development on this cohort, so validation is “Other.” No SHAP/LIME or hyperparameter-tuning process was reported.
section4_comments: Patients were required to have a qualifying thin-section inspiratory CT near CLAD diagnosis, and cases with failed segmentation were excluded, which is most consistent with complete-case/exclusion-based handling. Preprocessing was described in detail: lung segmentation, removal of large airways/central vasculature, voxel texture assignment, radiologist review of overlays, and normalization of ML variables by CT total lung capacity. No class-imbalance method, code release, or train/test split was reported because this was not a new model-training study in this cohort.
section5_comments: The main diagnostic outcome was CLAD phenotyping. ROC analysis showed that GGOML, RETML, and especially PVVML identified the RAS/mixed phenotype, with PVV having the strongest AUC of 0.85. Using a 3% cut-point, PVV had sensitivity 90.0% and specificity 70.1% for RAS/mixed phenotyping. Machine-learning hyperlucent lung identified BOS on inspiratory CT alone with AUC 0.76. Prognostically, PVV was the strongest independent CT predictor of graft failure in multivariable Cox analysis (HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.05–1.44; p = 0.01). Accuracy, PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, and DCA were not reported.

study_id: 36_Medved et al. - 2018 - Improving prediction of heart transplantation outcome using deep learning techniques
study_metadata:

Medved, D. et al.
Sci Rep / 2018
algorithm_name: International Heart Transplantation Survival Algorithm (IHTSA); comparator IMPACT
section1_comments: The study used “data from adult heart transplanted patients between January 1997 to December 2011… collected from the UNOS registry,” which is a U.S. national registry. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The study included “27,860 heart transplantations, corresponding to 27,705 patients.” Recipient mean age was “52 ± 13 years,” and 76% were male, implying 24% female. Race and numerous clinical-history variables were reported, including diabetes, infection, dialysis, previous transplant, previous cardiac surgery, ICU status, ventilation, ECMO, IABP, VAD, bilirubin, creatinine, PRA, and diagnosis.
section3_comments: The paper compared the deep-learning IHTSA model with the logistic-regression-based IMPACT score. IHTSA used recipient and donor tabular registry variables, whereas IMPACT used recipient variables only. The study split cohorts into pre-2009 derivation and 2009–2011 temporal test cohorts, which is best classified as external temporal validation relative to the derivation era. The text mentions CART was used by IHTSA developers to assess relative feature importance, but not as a main explainability framework in this paper. Hyperparameter tuning was not described in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The derivation cohort contained 22,263 transplants and the test cohort 5,597. The tables repeatedly report “N, number of transplants with non-missing values,” which indicates analysis on available cases rather than explicit imputation, so complete-case style handling is the best fit. No class-imbalance strategy or preprocessing/normalization details were reported. A web calculator for IHTSA is mentioned, but no code repository or released weights were identified, so code availability is marked Other.
section5_comments: In the 2009–2011 test cohort, recalibrated IHTSA achieved AUROC 0.65 (95% CI 0.63–0.68) for 1-year mortality, compared with 0.61 (0.58–0.63) for IMPACT. For long-term survival, recalibrated IHTSA had C-index 0.63 (0.61–0.65) versus 0.58 (0.56–0.61) for IMPACT. Calibration was reported through predicted versus actual mortality and Hosmer–Lemeshow statistics, with IHTSA closer to observed 1-year mortality than IMPACT. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported.

study_id: 37_Michelson-2024-Developing machine learning mod
study_metadata:
Developing machine learning models to predict primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation
Michelson, A. P. et al.
Am J Transplant / 2024
algorithm_name: K-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression (LR), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and support vector classifier (SVC); final selected model = KNN
section1_comments: The cohort included bilateral lung transplant recipients “at our center between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2019,” which makes this a U.S. single-center study. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: The final cohort “consisted of 576 patients.” Table 1 reports recipient sex as 237 female of 576 total recipients, or 41.15%. Recipient age was reported as median 59 years rather than mean, so mean age is NR. Race, BMI, diagnosis, LAS, ICU status, ventilation, ECMO, donor variables, and pulmonary artery pressure were reported.
section3_comments: The study used donor and recipient pretransplant structured data from UNOS, UNet, and the local EHR. Four prediction algorithms were trained: LR, KNN, XGB, and SVC. Feature reduction was done with lasso regression, and hyperparameters were optimized using 5-fold cross-validation with random grid search. Feature importance was assessed using SHAP. The cohort was split 75%/25% into train/test sets.
section4_comments: The paper states that “missing data were median imputed for continuous data and mode imputed for binary data,” which is simple imputation. Preprocessing included binary encoding of categorical variables and MinMax scaling fit on the training data and applied to the test data. The population was divided into a 75%/25% train-test split, which corresponds to about 432 training and 144 test patients from 576 total. I did not see explicit class-imbalance mitigation. The model was deployed on a secure website, but no source-code release was stated, so code availability is best classified as Other.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “PGD grade 3 at any time within 72 hours of transplantation,” which maps to PGD. The abstract states that the final selected KNN model had “an area under the receiver operating characteristics curve of 0.65.” Table 3 shows KNN among the better-performing models, and Table 4/Figure 4 show explicit calibration assessment using Cox intercepts, slopes, and calibration curves before and after sigmoid calibration. The retrieved text does not provide clear final held-out PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1 values for the selected final KNN model, so I leave those as NR. DCA was not reported.

study_id: 38_Miller et al. - 2019 - Predictive Abilities of Machine Learning Techniques May Be Limited by Dataset Characteristics Insig

algorithm_name: Neural networks, naïve-Bayes, tree-augmented naïve-Bayes, support vector machines, random forest, stochastic gradient boosting; compared with logistic regression, ridge regression, and LASSO
section1_comments: The study queried the “UNOS database… since its inception in 1987 through 2014” for adult cardiac transplant recipients, making this a U.S. national registry study. Disclosures were explicitly reported, and one author was “supported by grant K12 HS023000-04 from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality,” which fits government/public funding.
section2_comments: The final analytic cohort included “50,453/62,621 patients” after excluding those with >20% missing data. The retrieved text did not provide an overall age or sex summary for the full cohort, so these remain NR. The paper did report major clinical predictors such as age, renal function, BMI, liver function tests, bilirubin, creatinine clearance, hemodynamics, donor blood pH, and candidate diagnosis. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text.
section3_comments: The study explicitly compared traditional statistical methods with machine-learning methodologies and identified neural networks as the best-performing advanced model. Inputs were structured UNOS clinical variables, including donor and recipient factors. The data were “trained on 80% of the data and then tested on the remaining 20%,” so the validation method is internal split. No SHAP/LIME-style explainability or hyperparameter-tuning strategy was described in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: The authors “excluded patients with >20% missing data,” which is best classified as complete-case/exclusion-based handling. The train/test split was 80%/20%, corresponding to about 40,362 training and 10,091 test patients from 50,453 total. I did not find any explicit class-imbalance mitigation, code-release statement, or detailed preprocessing/normalization description in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “1-year survival.” The neural network had the highest C-statistic at 0.66, while logistic regression, ridge regression, and LASSO each had C-statistic 0.65. Calibration was evaluated using calibration curves, Hosmer–Lemeshow testing, and Brier scores; traditional models plus random forest and stochastic gradient boosting showed good calibration, whereas some other advanced models were inferior. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported in the retrieved text. DCA was not reported.

study_id: 39_Ozcan et al. - 2022 - Artificial intelligence-derived cardiac ageing is associated with cardiac events post-heart transpla
study_metadata:
Artificial intelligence-derived cardiac ageing is associated with cardiac events post-heart transplantation
Ozcan, I. et al.
Eur Heart J Digit Health / 2022
algorithm_name: AI-ECG age algorithm / ECG-age convolutional neural network
section1_comments: The study was performed “at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, MN” and included “564 consecutive cardiac transplant patients who underwent HTx in our institution between 1990 and 2018,” so this is a U.S. single-center cohort. I did not identify explicit funding or COI statements in the retrieved text.
section2_comments: “A total of 540 patients with available pre- and post-transplantation ECG data were included.” Table 1 reports recipient age 49 ± 14 years and recipient sex male in 366/540, implying 32% female. Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text. Clinical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, ischemic cardiomyopathy, lipid measures, ischemic time, immunosuppression, rejection, CAV grade, and pacemaker implantation.
section3_comments: The paper used “an AI-ECG algorithm that was previously developed and validated in the non-transplant population” and states that “the convolutional neural network model was developed using Keras with a TensorFlow and Python backend.” Raw 12-lead ECGs were input to estimate ECG age. The model was applied without additional training to this transplant cohort. No SHAP/LIME-type explainability or hyperparameter-tuning process for this study cohort was reported. Validation here is best marked as not reported because this paper is primarily an application/prognostic study of a previously developed model rather than a new derivation-validation paper.
section4_comments: The analysis included only patients “with available pre- and post-transplantation ECG data,” which is most consistent with complete-case inclusion. The ECG-age algorithm had been previously trained on 774,783 subjects outside this study, but this paper did not retrain or provide study-specific train/test counts for the transplant cohort. Data handling was described, including averaging ECG ages from ECGs obtained within 1 year before and after HTx and excluding ECGs used in the original training/validation sets. Class imbalance is not applicable to this prognostic exposure analysis. The network architecture was “available on request,” so code availability is best classified as Other rather than Yes.
section5_comments: The study outcome was MACE, defined as “any incident of coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, re-transplantation, and all-cause mortality,” so the closest allowed category is Adverse Events. During median follow-up of 8.8 years, 307 patients experienced MACE. The main reported performance/result metric was association strength rather than discrimination: ΔECG age ≥ 0 was associated with MACE in multivariable Cox analysis, HR 1.58 (95% CI 1.18–2.10, P = 0.002). No AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, or DCA were reported.

study_id: 40_Pelzer-2023-The Accuracy of Initial U.S. Heart

JACC Heart Fail / 2023
algorithm_name: Random survival forest (RSF); comparator Cox proportional hazards (CPH)
section1_comments: The data source was the “Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients,” with a prepolicy training set from “2010-2017” and a postpolicy test set from “November 1, 2018, and March 1, 2020.” I did not identify an explicit funding or COI statement in the retrieved text.

Race/ethnicity was not reported in the retrieved text. Clinical history included malignant disease, cerebrovascular disease, tobacco use, diabetes, diagnosis categories, and supportive treatments.
section3_comments: The study compared therapy-based “6-status” ranking with two multivariable methods: “Cox proportional hazards models and random survival forest models.” Predictors were clinically chosen listing-time variables including age, diagnosis, laboratory measurements, hemodynamics, and supportive treatment. Models were trained on prepolicy data and evaluated on a later postpolicy cohort, which is best classified as external temporal validation. No SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or hyperparameter-tuning details were reported in the retrieved text.
section4_comments: “Other missing data were imputed with the multiple imputation by chained equations algorithm,” so missing-data handling is multiple imputation. The prepolicy training cohort included 27,200 candidates and the postpolicy test cohort 5,094. The authors also specified assumptions for missing indicator variables and exclusion of obvious data-entry errors. I did not identify class-imbalance mitigation or code release.
section5_comments: The primary outcome was “death before receipt of a heart transplant,” which maps to waitlist mortality. In the postpolicy test set, the best-performing model was the Cox model with treatment variables, C-index 0.76, followed by the random survival forest with treatment variables, C-index 0.74; the 6-status system had C-index 0.67. Calibration was assessed with Kaplan–Meier survival by predicted 90-day risk groups and Brier scores. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. DCA was not reported.

study_id: 41_Raji and Safna - 2022 - Computational methods for predicting the outcome of thoracic transplantation
study_metadata:
Computational methods for predicting the outcome of thoracic transplantation

Journal of Big Data / 2022
algorithm_name: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with back-propagation; Radial Basis Function (RBF) network
section1_comments: The study states that data were collected from the “United Network for Organ Sharing database,” so the source is a U.S. national registry. The paper says “Funding: Not applicable,” but also notes the OPTN data source support contract in the ethics section; I therefore classify the study-specific funding as None. The exact calendar years of the included thoracic transplant records were not reported in the retrieved text. The paper uses the broad term “thoracic transplantation,” not a clearly separated heart-only or lung-only cohort.
section2_comments: The paper reports an initial UNOS thoracic dataset of 148,509 records, then after removing pediatric cases and validation steps, “24 important attributes with 485 records were extracted.” Age, donor age, creatinine, serum albumin, ECMO, IABP, rejection episodes, ischemic time, HLA mismatch, infection resistance, and graft-failure cause were included, so clinical history was incorporated. Mean age, sex distribution, and race/ethnicity were not reported for the final 485-case dataset.
section3_comments: The paper’s main proposed model is the “multi-layer perceptron algorithm,” and it also implemented “the Radial Basis Function Network model to prove the accuracy of proposed model.” Inputs were donor, recipient, and transplantation tabular variables selected from UNOS using InfoGain Attribute Eval with ranker search. The comparison was against an earlier published computational system rather than a clinical guideline or human reader. The paper discusses “validation” but the retrieved text does not clearly describe a standard split or CV protocol, so I classify validation as Other rather than guessing. No SHAP/LIME-style interpretability or explicit hyperparameter tuning was reported.
section4_comments: Data preprocessing was described extensively: multi-organ records were filtered to thoracic transplantation, pediatric records were removed, relevant attributes were selected, and InfoGain-based ranking reduced the feature space to 24 inputs. However, the retrieved text does not describe a missing-data method, class-imbalance handling, public code release, or explicit train/test counts. Because those details were not reported clearly, I left them as NR/No rather than inferring them.
section5_comments: The study outcome was graft/survival status after thoracic transplantation, represented by GRF_STAT, but the exact clinical horizon was not clearly specified in the retrieved text, so the safest category is Other. The paper reports “accuracy of 97.1%” for the MLP and “92.37%” for the RBF model. Table 6 reports sensitivity 0.966 and specificity 0.984 for the proposed MLP. AUC/C-statistic, PPV, NPV, F1, calibration, and DCA were not reported in the retrieved text.

The 40% validation set was used for the simulation, so internal split is the best validation label. The paper describes imputation of missing ABO and LAS-related variables and synthetic extension of trajectories, and explicitly uses “multiple imputation by chained equations” for some modeled quantities, so multiple imputation is the best fit. I did not find any class-imbalance strategy or code-release statement.
section5_comments: The modeled clinical decision was lung-transplant referral, and the downstream patient outcome was 5-year survival under different referral policies; because this does not map neatly to the preset categories, the best label is Other. The ML model’s baseline AUROC for 2-year mortality was 0.914 versus 0.876 for FEV1. Calibration is discussed because the paper states that the ML model had “better calibration than FEV1.” The paper’s main outcome results were survival and referral consequences in simulation rather than standard test-set accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1. The model was then examined in a retrospective blinded implementation study involving EVLP specialists, so human expert is the best comparator. Because the development cohort preceded two later consecutive validation cohorts, external temporal is the best validation category. SHAP importance values were explicitly used to assess feature importance. The retrieved text does not describe a separate feature-selection stage or explicit hyperparameter tuning.
section4_comments: The development dataset contained 504 EVLP cases, and the two independent temporal validation cohorts contained 97 and 124 cases, totaling 221 test cases. I did not find a clear missing-data strategy, class-imbalance method, or code-availability statement in the retrieved text.
section5_comments: The model predicted EVLP suitability and post-transplant duration of mechanical ventilation; within the extraction framework, the closest postoperative adverse-outcome category is PGD because the paper also linked predictions to PGD grade 3 at 72 h. External AUROCs were 0.734, 0.729, and 0.716. For multiclass ISHLT grades, the cross-validated AUROCs were 0.835 for 0R, 0.633 for 1R, and 0.905 for 2/3R. algorithm_name: Random forest variable-importance model with time-dependent multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis

Missing-data handling was not clearly reported. The paper states that “the complete analysis code is available” on GitHub, so code availability is affirmative under the available labels. No fixed train/test split sizes were reported.
section5_comments: The study outcome was post-transplant malignancy, which is not one of the preset transplant endpoints, so the best category is Other. The paper reports hazard ratios rather than standard predictive discrimination metrics: sirolimus HR 1.41, azathioprine HR 2.1, cyclosporine HR 1.59, and tacrolimus HR 0.59 for post-transplant malignancy. No AUC, accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, calibration, or DCA were reported in the retrieved text.

study_metadata:

The training set contained 911 slides, and the composite validation set contained 1447 slides: 395 internal and 1052 external. Missing-feature imputation was not described. section5_comments: Values above refer to the binary M1 classifier for low-grade 0R/1R versus high-grade 2R/3R rejection in the composite held-out validation set. A pooled overall age and female percentage were not reported; development-cohort mean age was 37.4 years and 31.6% were female, while validation-cohort mean age was 34.8 years and 71.7% were male. Race was reported, and clinical-history variables included previous cardiac arrest, cause of neurological injury, neurological examination findings, brain imaging, haemodynamic and ventilator variables, laboratory values, and sedative/analgesic use.
section3_comments: The study compared multivariate logistic regression with random forest, decision tree, radial-basis-function SVM, and Gaussian naïve Bayes. Candidate predictors were first identified by significant univariate logistic-regression associations, followed by backward elimination for the multivariable logistic model. Five-fold stratified cross-validation was used for candidate-model comparison, after which the selected logistic-regression model was trained on the full development cohort and externally validated at New York University. Interpretability was explicit: the authors preferred logistic regression partly because of its “greater interpretability,” and Table 4 provides model coefficients. No hyperparameter-search procedure was reported for the four machine-learning algorithms.
section4_comments: Regression imputation was used for missing development data. The primary external validation excluded offers with unavailable model inputs, while a sensitivity analysis used fivefold multiple imputation in an expanded validation cohort of 86 offers; therefore, missing-data handling was mixed. Outcome proportions were preserved using five-fold stratified cross-validation, although no resampling or class weighting was reported. Source code was not reported, but the full logistic-regression coefficients and intercept are provided in Table 4 and an online calculator is available. No predictor normalization or standardization procedure was described.
section5_comments: The outcome was progression to circulatory death after withdrawal of care among potential DCD heart donors. In the primary external-validation cohort of 53 offers, the final multivariate logistic-regression model achieved AUC 0.88 (95% CI 0.78–0.97), sensitivity 1.00, specificity 0.50, PPV 64%, and NPV 100%. Accuracy and F1-score were not explicitly reported. Calibration was evaluated using intercept, slope, and Brier score; external validation showed an intercept of −1.55, slope of 1.51, and Brier score of 0.19, indicating systematic overprediction. Decision-curve analysis was not reported.

study_id: 61_Dag et al. - 2026 - A data-guided analytical framework for assessing the value of additional variables in heart transpla

A data-guided analytical framework for assessing the value of additional variables in heart transplant decision making

Decis. Anal. J. / 2026
algorithm_name: Support Vector Machine with Random Under-Sampling (SVM_RUS; old-variable model)
section1_comments: The study used the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) heart transplant database. The source dataset covered October 1, 1987 to December 31, 2012, but transplantations before June 30, 2004 were excluded, giving an analysed period from 2004 through 2012. The authors declared no relevant competing interests. The work was supported in part by Health Resources and Services Administration contract 234-2005-370011C.
section2_comments: After data cleaning, the dataset contained 25,512 heart transplant cases and 161 variables. For the 1-year analysis, 19,704 observations were classified as survival, 2,693 as failure, and 3,115 were censored, resulting in 22,397 evaluable observations. Overall mean age, female proportion, and cohort race/ethnicity distributions were not reported. The predictor set included donor and recipient demographics, clinical history, haemodynamic and laboratory variables, life support, prior cardiac surgery, functional status, and procedural characteristics.
section3_comments: The authors compared Tree-Augmented Naïve Bayes, logistic regression, SVM, decision tree, and random forest models using five-fold cross-validation. SVM models were reported to outperform the other algorithms across the three time horizons; the selected balanced 1-year model was SVM_RUS using 33 old variables. Automated feature selection combined information-gain fast feature selection, LASSO, and Cox regression, supplemented by predictors identified from the literature. Feature selection was repeated within each training fold to reduce leakage. Interpretability was addressed through normalized sensitivity analysis, ranked variable-importance plots, and a TAN-derived directed acyclic graph. No explicit hyperparameter-tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Missing numerical values were imputed using the median, while missing categorical observations were assigned an “UNKNOWN” category. Invariant variables, outliers, identifiers, and variables considered unrelated to survival were checked and removed. Class imbalance was addressed using random under-sampling and cost-sensitive models; RUS was applied only to each training fold, leaving the corresponding test fold at its natural class distribution. Exact per-fold training and test counts were not reported, and neither source code nor trained model weights were reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for the highest-AUC balanced 1-year model presented in Table 6: SVM_RUS using the old-variable set. Across five-fold cross-validation, this model achieved AUC 0.6342, sensitivity 0.6263, specificity 0.5490, and accuracy 0.6167. The corresponding combined-variable SVM_RUS model achieved AUC 0.6285, indicating no improvement after adding the six selected post-2004 variables. AUC confidence intervals, PPV, NPV, F1-score, formal calibration assessment, and DCA were not reported.

study_id: 62_Ding Q et al. - 2026 - Machine learning-based prediction of high hospital charges after lung transplantation in chronic obs

BMC Health Serv Res / 2026
algorithm_name: Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM)
section1_comments: Data were obtained from the US Nationwide Inpatient Sample, part of the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project, and covered January 2005 through December 2014. The paper states “Funding: None” and “The authors declare no competing interests.”
section2_comments: The initial cohort contained 1,177 adult hospital admissions identified using ICD-9-CM lung-transplant procedure codes; 12 admissions with missing charge data were excluded, and 1,159 were included in the final analysis. Overall mean age and female percentage were not explicitly reported. Table 1 provides sex and race distributions by cost group and includes extensive clinical variables such as heart failure, coagulopathy, pulmonary vascular disease, acute kidney injury, sepsis, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, respiratory failure, and transplanted-lung complications.
section3_comments: The primary GBM was compared with logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM. Patients were divided into training and test cohorts in a 7:3 ratio, and ten-fold cross-validation was used within training to optimize hyperparameters. Feature selection used a two-stage automated process consisting of Pearson-correlation assessment followed by Random-Forest-based Recursive Feature Elimination, leaving 27 predictors. SHAP global and local analyses were used to interpret the selected GBM.
section4_comments: Missing Race and Zip-Code Income Quartile values were imputed using Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations with a Gradient Boosting Classifier for multiclass categorical imputation. Seven post-discharge or manually coded variables were excluded to reduce information leakage, and feature selection reduced the model to 27 variables. High-cost cases represented approximately 20% of the cohort, but no resampling, class weighting, or other explicit imbalance treatment was reported. The exact training count was not stated; the GBM test confusion matrix contains 348 observations. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The outcome was high-cost hospitalization, defined as total hospital charges at or above the cohort’s 80th percentile ($600,223.40). On the held-out test set, GBM achieved AUC 0.8078, accuracy 0.8164, precision 0.6944, recall 0.6657, and F1-score 0.6773. No AUC confidence interval, explicitly reported specificity, or NPV was provided. Calibration curves were presented, and GBM had a Brier score of 0.1360. Decision-curve analysis was not reported.

study_id: 63_Fessler J et al. - 2025 - Machine Learning for Predicting Pulmonary Graft Dysfunction After Double-Lung Transplantation A Sin

algorithm_name: eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
section1_comments: The study included all eligible double-lung transplant recipients treated at Hôpital Foch, France, from January 2012 through December 2019. Funding was provided by Hôpital Foch, with additional support acknowledged from the association “Vaincre la Mucoviscidose.” The authors declared that the research was conducted “in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.”
section2_comments: Of 510 double-lung transplant recipients, 477 met the inclusion criteria; 83 developed PGD3-T72 and 394 did not. Age was reported as median and interquartile range rather than an overall mean, and an overall female percentage was not explicitly stated. Clinical variables included primary lung disease, BMI, pulmonary hypertension, diabetes, prior thoracic surgery, waiting-list and ICU status, mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, laboratory values, Lung Allocation Score, donor characteristics, ECMO, and sequential intraoperative measurements.
section3_comments: XGBoost was compared with a baseline logistic-regression model. Models were developed at nine chronological stages using recipient, donor, and intraoperative variables. Hyperparameters were optimized through three-stage grid search with five-fold cross-validation. Automated feature selection used XGBoost Gain rankings and recursive addition of the highest-ranked predictors across 500 random train/test splits. SHAP dependence plots and a simplified logistic-regression score were used for interpretation.
section4_comments: Numerical variables were not transformed, categorical variables were one-hot encoded, and missing values were not imputed because “XGBoost treats missing data as a specific modality.” PGD3-T72 occurred in 83 of 477 recipients, but no class weighting, over-sampling, under-sampling, or other explicit imbalance method was reported. The primary XGBoost train/test split proportion and corresponding counts were not stated. The authors report that their “full codebase has been made publicly available.”
section5_comments: The primary outcome was grade 3 primary graft dysfunction at 72 hours according to the 2016 ISHLT definition. The optimal six-feature XGBoost model was evaluated at step 8, immediately after second graft implantation, and achieved a median AUROC of 0.84 with an IQR of 0.065; the abstract reports sensitivity 0.81 and specificity 0.68. Although bootstrap confidence intervals were said to have been generated, numeric lower and upper 95% CI limits were not reported. Accuracy, PPV, NPV, and F1-score were not provided in the main paper. The authors qualitatively described superior or well-calibrated risk estimates, but no calibration intercept, slope, Brier score, or calibration plot was reported. DCA was not reported.

study_id: 64_Kim DD et al. - 2026 - An integrated clinical-histopathologic prediction model for cardiac allograft rejection Translating
study_metadata:

algorithm_name: eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
section1_comments: The cohort was derived from adult heart transplant recipients at the University of Pennsylvania using four previously published digitized-biopsy datasets. Calendar years for patient inclusion were not reported. The study was supported by National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute grants K08HL159344, R01HL170152, and R01HL158071. The disclosure statement reads, “None to state.”
section2_comments: The final cohort comprised 484 recipients and 1,188 outpatient EMB-associated encounters. Mean recipient age was 52.6 years; 77.1% were male, but female percentage was not explicitly reported. Race was reported as White 70.7%, Black 19.2%, and Other 10.1%. Clinical history included BMI, retransplantation, CMV status, renal function, LVAD history, coronary disease, ischemic cardiomyopathy, diabetes, pulmonary hypertension, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, CKD, cPRA, medications, laboratory trends, and donor characteristics.
section3_comments: The primary model integrated structured EHR variables with quantitative pathology features extracted from digitized H&E-stained EMB slides. Data were split 80:20 by patient identifier, with 10-fold cross-validation during training and performance assessed exclusively on the held-out test set. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, clinical-only, morphology-only, and integrated configurations were compared. SHAP rankings were used to identify influential features and derive the Integrated Rejection Risk Index; no explicit hyperparameter-search or tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Patients were required to have at least 90% completeness of routinely collected clinical variables, and residual missingness was handled using multiple imputation by chained equations. The cohort was deliberately enriched for future-rejection patients, 26.9% versus a 15.1% institutional incidence, “to mitigate class imbalance.” Longitudinal predictors were constructed using time bins, change-from-baseline, change-from-prior-encounter, and rate-of-change features. Figure 2 reports 954 training encounters and 234 held-out test encounters; all splitting was performed at patient level. Code availability was not reported.
section5_comments: The primary feasibility outcome was future cardiac allograft rejection occurring more than 7 days and no more than 42 days after a CAR-free outpatient encounter. CAR included ISHLT cellular rejection greater than 1R, pAMR greater than 0, or clinically evident rejection. On the held-out test set of 234 encounters, the integrated longitudinal clinical-morphologic XGBoost model achieved AUROC 0.86, AUPRC 0.74, macro F1 0.83, sensitivity 0.72, specificity 0.94, PPV 0.74, and NPV 0.94. Numeric 95% confidence bounds for AUROC and accuracy were not reported. Formal calibration analysis and DCA were not reported.

study_id: 65_Koritsánszky KB et al. - 2025 - Shifting Determinants of Mortality Risk After Orthotopic Heart Transplantation Identified by Machine

algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: The study used the institutional database of the Heart and Vascular Center, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary, and included OHT recipients treated from 30 January 2012 to 23 December 2024. Funding was provided through a European Union-supported project, the Hungarian Ministry for Culture and Innovation/National Research, Development and Innovation Fund, and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. Conflicts were declared for two authors, including compensated work as Chief Medical Officer of Argus Cognitive, Inc. and advisory-board membership at GE Healthcare, both stated to be unrelated to the manuscript.
section2_comments: The cohort comprised 581 adolescent and adult OHT recipients; overall age was 50.7 ± 10.9 years and 155 patients (26.67%) were female. Race or ethnicity was not reported. The dataset included demographics, heart-failure diagnosis, comorbidities, functional status, mechanical circulatory support, right-heart catheterization, laboratory values, donor variables, medications, postoperative organ dysfunction, circulatory support, transfusion, ICU and ventilation duration, and postoperative complications.
section3_comments: Random forest models were developed separately for 30-day and 1-year all-cause mortality using either preoperative variables alone or all available preoperative and postoperative variables. A nested cross-validation design used a five-fold inner loop for hyperparameter optimization and a five-fold outer loop for feature selection, model selection, and performance evaluation. Feature selection retained 15–25 predictors. SHAP values quantified the magnitude and direction of predictor contributions, and the final ensemble comprised five classifiers trained on distinct outer folds.
section4_comments: Features with more than 40% missingness were excluded. Remaining continuous values were imputed using the mean, categorical values using the mode, and continuous predictors were standardized with z-score normalization. All preprocessing was fitted only within the training portion of the nested cross-validation. SMOTE was applied exclusively to training data within each fold. Exact outer-fold training and hold-out counts were not explicitly reported, and source code or trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for the 1-year random forest model using all preoperative and postoperative variables, evaluated across the outer hold-out folds of nested five-fold cross-validation. The model achieved AUC 0.86 (95% CI 0.80–0.92) and Brier score 0.10. Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. The preoperative-only 1-year model achieved AUC 0.67 (95% CI 0.56–0.78; Brier score 0.15). Formal calibration plots, calibration intercept or slope, and DCA were not reported.

algorithm_name: EHRFormer
section1_comments: The study used de-identified United Network for Organ Sharing Standard Transplant Analysis and Research File data, described as SRTR/OPTN data, from US lung transplant recipients. Transplants before 8 November 2022 were included, and the abstract describes the period as 1987–2022. The authors stated, “This research received no funding” and declared no competing interests.
section2_comments: The abstract reports 43,869 first-time lung transplant recipients, although the Results also describe an exploratory cohort of 47,864 recipients and Figure 1 reports 37,369 observations in the all-years modeling dataset. The study was restricted to first-time recipients older than 18 years. Overall mean age and female percentage were not reported. Recipient and donor ethnicity, transplant indication, functional status, infection, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, renal function, hemodynamics, lung function, and other clinical-history variables were included.
section3_comments: EHRFormer was a tabular BERT model with three transformer layers, 64-dimensional embeddings, an intermediate layer size of 128, and four attention heads. It was compared with XGBoost. Features were automatically filtered to those with less than 10% missingness within each era, producing 140–152 variables. The models used an 80:20 train/test split, five-fold cross-validation within training, and held-out test evaluation. EHRFormer hyperparameters were optimized with Optuna, while XGBoost used Bayesian optimization. Interpretability included SHAP for XGBoost and single- or multivariable in silico perturbations for EHRFormer.
section4_comments: Numerical variables were mean-imputed and categorical variables were mode-imputed. Categorical predictors were ordinal- or one-hot encoded, and EHRFormer numerical inputs were quantile-binned. The majority class was randomly downsampled to a 1:1 ratio separately in both training and test sets. Exact post-downsampling training and test counts were not explicitly reported. The authors provided a GitHub repository containing the underlying code; the UNOS-derived training and validation datasets were not publicly available.
section5_comments: Values were extracted for the best all-years held-out test model for 1-year mortality, EHRFormer. It achieved AUC 0.64 (95% CI 0.61–0.66), accuracy 0.60, F1-score 0.64, precision 0.58, recall 0.70, and specificity 0.49. NPV was not reported. The XGBoost comparator achieved AUC 0.63 (95% CI 0.60–0.67). Calibration assessment and DCA were not reported. Patients who died during or within 90 days of the index hospitalization were excluded from the mortality-prediction task.

study_id: 67_Mete M et al. - 2026 - Predicting Simultaneous Heart Kidney Allocation and Posttransplant Adverse Kidney Outcomes
