Kidney Int Rep / 2026
algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: The study used United Network for Organ Sharing Standard Transplant Analysis and Research files from the OPTN national registry. Model development used transplants from 18 October 2018 through 31 December 2020; temporal external validation used January–June 2021 and September 2023–March 2024 cohorts. The work was supported in part by a Health Resources and Services Administration contract. The disclosure states, “All authors declared no competing interests.”
section2_comments: The model was developed in 6,579 adult heart transplant recipients and evaluated in two external cohorts of 1,567 and 1,853 recipients, giving 9,999 participants across development and validation. The intended use was decision support at heart-transplant waitlisting. Age was reported as a median of 57 years rather than a mean, and 72.5% were male; an explicit female percentage was not reported. Race and clinical history were reported, including diabetes, heart-failure diagnosis, previous transplantation, dialysis, mechanical support, renal function, biomarkers, and right-heart catheterization measurements.
section3_comments: An expert panel initially selected 44 clinically relevant variables from 531 registry variables. Random-forest Gini importance was then used to select the final 15 predictors. Hyperparameters were exhaustively searched across numbers of trees, maximum depth, maximum features, positive-class weights, and random seeds. Internal five-fold cross-validation was followed by validation in two later temporal cohorts. Interpretability was provided through feature-importance distributions and a patient-level web calculator.
section4_comments: Missing predictor values were imputed with a K-nearest-neighbors imputer using K = 50, primarily for right-heart catheterization measurements, BNP, and blood urea nitrogen. Class imbalance was addressed through positive-sample class-weight tuning from 3 to 10, and precision-recall performance was reported for the 13.4% adverse-outcome prevalence. The primary temporal external test cohort contained 1,567 recipients; a second external cohort contained 1,853. Study code or trained model weights were not reported, although the model was implemented as an online calculator.
section5_comments: The composite adverse outcome comprised receipt of simultaneous heart-kidney transplantation or, after heart transplantation alone, chronic dialysis, eGFR below 20 ml/min per 1.73 m², or kidney-transplant listing/transplantation within 1 year. In the first temporal external-validation cohort of 1,567 recipients, the random forest achieved c-statistic 0.899, sensitivity 0.680, specificity 0.941, PPV 0.680, NPV 0.941, and F1-score 0.680. A 95% confidence interval for the c-statistic and model accuracy were not reported. Calibration and DCA were not reported. The second postpolicy validation cohort achieved a c-statistic of 0.874.

algorithm_name: Multilayer Perceptron

section2_comments: Of 303 initially enrolled recipients, patients who withdrew, underwent heart-lung transplantation, were lost to follow-up, or had incomplete data were excluded, leaving 240 recipients. Clinical variables included transplant indication, diabetes, hypertension, CKD, malignancy, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease, infection, steroid exposure, pulmonary function, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, laboratory values, HLA crossmatch, donor-specific antibodies, and panel-reactive antibodies.
section3_comments: The primary MLP was compared with logistic regression, SVM, random forest, gradient boosting machine, and balanced random forest. Twenty-five preoperative variables associated with graft failure in univariate analyses were ranked using averaged logistic-regression coefficients across repeated 5-fold cross-validation, and the top nine variables with normalized absolute coefficients above 0.25 were retained. Grid-search hyperparameter optimization was reported. The MLP contained two 60-unit ReLU dense layers with dropout of 0.7 and a sigmoid output. SHAP DeepExplainer was used for interpretation.
section4_comments: Only patients with complete data for all selected preoperative variables were analysed, and no imputation was performed. Class imbalance was addressed using balanced class weights for several models and a balanced-random-forest implementation; the exact imbalance method used for the final MLP was not explicitly specified. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation preserved the graft-failure proportion in each fold. Exact fold-specific training and validation counts were not reported. Feature-selection and model-preparation procedures were described, but predictor scaling or normalization before MLP training was not explicitly reported. Source code and model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The outcome was 1-year graft failure, defined as death or retransplantation due to graft failure within 1 year; retransplantation date was treated as equivalent to the date of death. Across stratified 5-fold cross-validation, the MLP achieved AUC 0.780, accuracy 0.733, sensitivity 0.673, specificity 0.751, PPV 0.449, NPV 0.886, and F1-score 0.537. study_id: 69_Peyster et al. - 2021 - An automated computational image analysis pipeline for histological grading of cardiac allograft rej
study_metadata:

Eur Heart J / 2021
algorithm_name: Computer-Assisted Cardiac Histologic Evaluation-Grader (CACHE-Grader)
section1_comments: Archived biopsy slides were obtained from the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, and Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center during usual care between 2005 and 2018. Funding was predominantly from US public agencies, including the NIH, Department of Veterans Affairs, and Department of Defense, with additional foundation and institutional support. Multiple authors declared consultancy, equity, patent, licensing, advisory-board, or sponsored-research interests.
section2_comments: The analytic units were 2,472 archived H&E-stained endomyocardial-biopsy slides originating from 546 heart transplant recipients. Biopsies were obtained 7–6,415 days after transplantation during scheduled surveillance or for-cause assessment. Recipient-level age, sex, race/ethnicity, and comorbidity distributions were not reported.
section3_comments: The pipeline extracted 154 biologically inspired, hand-crafted histologic features describing lymphocyte foci, tissue compartments, densities, and spatial interactions. Support vector machine classifiers were selected for binary low- versus high-grade rejection (M1) and four-grade rejection classification (M2). Features were ranked using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test for M1 and a t-test for M2, resulting in models with 2 and 15 features, respectively. Validation included 395 held-out slides from the development center and 1,052 geographically external slides from two other centers; no explicit SVM hyperparameter-search procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Slides underwent automated HistoQC assessment, stain deconvolution, tiling, K-means tissue segmentation, lymphocyte-cluster detection, and feature normalization relative to tissue-compartment size. The authors deliberately enriched the cohort for grades 2R/3R to approximately 20%, compared with approximately 8% in routine practice, to ensure sufficient high-grade cases; this addressed imbalance through cohort construction rather than algorithmic weighting or resampling. The training set contained 911 slides, and the composite validation set contained 1,447 slides: 395 internal and 1,052 external. Missing-feature imputation was not described. Source code was publicly available through the CACHE-Grader repository.
section5_comments: Values refer to the binary M1 classifier for low-grade 0R/1R versus high-grade 2R/3R rejection in the composite independent validation set. It achieved 84.5% agreement with the grade of record, AUC 0.92, sensitivity 0.85, and specificity 0.84; no AUC confidence interval was reported. The four-grade M2 classifier achieved 65.9% agreement (95% CI 63.4–68.3%), with similar internal and external agreement of 66.1% and 65.8%. Numeric PPV, NPV, F1-score, formal probabilistic calibration metrics, and DCA were not reported.

study_id: 70_Sharma G et al. - 2025 - Development and Validation of a Hybrid Machine Learning Model to Predict Lung Transplant Outcomes
study_metadata:
Development and Validation of a Hybrid Machine Learning Model to Predict Lung Transplant Outcomes.
Sharma, G. et al.
JAMA Netw Open / 2025
algorithm_name: AutoScore-Survival
section1_comments: The study used the United Network for Organ Sharing–Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network registry and included US lung transplants performed between October 16, 1987, and March 26, 2025. Dr Sharma was supported by three American Heart Association awards. The article states, “Conflict of Interest Disclosures: None reported.”
section2_comments: The cohort comprised 51,933 adults undergoing their first lung transplant. Age was reported as a median of 59 years rather than a mean; 22,028 recipients (42.4%) were women. Race and ethnicity were reported. Candidate predictors included recipient demographics, functional status, prior cardiac surgery, laboratory measures, donor characteristics, transplant type, ischemic time, inotropic support, hospital length of stay, and posttransplant ventilation support.
section3_comments: AutoScore-Survival is a hybrid framework that used a random survival forest to rank 61 candidate variables and Cox proportional hazards regression to generate an interpretable integer-based score. A parsimony plot in the development validation cohort selected nine predictors. The cohort was temporally split into development and contemporary testing periods; the development cohort was further divided into training and validation sets for model selection and hyperparameter tuning. Interpretability was provided through a nine-variable point score, hazard ratios, risk groups, and a web calculator.
section4_comments: Missing values were retained as an “unknown” or “not reported” category rather than imputed. Continuous predictors were categorized to generate the point-based score, and the model-development workflow and temporal allocation were described. The development cohort contained 24,014 training recipients and 2,668 validation recipients; the temporal testing cohort contained 25,251 recipients. Class imbalance treatment was not applicable to the time-to-event survival framework, which incorporated censoring and had an overall event rate of 61.4%. Source code or trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The outcome was time from lung transplantation to death or retransplantation, evaluated at 1, 5, and 10 years. In the temporal testing cohort, the 1-year time-dependent AUC was 0.61 (95% CI 0.52–0.70). The testing-set integrated AUC was 0.61 (95% CI 0.60–0.63) and C-index was 0.64 (95% CI 0.63–0.64). Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. Calibration was assessed using plots, calibration slope, observed-to-expected ratios, and Brier scores; decision-curve analysis showed net benefit across clinically relevant thresholds.

study_id: 71_Tran-Dinh A et al. - 2026 - Early identification of high-risk individuals for mortality after lung transplantation A retrospect
study_metadata:
Early identification of high-risk individuals for mortality after lung transplantation: A retrospective cohort study with topological feature engineering.

PLOS Digit Health / 2026
algorithm_name: Topological Attention Multilayer Perceptron
section1_comments: The study included consecutive lung transplant recipients at Bichat-Claude Bernard Hospital in Paris, France, between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2020. Funding included the French Agence Nationale de la Recherche and regional Spanish public/FEDER funding, with Institute Mutualiste Montsouris covering article-processing charges. The authors declared that no competing interests existed.
section2_comments: Of 287 consecutive recipients screened, 24 were excluded for more than 20% missing key variables and 11 for insufficient follow-up without documented death, leaving 252 patients: 189 survivors and 63 non-survivors at 1 year. Overall mean age and female percentage were not explicitly reported in the article text. Clinical variables included diabetes, ischemic heart disease, primary lung disease, pulmonary arterial pressure, BMI, CMV mismatch, preoperative and intraoperative ECMO, transplant type, ICU severity scores, postoperative organ support, infections, primary graft dysfunction, renal failure, and rejection.
section3_comments: The primary classifier was a regularized MLP using 49 clinical variables and 27 topological features generated from persistent-homology representations. It was compared with the Lung Transplant Risk Index, Charlson Comorbidity Index, FEV1, clinical-only MLP, random forest, gradient boosting, logistic regression, and other classifiers. Validation used nested stratified cross-validation with five outer folds for performance estimation and three inner folds for hyperparameter tuning. Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation was performed within each training fold, retaining a mean of 34 ± 6 features. SHAP, partial-dependence plots, effect sizes, and an interpretable risk score were used for explanation.
section4_comments: Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations with ten iterations and five imputed datasets, using predictive mean matching for continuous variables and logistic regression for binary variables. Scaling, imputation, topological extraction, and feature selection were fitted exclusively within training folds. Class imbalance was addressed with inverse-frequency class weights of 1 for survivors and 3 for non-survivors; SMOTE was evaluated in sensitivity analysis. Exact per-fold training and test counts were referenced in Supplementary Table S2 but were not stated numerically in the article text. The data, code, and split manifest were made publicly available in the TopoAttention repository.
section5_comments: The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality within 365 days after transplantation. Table 2 reports AUC 0.87 (95% CI 0.81–0.93), accuracy 0.90 (95% CI 0.85–0.95), sensitivity 0.84, specificity 0.90, PPV 0.82, NPV 0.91, F1-score 0.83, and PR-AUC 0.71 for the Topological Attention model. The abstract separately reports 87.4% accuracy, 84.1% sensitivity, and 89.6% specificity on the test dataset, indicating minor inconsistency or different rounding/evaluation summaries. Calibration was evaluated with curves, Expected Calibration Error 0.08, Brier score 0.12, calibration slope 0.91, and intercept −0.15. DCA showed positive net benefit across thresholds from 0.1 to 0.5 and benefit relative to treat-all and treat-none strategies above approximately 0.15.

study_id: 72_Weigt SS et al. - 2025 - Development and validation of a bronchoalveolar lavage genomic classifier for acute cellular rejecti
study_metadata:
Development and validation of a bronchoalveolar lavage genomic classifier for acute cellular rejection.
Weigt, S. S. et al.
EBioMedicine / 2025
algorithm_name: 31-gene bronchoalveolar-lavage cell-pellet genomic ACR Random Forest classifier
section1_comments: CTOT-20 was a prospective observational cohort enrolling adult lung transplant recipients at five North American centres: Duke University, UCLA, University of Toronto, Johns Hopkins, and Cleveland Clinic. Participants were transplanted between December 2015 and August 2018; the consecutively sampled study subset was transplanted from August 2016 to April 2017, with follow-up through July 2021. Funding included National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases awards, with additional Cystic Fibrosis Foundation and Saul and Joyce Brandman Foundation support. Multiple author conflicts were declared, including research grants, consulting, honoraria, advisory roles, and a provisional patent related to allograft injury or rejection.
section2_comments: The primary CTOT-20 analytic cohort contained 181 recipients contributing 806 pre-CLAD BAL-cell-pellet samples that passed RNA quality control. Mean age was 55.2 years and 80 of 181 recipients (44.2%) were female. Race and ethnicity, native lung-disease category, transplant type, Lung Allocation Score, HLA mismatch, induction therapy, and grade 3 primary graft dysfunction were reported. The independent UCLA cohort contained 219 recipients, although external diagnostic validation was performed in 78 samples meeting the clinically significant ACR or stable-control phenotype definitions.
section3_comments: RNA-seq-derived gene-expression features were used to classify clinically significant ACR versus stable controls defined by bronchoscopy, microbiology, donor-specific antibodies, and pathologist-assigned transbronchial-biopsy grades. Logistic regression, Elastic-Net, and Random Forest were evaluated; Random Forest was selected. Ten-fold cross-validation tuned mtry from 1–15 and ntree from 100–5000. Boruta automated all-relevant feature selection reduced 62 differentially expressed genes to a locked 31-gene model. Interpretability was provided through individual gene-importance rankings and biologic pathway analysis. Validation included a held-out internal test set and an independent geographically separate UCLA cohort.
section4_comments: RNA quantity and integrity thresholds were prespecified; 185 of 991 pre-CLAD samples failed quality control, predominantly because of insufficient RNA quantity. Sequencing preprocessing included fastp read cleaning, quality metrics, STAR alignment, FeatureCounts quantification, RPKM calculation, low-expression filtering, and LIMMA-voom differential-expression analysis. No missing-predictor imputation was described. Clinically significant ACR was substantially less frequent than stable control in the model-development sample, but no class weighting, over-sampling, under-sampling, or other imbalance method was reported. The development split contained 150 training and 38 internal-test samples; the independent external validation analysis contained 78 samples. Gene-expression and clinical data were deposited in Mendeley Data, but source code or trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted from the independent UCLA validation cohort for distinguishing clinically significant ACR from stable controls. The 31-gene Random Forest classifier achieved AUC 0.90 (95% CI 0.83–0.96), accuracy 82.1%, sensitivity 73.3%, and specificity 87.5%. PPV, NPV, and F1-score were not reported for the external cohort. The internal held-out test set contained 38 samples and achieved AUC 0.72 (95% CI 0.53–0.88). Formal probability calibration and decision-curve analysis were not reported. As a secondary prognostic finding, late genomic ACR was associated with subsequent CLAD risk.

study_id: 73_White JP et al. - 2026 - Predicting expiration among potential donation after circulatory death donors at 30- and 120-min pos
study_metadata:
Predicting expiration among potential donation after circulatory death donors at 30- and 120-min post extubation.
White, J. P. et al.
J Heart Lung Transplant / 2026
algorithm_name: Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), max variable model
section1_comments: Data were collected from three geographically distinct US organ procurement organizations: HonorBridge, Gift of Life Donor Program, and OneLegacy, covering January 2014 through June 2025. The study was supported by the Sam Malik Foundation. The authors included a conflict-of-interest declaration stating that they had no conflicts of interest.
section2_comments: The overall cohort contained 4,464 potential DCD donors for whom withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy was initiated with intent for organ donation. Median age was 46 years rather than a reported mean, and 37% were female. Race was reported, and clinical history included diabetes, hypertension, cause and mechanism of death, neurologic reflexes, ventilatory variables, hemodynamics, laboratory values, and whether a lung offer had been made.
section3_comments: Separate XGBoost models were developed for 30- and 120-minute expiration using a 14-variable max-sample cohort and a 61-variable max-variable cohort. Each dataset was randomly divided 80:20 into training and held-out test sets. Multivariable logistic regression served as the baseline comparator. Predictors contributing less than 5% of the importance of the highest-ranked variable were removed and the model was rerun. Feature-importance analysis and an interactive probability calculator supported interpretation, but a specific hyperparameter-search procedure was not reported.
section4_comments: Variables were required to have at least 85% completeness. Missing numerical values were imputed using medians and categorical values using the mode. The max-variable model used 2,092 donors and 61 predictors; the exact integer training and test counts resulting from the reported 80:20 random split were not stated. Expiration occurred in 59% and 82% of the max-variable cohort at 30 and 120 minutes, respectively, but no class weighting, resampling, or other explicit class-imbalance method was reported. A web application was provided, but source code or model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for the best held-out test model: the 61-variable XGBoost model predicting circulatory death within 120 minutes after extubation. It achieved ROC-AUC 0.89 and PR-AUC 0.97; no 95% confidence interval, accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, or F1-score was reported. The corresponding 30-minute max-variable test model achieved ROC-AUC 0.76 and PR-AUC 0.80. Calibration curves and Brier scores were reported in supplementary figures, but decision-curve analysis was not reported.

study_id: 74_Yim WY et al. - 2026 - Bridging machine learning and clinical practice a multicentre nomogram for 90-day graft failure ris
study_metadata:
Bridging machine learning and clinical practice: a multicentre nomogram for 90-day graft failure risk stratification in heart transplantation.
Yim, W. Y. et al.
Open Heart / 2026
algorithm_name: XGBoost-derived eight-variable logistic-regression nomogram
section1_comments: The primary derivation cohort came from the US UNOS/OPTN registry between 2008 and 2020, and geographic external validation was performed at Wuhan Union Hospital in China. The main Results section reports the WHUH period as 2015–2024, although the abstract reports 2018–2023 and Figure 1 reports 2015–2020; 2024 was retained as the latest explicitly stated year. Funding was provided by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Hubei Provincial Natural Science Foundation. The paper states, “Competing interests None declared.”
section2_comments: After inclusion, exclusion, and preprocessing, 25,200 UNOS recipients and 563 WHUH recipients were analysed, for a total of 25,763. Age was reported as median and IQR by outcome or risk group rather than as an overall mean, and an overall female percentage was not explicitly reported. Race mismatch was reported, and the candidate variables included donor and recipient age, sex, BMI, medical history, diagnosis, previous cardiac surgery, HLA mismatch, bilirubin, renal markers, mechanical support, donor medication use, centre volume, and cold ischaemia time.
section3_comments: XGBoost and Random Forest were developed from 32 pretransplant donor-recipient variables and compared with the IMPACT score. Five-fold cross-validation was used for hyperparameter optimisation. Global SHAP importance automatically selected the eight highest-impact predictors: previous cardiac surgery, recipient age, recipient bilirubin, recipient BMI, donor age, donor sex, donor BMI, and cold ischaemia time. These ML-selected variables were translated into an interpretable logistic-regression nomogram and externally validated in China. SHAP summary plots, force plots, clustering, and the nomogram provided global and patient-level interpretability.
section4_comments: Figure 1 lists missing baseline variables among the exclusions, supporting complete-case analysis, although detailed missing-data procedures were deferred to the online supplement. The main article states that missing-data handling and normalisation were performed but does not describe the exact normalisation method. The UNOS cohort was split 70:30, corresponding to 17,640 training and 7,560 internal test recipients; the final nomogram was additionally evaluated in 563 external-validation recipients. Graft failure occurred in 1,444 of 25,200 UNOS recipients, but no class weighting, resampling, or other explicit imbalance method was reported. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The target outcome was graft failure within 90 days after heart transplantation; the exact operational definition was deferred to the online supplemental methods and was not stated in the main article. Performance was extracted for the final eight-variable nomogram in the independent WHUH external-validation cohort: AUC 0.671 (95% CI 0.6025–0.7386). Accuracy, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and F1-score were not reported. Calibration was assessed and the nomogram had a reported Brier score of 0.0472 in development. DCA in the external cohort showed net benefit over treat-all and treat-none strategies across risk thresholds from 0.0 to 0.4.

study_id: 75_Zadeh et al. - 2025 - Predictive analytics for de novo malignancies after lung transplantation
study_metadata:
Predictive analytics for de novo malignancies after lung transplantation
Zadeh, A. et al.
Intelligent Decision Technologies / 2025
algorithm_name: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
section1_comments: The study used the Standard Transplant Analysis and Research (STAR) data sources overseen by UNOS/OPTN and containing US transplantation records. The authors state that lung transplant recipient records from 1984 to 2021 were used, although the Methods also describe the STAR source as covering US transplants since 1987. The paper states that the authors received no financial support for the research and declared no potential conflicts of interest.
section2_comments: The investigators identified 66,590 lung transplant records, excluded recipients with a documented pretransplant malignancy, leaving 38,788, and then excluded those lost to follow-up, producing a final cohort of 30,917 recipients. Twenty-five percent developed a post-transplant malignancy. Figure 2 reports 43% female and presents ethnicity and age distributions, but an overall mean age was not reported. The registry variables included demographics, HLA/PRA, serology, donor characteristics, laboratory values, transplantation details, hospital course, rejection, survival, and other complications.
section3_comments: Gradient Boosting was compared with Random Forest, Decision Tree, LARS, Neural Network, logistic regression, rule induction, and SVM. The dataset was divided into 70% training and 30% testing. Medical experts reviewed 544 candidate variables and excluded 173 because of irrelevance, redundancy, excessive missingness above 30%, or excessive correlation. Gradient Boosting variable-importance rankings were used for interpretation. Reported model settings included shrinkage 0.1, 50 iterations, and use of 60% of observations for fitting individual boosted trees.
section4_comments: Variables with more than 30% missing data were removed during expert preprocessing, but the handling of residual missing values was not described; this was therefore classified as Other rather than imputation. Class imbalance was explicitly addressed by oversampling and replicating minority-class observations. Data cleaning, consolidation, variable filtering, and transformation were described, and SAS Enterprise Miner was used. The paper states a 70:30 split but does not report exact integer training and test counts. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The target was occurrence of de novo malignant cancer after lung transplantation among recipients with no prior malignancy. In the held-out test set, Gradient Boosting achieved AUC 0.746, accuracy 0.690, sensitivity 0.731, specificity 0.649, and precision 0.676. No AUC confidence interval, NPV, or F1-score was reported. The study did not report formal calibration assessment or decision-curve analysis.

study_id: 76_Zhou X et al. - 2026 - Predicting heart transplant outcomes using explainable artificial intelligence a multicenter study
study_metadata:
Predicting heart transplant outcomes using explainable artificial intelligence: a multicenter study.
Zhou, X. et al.
Front Cardiovasc Med / 2026
algorithm_name: Generalizable Interpretable Neural Network (GINN)
section1_comments: The primary dataset was the US UNOS registry from 1994–2024. Geographic external validation used Eurotransplant, Scandiatransplant, and a 14-patient Chinese cohort from Jiangxi Provincial People’s Hospital; the abstract reports Scandiatransplant data from 1997–2018, while study periods for Eurotransplant and External-CN were not explicitly stated. The authors declared that no financial support was received and that no commercial or financial conflicts of interest existed.
section2_comments: The analytic cohorts comprised 81,327 eligible UNOS recipients, 3,061 Eurotransplant recipients, 1,546 Scandiatransplant recipients, and 14 External-CN recipients, totalling 85,948. The UNOS cohort was divided into derivation (n=45,927), temporal test (n=20,200), and out-of-time validation (n=15,200) cohorts. Age and female sex were reported separately by UNOS era rather than as pooled overall values. Race and extensive donor-recipient clinical characteristics were reported, including diagnoses, prior surgery and transplantation, mechanical support, dialysis, donor hypertension and diabetes, creatinine, and ischemic time.
section3_comments: GINN used an additive Risk Response Network in which each of nine structured clinical variables was processed by a separate lightweight MLP and combined into a mortality-risk logit. The nine inputs were specified a priori from clinical relevance and established heart-transplant risk models; an embedded Lasso-style regularizer promoted sparsity but was not used as preliminary feature screening. Comparators included IMPACT, IHTSA, recalibrated IHTSA, and EBM. Interpretability was intrinsic through feature-specific partial-response curves and additive patient-level risk contributions. Temporal UNOS evaluation and geographic validation in Eurotransplant, Scandiatransplant, and External-CN were performed, but no explicit hyperparameter-search or tuning procedure was reported.
section4_comments: Continuous variables were median-imputed, categorical variables were mode-imputed, and numerical variables were standardized using z-score normalization. Variable coding was harmonized across centers, and SMOTE was applied to the minority mortality class in the training set. The derivation cohort contained 45,927 recipients, an intermediate temporal test cohort contained 20,200, and the primary out-of-time validation cohort contained 15,200. The pipeline was implemented in Python/PyTorch using a fixed random seed. Data access procedures were described, but source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: Performance was extracted for GINN in the 15,200-recipient out-of-time UNOS validation cohort: AUROC 0.827 (95% CI 0.821–0.833), accuracy 0.80, reported precision 0.82, recall 0.80, and F1-score 0.81. Specificity and NPV were not explicitly reported. Calibration was assessed using calibration plots, slope, calibration-in-the-large, Brier score, and expected-to-observed ratio; Table 4 reports slope 1.02, CITL 0.02, Brier score 0.115, and E/O 1.01. DCA was not reported. The reported precision of 0.82 is not reconcilable with the death-class PPV implied by the displayed confusion matrix, and external-cohort AUROCs differ between the narrative/Figure 6 and Table 4.

study_id: 77_Zhu Y et al. - 2026 - Construction and validation of a machine learning-based prediction model for venous thromboembolism
study_metadata:
Construction and validation of a machine learning-based prediction model for venous thromboembolism in lung transplant recipients supported by ECMO.
Zhu, Y. et al.
Front Med (Lausanne) / 2026
algorithm_name: Random Forest
section1_comments: The study used electronic medical records from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine, China. The internal cohort covered May 2023–May 2024 and the temporal validation cohort covered June–November 2024. Funding was provided by the Health Commission of Zhejiang Province, China (No. 2025KY865). The authors declared no commercial or financial conflicts of interest.
section2_comments: The cohort included 189 elective lung transplant recipients receiving postoperative ECMO, comprising 117 patients with postoperative DVT and 72 without DVT. Age was reported only in categories of ≤60 and >60 years, so an overall mean was unavailable. There were 37 women (19.58%). Clinical variables included diagnosis, hypertension, diabetes, prior tumour, coronary disease, prior thrombosis, respiratory support, BMI, anticoagulant use, laboratory values, respiratory failure, and pulmonary-function measures.
section3_comments: Random Forest was compared with logistic regression, SVM, KNN, XGBoost, and AdaBoost, as well as the clinical Caprini risk score. Recursive Feature Elimination reduced 22 candidate variables to six predictors: anticoagulant therapy, BMI, history of thrombosis, procalcitonin, concomitant respiratory failure, and white-blood-cell count. Grid search with five-fold cross-validation selected hyperparameters using mean cross-validated AUC. SHAP summary, importance, and patient-level waterfall plots were used for interpretation. The validation cohort came from a later period at the same institution and was therefore classified as external temporal validation.
section4_comments: Patients with incomplete case data were excluded, variables with more than 10% missingness were removed, and the remaining variables contained no missing values; no imputation was performed. Categorical variables were one-hot encoded. SMOTE oversampling was applied to the minority class in the training dataset. The article and Figure 1 refer to a 70:30 training-validation division, while the Methods describe calendar-based internal and temporal cohorts; exact integer split counts were not reported. Source code and trained model weights were not reported.
section5_comments: The target outcome was postoperative venous thrombosis, operationally assessed as lower-extremity DVT using serial colour Doppler ultrasonography. In the temporal validation set, the Random Forest model achieved AUC 0.895 (95% CI 0.788–1.000), accuracy 0.897, sensitivity 0.897, specificity 0.895, PPV 0.946, NPV 0.810, and F1-score 0.921. The abstract writes “PPV 0.946%,” but Table 3 reports 0.946, corresponding to 94.6%. Calibration curves were presented, and DCA indicated net clinical benefit over relevant threshold probabilities.
